title: Crisp design, colorful action photos and star players make 1956 Topps Baseball a popular vintage set for collectors
author: Greg Bates
body:
Cards
Crisp design, colorful action photos and star players make 1956 Topps Baseball a popular vintage set for collectors
The 1956 Topps set is arguably one of the most aesthetically pleasing baseball card sets of all time.
A crisp design, full-color artwork featuring dual action and profile shots, clean white borders and all the best players in the game make the set truly iconic.
It is instantly recognizable to any vintage baseball card buff.
Related Content:
Add in the fact that over half the players come in white and gray back variations—some cards rarer than others—and every card is widely available 70 years after production, the set’s lasting impact on the hobby is no surprise.
“I think you’re not going to get a lot of pushback from a lot of collectors that know that era. It would be hard to battle that set, because it’s got everything,” said Mike Baker, founder of Mike Baker Authenticated.
New York Yankees great Mickey Mantle is the crown jewel of the 340-card set. But there isn’t a lack of star power.
“It’s one of those weird sets from the ’50s that even though there’s a Luis Aparicio rookie, it’s really not anchored by that,” said Leighton Sheldon, owner of Vintage Breaks and Just Collect. “It’s anchored by the fact there’s just every available star of the day: Ted Williams, Jackie Robinson, Al Kaline, Willie Mays. The list just goes on and on. And those cards are highly coveted because of the design, because it shows a few different aspects of the player.”
Former Heritage Auctions Executive Vice President of Sports Joe Orlando agrees. The 1956 set features second-year cards of Sandy Koufax, Roberto Clemente and Harmon Killebrew and early cards of Mantle, Mays and Hank Aaron.
“The star combination across the board is so terrific,” Orlando said. “If you were to ask what’s the one relatively weak spot of this set, it doesn’t have as strong of a rookie card class as some of the sets around it. In 1955, you have one of the all-time great rookie card selections in Koufax, Clemente and Killebrew. In 1957, a year later, you have Don Drysdale, Frank Robinson, Brooks Robinson, it just keeps going with great rookie cards in that set. But in ’56 you have Luis Aparicio, a Hall of Fame shortstop, great player, but that’s basically the extent of the major names.”
MANTLE RETURNS
One main reason the set is so special and adored by collectors is it featured the reintroduction of Mantle back into Topps. The slugger was included in Topps’ 1952 and ’53 sets, but rival card company Bowman inked Mantle to an exclusive contract. He was noticeably excluded from Topps’ 1954 and ’55 releases. However, after Topps bought out its only competitor in January 1956, Mantle, Yankees pitcher Whitey Ford and Cleveland Indians pitcher Bob Feller all made their way back to Topps.
“Having Mantle back in Topps was such a huge moment for the company, because Mickey Mantle was the most popular player in baseball,” Orlando said. “Having him back in the set is a huge, huge part of its appeal. And, of course, in 1956 he just happens to reach the Triple Crown, which is like the stars aligned for Mantle that year.”
The ’56 Mantle is his only horizontal card during his illustrious Topps run. Mantle’s first ever Topps card in 1952 always receives accolades as one of the most iconic cards in the hobby. But his ’56 card is right up there with the ’53 release as being in the top three of Mantle’s most coveted cards.
“If you look at the card, it’s such a great looking card,” Orlando said. “He’s smiling ear to ear on his portrait side of the picture, there’s a beautiful action shot of him going into the stands, making a leaping grab in the background. Sometimes the design comes together in a way that just creates such a visually appealing card, and in this case, I think that’s a huge part of it. It’s just such a great looking card of Mantle, coupled with the other attributes that it’s absolutely one of his most popular issues.”
Having Mantle back in its product was monumental for Topps. And the company, in just its sixth year of making cards, took full advantage of having the face of America’s Pastime in its set.
After a successful year with the 1955 set, which featured a very similar look the following year, Topps upped its print run in ’56. That is evident in PSA’s Population Report from that year.
As of the end of January 2026, PSA had graded 212,795 cards from the 1955 set. The number of slabs jumped to 391,296—nearly double—for the 1956 set.
Having so much product around even 70 years after its release is advantageous for set collectors. The ’56 set can be achieved in high grades since there are so many prime examples.
“In 1956, because it is more attainable than 1955 or 1954, it actually invites more participation, more competition because there’s more product out there,” said Orlando, who used to be the president of PSA. “So, while it isn’t the toughest of the ’50s Topps sets, because the design is so appealing and the star selection is also so appealing and the cards are attainable in high grade, it actually makes for a nice combination and an inviting one for a lot of collectors.”
Collectors seemed to have taken care of their ’56 Topps cards, even seven decades ago. Remarkably, there are just shy of 80,000 copies that have received PSA 8 grades or higher. There are 305 cards that have reached Gem Mint PSA 10 status.
“The fact that they’ve got white borders, too, generally those cards are going to grade a tad bit better,” longtime baseball card collector Ryan Hoge said. “If you look at the population, there’s a heavy concentration of grades between 6 and 8, which is good for vintage. If you fast forward to say I want to look at like ’71 as a counterpoint, black borders, your percentage of 8s and 9s is infinitely smaller, if you look at the overall split across the PSA grades.”
Hoge, who is President of Grading at Collectors, the parent company of PSA, SGC and Beckett, noted that 1956 Topps baseball is one of the most popular vintage sets for passionate collectors who use the PSA Registry.
Hoge personally loves the ’56 release. He doesn’t collect the set, but he considers four 1956 cards he owns among the favorites in his collection. Hoge has a Mantle PSA 8.5 and Robinson, Mays and Aaron cards all slabbed in PSA 8.
“These are some of the coolest cards in my collection, the Mantle in particular is awesome. It was his Triple Crown year,” Hoge said. “I think the innovation with the profile shot and the action shot just adds to the eye appeal on the front of the card. Then on the back it has the information, the storytelling; the backs of these cards had all sorts of fun trivia type nuggets about the players and then their stats. Just awesome stuff.”
For how accessible single cards—raw and graded—and sets are from 1956, sealed wax and even wrappers are impossible to find, noted Sheldon. Over the years, there haven’t been any major finds unearthing a large offering of unripped packs.
SET COLLECTORS UNITE
A longtime set collector whose name is plastered all over the PSA Set Registry, John Evanoff has finished off Topps baseball set runs from 1952-67 and 1969-72.
It has been Evanoff’s goal to have every set he completes rank in the top 10 on PSA’s registry. In order to achieve that, all the cards need to be in high grades, 8s and up.
“It became a challenge,” Evanoff said. “That registry is addictive.”
Since he was on the verge of retirement, to financially afford to complete the high-graded sets, he needed to sell off some of his cards. One of the five sets he held onto was 1956 Topps.
Evanoff initially pieced together the ’56 set in just five months in fall 2015.
“It’s an easy set to finish in high grade, 8 or up, if you’ve got the money,” Evanoff said. “But back then they weren’t all that expensive. For example, I got the Mantle in an 8.5 for $5,700 at the 2015 National.”
Evanoff also acquired a number of the big stars in the set from Memory Lane Inc. He picked up Robinson and Aaron in PSA 8.5 for $2,000 apiece. Now those examples sell in the five-figure range.
Once Evanoff knocked off some of the most expensive cards, his new goal was to crack the top five in the PSA Set Registry.
“Which means, now you’ve got to go for 9s,” Evanoff said. “Now, look at the price of those cards; they’re crazy expensive.”
Evanoff—who has the No. 3-ranked Current Finest set in the PSA Set Registry for 1956 Topps—is constantly upgrading his cards. He owns 236 cards graded a PSA 9, 29 in PSA 8.5 and 77 in PSA 8.
Evanoff has invested a great deal of time and money into his ’56 set. He recently spent $29,000 on a PSA 9 of Roy Campanella. The toughest 9 for Evanoff to track down has been of Red Schoendienst. There are 17 Gray backs in a 9, but Evanoff has been chasing that grade for six years to no avail.
Evanoff makes it a point to meet up with 1956 Topps set collectors at the National Sports Collectors Convention. He planned to sell a PSA 8 at the show when he upgrades to a 9. Evanoff also sells a lot on the Facebook group for 1956 Topps set collectors.
“It’s a competition,” said Evanoff, whose set is GPA weighted at 8.78. “I love it. That’s why I do it.”
For set collector Lanny Ribes, the 1956 set has really grown on him over the years. He’s a huge fan of the ’55 release but the ’56 set wasn’t his favorite for quite some time.
Ribes’ son, Anthony, plays college baseball at the University of Illinois Springfield. Ribes uses different Topps card designs from over the years to make cards of his son.
“Whenever I design a different one, I fall in love with it just because of the colors and the fonts and everything else,” Ribes said. “So, ’56 for me it was pretty much exactly like 1955, except it had that action photo in the background. I thought that was cool.
“That was like the first action photos. I know it’s artwork, but the first action on a card you could really see. The Mickey Mantle and the Hank Aaron making plays over the wall and sliding plays at home plate. So, for me it was a combination of the artwork is absolutely gorgeous, the colors really pop and you’ve got that action part on every card—it was the first of its kind.”
WHITE VS GRAY
One aspect that separates the 1956 set from other vintage sets is it was the final year Topps produced larger cards. The dimensions were 2 5/8-by- 3 3/4. The following year Topps transitioned to 2½-by-3½, which is the size that has been used ever since.
Topps also experimented with different backs for its cards. Cards numbered #1-180 have cardboard backs with both white and gray. For numbers #1-100, the white backs are more common; for numbers #101-180, the gray backs are more common.
For example, Ted Williams’ card #5 has a PSA population of 5,319 for white backs and 2,344 for gray backs. Mantle’s card #135, on the other hand, has been graded 10,334 times in a gray back and just 1,109 in a white back.
The rarer cards certainly demand a higher premium. A Mantle white back in a PSA 5 sold in October 2025 for $4,500. A Mantle in a gray in the same grade went for $2,800 in January 2026.
“Having the gray back and the white back varieties is definitely a challenge,” Baker said. “The white backs are incredibly more challenging than their gray back counterparts—the population report shows that. But I think it adds another little flare to it. Having as many varieties in that set is kind of fun.”
The ’56 set has stood the test of time with collectors 70 years after its release. The great designs and star players keep the set extremely popular.
“Certainly, I mean no disrespect in saying this, but I’ve heard this expression that a ’56 Topps set is a poor man’s ’52,” Sheldon said. “The reason being is you had the stars of the day, but there’s no high numbers. In other words, you don’t have to buy a random common that costs you hundreds of dollars in VG, even like a ’52 Topps, because there’s no high-number series. So, for collectors on a budget, still being able to access a Jackie Robinson or Mickey Mantle that are not high numbers that are beautiful cards, you have to pay a fraction of what the ’52s go for.”

rss_title: Crisp design, colorful action photos and star players make 1956 Topps Baseball a popular vintage set for collectors
rss_body:
Cards
Crisp design, colorful action photos and star players make 1956 Topps Baseball a popular vintage set for collectors
The 1956 Topps set is arguably one of the most aesthetically pleasing baseball card sets of all time.
A crisp design, full-color artwork featuring dual action and profile shots, clean white borders and all the best players in the game make the set truly iconic.
It is instantly recognizable to any vintage baseball card buff.
Related Content:
Add in the fact that over half the players come in white and gray back variations—some cards rarer than others—and every card is widely available 70 years after production, the set’s lasting impact on the hobby is no surprise.
“I think you’re not going to get a lot of pushback from a lot of collectors that know that era. It would be hard to battle that set, because it’s got everything,” said Mike Baker, founder of Mike Baker Authenticated.
New York Yankees great Mickey Mantle is the crown jewel of the 340-card set. But there isn’t a lack of star power.
“It’s one of those weird sets from the ’50s that even though there’s a Luis Aparicio rookie, it’s really not anchored by that,” said Leighton Sheldon, owner of Vintage Breaks and Just Collect. “It’s anchored by the fact there’s just every available star of the day: Ted Williams, Jackie Robinson, Al Kaline, Willie Mays. The list just goes on and on. And those cards are highly coveted because of the design, because it shows a few different aspects of the player.”
Former Heritage Auctions Executive Vice President of Sports Joe Orlando agrees. The 1956 set features second-year cards of Sandy Koufax, Roberto Clemente and Harmon Killebrew and early cards of Mantle, Mays and Hank Aaron.
“The star combination across the board is so terrific,” Orlando said. “If you were to ask what’s the one relatively weak spot of this set, it doesn’t have as strong of a rookie card class as some of the sets around it. In 1955, you have one of the all-time great rookie card selections in Koufax, Clemente and Killebrew. In 1957, a year later, you have Don Drysdale, Frank Robinson, Brooks Robinson, it just keeps going with great rookie cards in that set. But in ’56 you have Luis Aparicio, a Hall of Fame shortstop, great player, but that’s basically the extent of the major names.”
MANTLE RETURNS
One main reason the set is so special and adored by collectors is it featured the reintroduction of Mantle back into Topps. The slugger was included in Topps’ 1952 and ’53 sets, but rival card company Bowman inked Mantle to an exclusive contract. He was noticeably excluded from Topps’ 1954 and ’55 releases. However, after Topps bought out its only competitor in January 1956, Mantle, Yankees pitcher Whitey Ford and Cleveland Indians pitcher Bob Feller all made their way back to Topps.
“Having Mantle back in Topps was such a huge moment for the company, because Mickey Mantle was the most popular player in baseball,” Orlando said. “Having him back in the set is a huge, huge part of its appeal. And, of course, in 1956 he just happens to reach the Triple Crown, which is like the stars aligned for Mantle that year.”
The ’56 Mantle is his only horizontal card during his illustrious Topps run. Mantle’s first ever Topps card in 1952 always receives accolades as one of the most iconic cards in the hobby. But his ’56 card is right up there with the ’53 release as being in the top three of Mantle’s most coveted cards.
“If you look at the card, it’s such a great looking card,” Orlando said. “He’s smiling ear to ear on his portrait side of the picture, there’s a beautiful action shot of him going into the stands, making a leaping grab in the background. Sometimes the design comes together in a way that just creates such a visually appealing card, and in this case, I think that’s a huge part of it. It’s just such a great looking card of Mantle, coupled with the other attributes that it’s absolutely one of his most popular issues.”
Having Mantle back in its product was monumental for Topps. And the company, in just its sixth year of making cards, took full advantage of having the face of America’s Pastime in its set.
After a successful year with the 1955 set, which featured a very similar look the following year, Topps upped its print run in ’56. That is evident in PSA’s Population Report from that year.
As of the end of January 2026, PSA had graded 212,795 cards from the 1955 set. The number of slabs jumped to 391,296—nearly double—for the 1956 set.
Having so much product around even 70 years after its release is advantageous for set collectors. The ’56 set can be achieved in high grades since there are so many prime examples.
“In 1956, because it is more attainable than 1955 or 1954, it actually invites more participation, more competition because there’s more product out there,” said Orlando, who used to be the president of PSA. “So, while it isn’t the toughest of the ’50s Topps sets, because the design is so appealing and the star selection is also so appealing and the cards are attainable in high grade, it actually makes for a nice combination and an inviting one for a lot of collectors.”
Collectors seemed to have taken care of their ’56 Topps cards, even seven decades ago. Remarkably, there are just shy of 80,000 copies that have received PSA 8 grades or higher. There are 305 cards that have reached Gem Mint PSA 10 status.
“The fact that they’ve got white borders, too, generally those cards are going to grade a tad bit better,” longtime baseball card collector Ryan Hoge said. “If you look at the population, there’s a heavy concentration of grades between 6 and 8, which is good for vintage. If you fast forward to say I want to look at like ’71 as a counterpoint, black borders, your percentage of 8s and 9s is infinitely smaller, if you look at the overall split across the PSA grades.”
Hoge, who is President of Grading at Collectors, the parent company of PSA, SGC and Beckett, noted that 1956 Topps baseball is one of the most popular vintage sets for passionate collectors who use the PSA Registry.
Hoge personally loves the ’56 release. He doesn’t collect the set, but he considers four 1956 cards he owns among the favorites in his collection. Hoge has a Mantle PSA 8.5 and Robinson, Mays and Aaron cards all slabbed in PSA 8.
“These are some of the coolest cards in my collection, the Mantle in particular is awesome. It was his Triple Crown year,” Hoge said. “I think the innovation with the profile shot and the action shot just adds to the eye appeal on the front of the card. Then on the back it has the information, the storytelling; the backs of these cards had all sorts of fun trivia type nuggets about the players and then their stats. Just awesome stuff.”
For how accessible single cards—raw and graded—and sets are from 1956, sealed wax and even wrappers are impossible to find, noted Sheldon. Over the years, there haven’t been any major finds unearthing a large offering of unripped packs.
SET COLLECTORS UNITE
A longtime set collector whose name is plastered all over the PSA Set Registry, John Evanoff has finished off Topps baseball set runs from 1952-67 and 1969-72.
It has been Evanoff’s goal to have every set he completes rank in the top 10 on PSA’s registry. In order to achieve that, all the cards need to be in high grades, 8s and up.
“It became a challenge,” Evanoff said. “That registry is addictive.”
Since he was on the verge of retirement, to financially afford to complete the high-graded sets, he needed to sell off some of his cards. One of the five sets he held onto was 1956 Topps.
Evanoff initially pieced together the ’56 set in just five months in fall 2015.
“It’s an easy set to finish in high grade, 8 or up, if you’ve got the money,” Evanoff said. “But back then they weren’t all that expensive. For example, I got the Mantle in an 8.5 for $5,700 at the 2015 National.”
Evanoff also acquired a number of the big stars in the set from Memory Lane Inc. He picked up Robinson and Aaron in PSA 8.5 for $2,000 apiece. Now those examples sell in the five-figure range.
Once Evanoff knocked off some of the most expensive cards, his new goal was to crack the top five in the PSA Set Registry.
“Which means, now you’ve got to go for 9s,” Evanoff said. “Now, look at the price of those cards; they’re crazy expensive.”
Evanoff—who has the No. 3-ranked Current Finest set in the PSA Set Registry for 1956 Topps—is constantly upgrading his cards. He owns 236 cards graded a PSA 9, 29 in PSA 8.5 and 77 in PSA 8.
Evanoff has invested a great deal of time and money into his ’56 set. He recently spent $29,000 on a PSA 9 of Roy Campanella. The toughest 9 for Evanoff to track down has been of Red Schoendienst. There are 17 Gray backs in a 9, but Evanoff has been chasing that grade for six years to no avail.
Evanoff makes it a point to meet up with 1956 Topps set collectors at the National Sports Collectors Convention. He planned to sell a PSA 8 at the show when he upgrades to a 9. Evanoff also sells a lot on the Facebook group for 1956 Topps set collectors.
“It’s a competition,” said Evanoff, whose set is GPA weighted at 8.78. “I love it. That’s why I do it.”
For set collector Lanny Ribes, the 1956 set has really grown on him over the years. He’s a huge fan of the ’55 release but the ’56 set wasn’t his favorite for quite some time.
Ribes’ son, Anthony, plays college baseball at the University of Illinois Springfield. Ribes uses different Topps card designs from over the years to make cards of his son.
“Whenever I design a different one, I fall in love with it just because of the colors and the fonts and everything else,” Ribes said. “So, ’56 for me it was pretty much exactly like 1955, except it had that action photo in the background. I thought that was cool.
“That was like the first action photos. I know it’s artwork, but the first action on a card you could really see. The Mickey Mantle and the Hank Aaron making plays over the wall and sliding plays at home plate. So, for me it was a combination of the artwork is absolutely gorgeous, the colors really pop and you’ve got that action part on every card—it was the first of its kind.”
WHITE VS GRAY
One aspect that separates the 1956 set from other vintage sets is it was the final year Topps produced larger cards. The dimensions were 2 5/8-by- 3 3/4. The following year Topps transitioned to 2½-by-3½, which is the size that has been used ever since.
Topps also experimented with different backs for its cards. Cards numbered #1-180 have cardboard backs with both white and gray. For numbers #1-100, the white backs are more common; for numbers #101-180, the gray backs are more common.
For example, Ted Williams’ card #5 has a PSA population of 5,319 for white backs and 2,344 for gray backs. Mantle’s card #135, on the other hand, has been graded 10,334 times in a gray back and just 1,109 in a white back.
The rarer cards certainly demand a higher premium. A Mantle white back in a PSA 5 sold in October 2025 for $4,500. A Mantle in a gray in the same grade went for $2,800 in January 2026.
“Having the gray back and the white back varieties is definitely a challenge,” Baker said. “The white backs are incredibly more challenging than their gray back counterparts—the population report shows that. But I think it adds another little flare to it. Having as many varieties in that set is kind of fun.”
The ’56 set has stood the test of time with collectors 70 years after its release. The great designs and star players keep the set extremely popular.
“Certainly, I mean no disrespect in saying this, but I’ve heard this expression that a ’56 Topps set is a poor man’s ’52,” Sheldon said. “The reason being is you had the stars of the day, but there’s no high numbers. In other words, you don’t have to buy a random common that costs you hundreds of dollars in VG, even like a ’52 Topps, because there’s no high-number series. So, for collectors on a budget, still being able to access a Jackie Robinson or Mickey Mantle that are not high numbers that are beautiful cards, you have to pay a fraction of what the ’52s go for.”

title: Should the Yankees use Cam Schlittler in Game 1 or 2 of the Wild Card Series?
author: Andrés Chávez
body:
The New York Yankees have punched their ticket to the 2026 MLB Playoffs and, barring a late surprise, will face the Boston Red Sox in the AL Wild Card Series with all games being played in Yankee Stadium. There are legitimate questions surrounding the Yanks’ offense and bullpen, but their rotation appears to be in a very good place heading into October: it boasts leading AL Cy Young candidate Cam Schlittler, former winner of the award Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, and Carlos Rodón, plus other solid depth options.
Should the Yankees use Cam Schlittler in Game 1 or 2 of the Wild Card Series?
The Yankees have a nice problem on their hands for Game 1 of a still-hypothetical, but likely Wild Card Series.
It’s safe to assume that Schlittler, Cole, and one of Rodón or Fried will be the ones in charge of taking the ball in the Wild Card round. How will manager Aaron Boone deploy them, though? And who will be the starter for Game 1: Schlittler, the best pitcher on the team and potentially the league; or Cole, the nominal ace with a myriad of postseason battles under his belt?
Right now, the Yankees’ rotation is lined up for Cole to take the ball in Game 1 against the Red Sox on Tuesday, on five days’ rest. Schlittler would be the Game 2 starter, also with five days between games to rest. One of Fried or Rodón will be available for a potential Game 3 on four days’ rest, depending on how they’re used this weekend.
What should the Yankees do in Games 1 and 2 regarding their starter? Let’s examine the case for each potential path:
The case for starting Cole in Game 1:
Cole, as explained, is lined up to get the ball in the AL Wild Card Series opener at home on Tuesday with five days’ rest. Traditionally, at least in recent years, the Yankees have preferred to give their pitchers five days to recharge between starts in the postseason whenever possible.
Maybe Cole didn’t have the best regular season statistically, and he did allow eight home runs in his last three starts, but he showed in 2024 that he could be solid in regular season play (3.41 ERA, against a similar 3.63 mark this year) only to lock in during October, when he had a 2.17 ERA in 29 frames and a 0.71 World Series ERA against the Dodgers.
Additionally, opening the Wild Card series with Cole as the Game 1 starter would allow the Yankees to save Schlittler for a pivotal Game 2 in which they could either clinch their spot in the Division Series or tie the best-of-three matchup with Boston. Having the AL Cy Young candidate in the second game could represent a nice way to either save the season or have him as the ‘closer’ of the matchup, depending on Game 1’s result.
On top of that, using Cole in Game 1 and saving Schlittler for the second would, in theory, mean the Yankees could still have Schlittler start Game 2 of the ALDS against the Rays on standard four days’ rest on October 5th, and be available on four days’ rest again for a potential Game 5 on October 10th.
The case for starting Schlittler in Game 1:
If Schlittler toes the rubber in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, the Yankees would have a better chance to go up 1-0 in the best-of-three matchup. He is the best pitcher in the Junior Circuit and has a knack for getting it done against the Red Sox. You can’t underestimate the obvious advantages of going up in the series.
It’s not that Cole can’t toss seven scoreless and guide the Yankees to a 1-0 start, but Schlittler’s chances of doing that are objectively better. After all, the latter has a 1.94 regular-season ERA, and the 2023 AL Cy Young Award winner is at 3.63. Some would also say that not using your absolute best pitcher in Game 1 of such a short series can be counterproductive and extremely risky.
In short, deploying Schlittler as the starting pitcher for the Wild Card series opener could increase the chances of the Yankees taking the field on Wednesday with a 1-0 lead. In any case, he would be slated to pitch two games in the AL Division Series should the Yankees advance.

title: Luis Gil Has a Lot to Prove to Yankees During Final Week of Regular Season
author: Joseph Randazzo; Unknown
body:
It's funny to think that at one point it felt like sacrilege to even consider trading Luis Gil for anyone. Here was the prospective American League Rookie of the Year who held it down in the rotation while Gerrit Cole was sidelined for much of 2024, and the Houston Astros wanted him as the centerpiece of a trade for Kyle Tucker. The New York Yankees scoffed at the idea and opted to keep Gil.
In hindsight, they should have landed Tucker and sent Gil to Houston. Gil immediately broke down, and his velocity has never been what it was during his first full season, when he earned rookie honors. It's a trade they likely would have won even if Tucker ended up still going to the Los Angeles Dodgers.
That one successful year feels like a lifetime ago, but now the Yankees have a chance to salvage some of his value. With injuries to Ryan Weathers, a Clarke Schmidt scare this past week, and Brent Headrick's velocity alarmingly down over the weekend, the bullpen is looking shaky heading into the postseason. With just a week left in the regular season, they should use this opportunity to see what they have in Gil.
In the best-case scenario, Gil would be relegated to lower-leverage situations. That is how they have used him, too. Gil has seen just five appearances over the last month, but things feel a little more dire, and Boone used him twice in their most recent series against the Arizona Diamondbacks. It could be a signal that they're giving Gil one last chance to prove himself. There might not be another choice, either.
The best use of Gil moving forward
Call it a bit of a Hail Mary, but it wouldn't hurt the Yankees at this point if they used Gil in medium- to high-leverage situations against the Tampa Bay Rays and Baltimore Orioles. If he can hack it, at least they know what they have. The same goes if he fails there. At least they know not to use him in that role in the postseason.
Better to find out now, when the games don't matter and the postseason is already set. Chances are the Rays aren't losing the next seven games and blowing the division, either.
One thing about Gil is that his velocity looks like it's up. He averaged 95.4 MPH on his fastball this season. Since being called up on August 31st, Gil has averaged 96.1 MPH. His slider velocity is up as well. He's averaging 87.1 MPH on it since the call-up. He is sitting at 85.8 MPH this season.
Gil's strikeout numbers are also slightly up in this small sample size. Since his call-up, he has pitched six innings and struck out eight with just three walks. He has allowed one earned run, but that was back in his first start.
Another thing about Gil is that the Yankees are waiting for his arm to return to what it used to be. He may never be what he once was, and with a stacked rotation, his only role as a Yankee is likely in the bullpen. That said, this final week could be one of Gil's most important.
It's an opportunity to show that he still has some value to the team, and if he's able to get outs, blowing heaters by batters this week and into the postseason, they don't have to feel all that bad about watching Tucker go elsewhere in 2025 — not that it would have mattered in the long run anyway.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

That one successful year feels like a lifetime ago, but now the Yankees have a chance to salvage some of his value. With injuries to Ryan Weathers, a Clarke Schmidt scare this past week, and Brent Headrick's velocity alarmingly down over the weekend, the bullpen is looking shaky heading into the postseason. With just a week left in the regular season, they should use this opportunity to see what they have in Gil.
In the best-case scenario, Gil would be relegated to lower-leverage situations. That is how they have used him, too. Gil has seen just five appearances over the last month, but things feel a little more dire, and Boone used him twice in their most recent series against the Arizona Diamondbacks. It could be a signal that they're giving Gil one last chance to prove himself. There might not be another choice, either.
The best use of Gil moving forward
Call it a bit of a Hail Mary, but it wouldn't hurt the Yankees at this point if they used Gil in medium- to high-leverage situations against the Tampa Bay Rays and Baltimore Orioles. If he can hack it, at least they know what they have. The same goes if he fails there. At least they know not to use him in that role in the postseason.
Better to find out now, when the games don't matter and the postseason is already set. Chances are the Rays aren't losing the next seven games and blowing the division, either.
One thing about Gil is that his velocity looks like it's up. He averaged 95.4 MPH on his fastball this season. Since being called up on August 31st, Gil has averaged 96.1 MPH. His slider velocity is up as well. He's averaging 87.1 MPH on it since the call-up. He is sitting at 85.8 MPH this season.
Gil's strikeout numbers are also slightly up in this small sample size. Since his call-up, he has pitched six innings and struck out eight with just three walks. He has allowed one earned run, but that was back in his first start.
Another thing about Gil is that the Yankees are waiting for his arm to return to what it used to be. He may never be what he once was, and with a stacked rotation, his only role as a Yankee is likely in the bullpen. That said, this final week could be one of Gil's most important.
It's an opportunity to show that he still has some value to the team, and if he's able to get outs, blowing heaters by batters this week and into the postseason, they don't have to feel all that bad about watching Tucker go elsewhere in 2025 — not that it would have mattered in the long run anyway.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

title: Aaron Judge podría no volver a jugar en 2026 con los Yankees
author: José Moreno
body:
Aaron Judge volvió a encender las alarmas en los New York Yankees después de sufrir una nueva lesión que lo mandó nuevamente a la lista de lesionados, apenas unos días después de regresar tras una larga ausencia.
La situación genera preocupación en New York, pues el pelotero presenta una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha y ahora existe la posibilidad de que no vuelva a disputar un encuentro durante lo que resta de la temporada.
Aaron Judge vuelve a quedar fuera por lesión
Judge fue colocado nuevamente en la lista de lesionados después de presentar molestias durante el encuentro ante los Minnesota Twins. El problema físico fue confirmado posteriormente mediante estudios médicos.
El regreso del capitán había ocurrido el pasado 8 de septiembre, después de permanecer fuera durante más de tres meses por una fractura en las costillas. Sin embargo, solo pudo disputar siete encuentros antes de volver a quedar fuera.
El momento de la lesión complica todavía más el panorama, ya que Judge podría ser elegible para regresar hasta el 27 de septiembre, cuando los Yankees estarán prácticamente en el cierre de su calendario de temporada regular.
Crece la preocupación en los Yankees
De acuerdo con reportes citados por medios estadounidenses, existe una posibilidad importante de que Judge no vuelva a jugar durante esta temporada. La situación también pone en duda su participación en la postemporada.
El propio jugador mantiene la intención de regresar para los playoffs, aunque todavía no existe un calendario definido para su recuperación. Los Yankees tendrán que esperar la evolución de la lesión antes de tomar una decisión.
La ausencia de Judge representa un problema para New York, especialmente porque el capitán es una de las principales figuras ofensivas del equipo. Ahora, los Yankees deberán esperar para saber si podrá regresar a tiempo para octubre.

title: Red Sox platoon issues could play right into Yankees hands in potential playoff tilt
author: Stephen Parello
body:
The New York Yankees' hopes for a deep playoff run took a huge hit when Aaron Judge landed on the IL with a strained calf. Judge says that he'd like to be back in time for the start of the playoffs, but refused to lay out a timeline. While Giancarlo Stanton and his calf strain that never ends (it goes on and on, my friends) is a special case, depending on the severity, this can be a tricky injury.
New York's playoff journey is most likely set to begin with a matchup against the archrival Boston Red Sox. Missing Judge, or having him in a diminished capacity, will be a big blow, but there is still an advantage that the Yankees can leverage.
Several key Red Sox bats are left-handed hitters. Last season, Boston employed a lefty-mashing platoon duo of Rob Refsnyder and Romy Gonzalez to protect those hitters and neutralize any advantage southpaws might hold over them.
However, this year is a different story, as Refsnyder bolted to the Mariners and then retired after a putrid performance led to him being cut, and Gonzalez missed much of the season recovering from shoulder surgery and is currently in Triple-A.
Boston's new lefty-mashing crew has taken some hits lately. Eli White is done for the season with a torn ligament in his right foot. Andruw Monasterio has a .798 OPS against lefties this season, but he's cooled substantially with a .115/.179/.115 line against left-handed pitching since August 1. Jahmai Jones struggled mightily earlier in the season with the Tigers, heated up once picked up by the Red Sox and then slowed back down with a 3-for-18, eight-strikeout performance to begin September.
Yankees are set up to take advantage of Red Sox's recent platoon struggles with Max Fried, Carlos Rodon
The Red Sox's platoon issues play right into the Yankees' hands with Max Fried and Carlos Rodón lurking in the playoff rotation. Fried has battled injuries, but when he's been on the mound, he's been dominant. Seeing him go seven strong in his September 15 start against the Minnesota Twins was a great sign that he's going to be at full strength in time for October.
Rodón is a different case. His velocity drop against the Twins was concerning, but he did rebound later in the start and began pumping 95-plus heat. Overall, though, he doesn't get enough credit for how solid he's been as a Yankee. Most fans' opinions are colored by how his tenure began, but over his last 61 starts in pinstripes, he has a 3.04 ERA.
If Tim Hill can get back on track (outcome hazy, ask again later), the advantage will only grow as the New York can match up following their right-handed starters and later in the game.
There might be a couple of other advantages that the Yankees can exploit. Aroldis Chapman is dealing with a lat issue that hasn't landed him on the IL, but could make him vulnerable. Meanwhile, Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch and suffered a hand injury on September 17 against the Texas Rangers. While X-rays were negative and the hand doesn't appear to be fractured, it could carry over and impact his ability to be a threat at the plate.
The Yankees will need every advantage they can get given Judge's uncertainty. If this matchup comes to fruition, they'll be fortunate enough that the Red Sox are dealing with a number of issues of their own that New York can exploit.

title: Carlos Rodon explains how Cam Schlittler is ‘rage baiting’ Yankees manager Aaron Boone
author: Brogan Clasper
body:
The New York Yankees appear to be in a relaxed mood as they gear up for the playoffs ahead of the final regular games of the season.
Although the Yankees have failed to win either of their last two games against the Arizona Diamondbacks, Aaron Boone's victory celebration has been thrown into the spotlight.
Second-year pitcher Cam Schlittler has been in fine form this season and will be among the names to pick up one of the awards at the end of the season.
However, it is what the pitcher has been doing to Boone that has made some of his teammates laugh back at Yankee Stadium.
How Cam Schlittler has been rage baiting Yankees manager Aaron Boone
After every Yankees win – and there has been 89 this season – Boone has looked to the stands and hit his clenched fists together up in the air.
The reason behind it remains a mystery, even for the players, with Carlos Rodon providing some insight on how Schlittler has been using the celebration to rage bait Boone.
"I don't even know what it is. At some point was it brought to my attention, from Cam himself, because Cam kind of does the same thing when he does it, just to be funny, to rage bait him," said Rodon.
"But I have no idea what it means or what it signifies. I don't even know. I don't even think he's really looking at anybody in the stands. He says he's looking at someone, but I have no idea what's going on there."
Only seven games remain for the Yankees in the regular season, with second spot in the AL East still needing to be wrapped up.
The third-placed Boston Red Sox have only six games remaining, which could see them end their season with 90 wins if they were to go unbeaten.
Boone's Yankees are already on 89 victories for the season, which would mean a couple more celebrations from the manager would be enough to secure second spot.

title: The Yankees’ Aaron Judge double-talk is cheating those who care the most
author: Joel Sherman
body:
The Yankees and Aaron Judge have two basic public postures when it comes to his injuries — dissembling and disrespectful.
It lowers both team and player. Does nothing for their reputations. And certainly gives no thoughts to their fan base.
I could get it if this was a high-minded defense of HIPAA rights. But this feels tied up in paranoia and gripes. And, again, cares not a whit about the paying customer.
Because Judge and his bosses should read this sentence with the utmost sincerity with which it is offered: I personally don’t care what the status of his current injury is, except to the extent that I would always prefer all the best players play since that usually provides a more enjoyable sport to cover.

title: Yankees' playoff picture, Aaron Judge update and potential rotation
author: Pete Caldera
body:
Yankees' playoff picture, Aaron Judge update and potential rotation
This wasn’t how the Yankees wanted to move into the regular season’s final week, with a four-game set against Tampa Bay.
Beginning with Tuesday’s day-night doubleheader, they’ll need to sweep the AL East leaders just to prevent the Rays from spilling champagne inside Yankee Stadium’s visiting clubhouse.
And there’s uncertainty surrounding Yankees captain Aaron Judge’s availability next week – the start of postseason − due to a right calf strain.
“We’ve been through a lot as a team this year already and we’ve answered the bell at mostly all the turns,’’ Yanks manager Aaron Boone told reporters, including the YES Network, after Sunday’s 8-4 loss at Arizona.
“(We’re) looking forward to hopefully playing a good week of baseball and building some momentum going into the postseason.’’
Here’s a look at the Yankees’ week ahead:
Yankees vs Rays with AL East race nearing its end
In winning 12 of their last 15 games, the Rays (95-60) have opened a six-game divisional lead on the Yanks (89-66).
On the verge of its first AL East title since 2021, Tampa Bay could clinch it with one win on a long Tuesday in the Bronx.
Tuesday’s opener has Rays right-hander Nick Martinez (15-4, 2.94) scheduled to oppose lefty Carlos Rodon (6-3, 2.95), with righty Drew Rasmussen (15-5, 2.72) vs. lefty Max Fried (5-4, 2.63) in the nightcap.
The Yanks are scheduled to start Gerrit Cole on Wednesday and Cam Schlittler on Thursday.
In the wider picture, Boone acknowledged the need to prep for next week, which includes giving important bullpen arms like Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn some added rest.
“You’ve got to make sure guys are in a good spot going in (to postseason),’’ Boone told reporters, speaking generally on Sunday.
“But we’re going to show up and try to win the games on Tuesday.’’
Aaron Judge injury update
Judge’s availability for the first playoff round remains a mystery.
This past weekend, Judge told reporters: “I’d like to be back by the postseason. That’s definitely the plan.’’
Judge said he’s played through minor calf strains before, but this current injury to the soleus muscle is a more problematic spot.
So, this will be a key week of treatment and testing to see if Judge could be available in any capacity for a first-round playoff series.
Yankees injury news as Jazz Chisholm Jr. might return
Sidelined since Sept. 9, lefty-hitting second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. (right thumb sprain) could be activated from the injured list to start the Tampa Bay series.
Though he’s unlikely to be activated this week, lefty reliever Ryan Weathers (flexor strain) could find himself on a playoff roster next week in a bullpen capacity.

title: Monday Stat Party: Put him in the books
author: Linus Lawrence
body:
Welcome back to Monday Stat Party, a weekly series showcasing some of the most curious and nostalgia-inducing statistical developments from the past week of Mets baseball. What unites each entry is the sense of intrigue which they aim to spark, and the unbridled love of the game’s anomalies from which they arise. Without further ado, let the stat party begin.
MONDAY
A.J. Ewing hit his 10th home run of the season, giving the Mets 11 players with 10+ homers and setting a new record for most 10-homer players in a season in franchise history (the 2017 team previously held the record with 10 10-homer players). They are now tied for the fifth-most 10-homer players on a team in baseball history, behind the 2019 Yankees (14), 2019 Blue Jays (13), 2018 Yankees (12), and 2023 Twins (12).
TUESDAY
Pete Alonso became the 20th player to record their 300th homer against a team for which they previously played, and the third to do so against a team for which they played 1,000 or more games (along with Willie Horton against the Tigers and Torii Hunter against the Twins). (source: Sarah Langs on X, per Elias Sports Bureau)
Alonso became the second player to hit their 300th homer at Citi Field, as Curtis Granderson reached the milestone with a go-ahead homer in the eighth inning on June 14, 2017, against the Cubs.
The homer marked Alonso’s first game-tying or go-ahead home run while trailing in the ninth inning or later since Game 3 of the 2024 Wild Card Series.
Alonso was actually the second former Met to hit a game-tying or go-ahead home run at Citi Field while trailing in the ninth inning or later. It may not have received the same fanfare as the Polar Bear’s blast, but Adeiny Hecchavarría accomplished the feat with the Braves off Paul Sewald on September 29, 2019 — exactly one day after Alonso set a new MLB rookie record with his 53rd home run of the season. Hechavarría’s homer set up Dom Smith’s memorable walk-off homer on the final pitch of the regular season.
Alonso’s homer snapped Kodai Senga’s streak of seven consecutive saves successfully converted, the fourth-most by a Met to begin their career behind Tug McGraw (15), Anthony Young (12), and Hisanori Takahashi (8).
A.J. Ewing’s second-inning single marked the 100th hit of his career. Ewing and Carson Benge are just the third pair of Mets rookies to record 100 hits in the same season, joining Steve Henderson and Lee Mazzilli in 1977 and Jason Phillips and Ty Wigginton in 2003.
Since 2015, there have been four extra-inning inside-the-park homers in MLB. Three of those four have been hit by an opposing player at Citi Field: Blake Swihart of the Red Sox on August 28, 2015, Daylen Lile of the Nationals on September 20, 2025, and now Coby Mayo of the Orioles on September 15, 2026. The only other extra-inning inside-the-park homer in that span was hit by another Oriole, Austin Hays, on August 11, 2020, at Citizens Bank Park.
Mayo’s inside-the-park homer was a wind-prevented traditional homer, marking the first time a wind-prevented traditional homer has resulted in an inside-the-parker since…Daylen Lile’s on September 20, 2025, at Citi Field. (source: Sarah Langs on X, per Weather Applied Metrics)
The Mets played their 18th extra-inning game of the season, marking the fourth-most in the majors behind the Angels (20), Cubs (19) and Cardinals (19). It’s the most extra-inning games the Mets have played in a season since 2018 (18).
WEDNESDAY
With his 24th stolen base of the season, A.J. Ewing tied Mookie Wilson’s 1981 record for the most stolen bases by a rookie in franchise history.
By allowing homers to Pete Alonso, Christian Encarnacion-Strand, and Jeremiah Jackson, the Mets allowed homers to the same three players in back-to-back games for the first time in franchise history.
The Orioles hit three homers at 106+ mph against the Mets for the second day in a row. Prior to this series, the Mets hadn’t allowed three such homers in a game since April 4, 2023, during a 9-0 loss in Milwaukee.
Chris Bassitt completed six innings at Citi Field for the 16th time since 2022. He is tied with David Peterson for the most six-inning outings at Citi Field during that span, despite the fact that Bassitt played just one season as a Met.
Alonso hit his 125th homer at Citi Field. No other player has more than 80 (Francisco Lindor). It was also Alonso’s 58th homer of a Statcast-projected 410+ feet at Citi Field. No other player has more than 23 (Michael Conforto).
The Mets have now lost five games in a row against the Orioles, and nine of their last 12.
THURSDAY
Nolan McLean has a 0.71 ERA over his first four career starts against the Phillies. That’s tied with Chuck Taylor for the fourth-lowest ERA in a pitcher’s first four starts against the Phillies since the mound was lowered in 1969 (min. 20 IP), behind Rick Honeycutt (0.38), Bob Sykes (0.42), and Hiroki Kuroda (0.68).
McLean recorded his 19th quality start this season, tied with Sonny Gray and Chris Sale for sixth-most in the majors behind Sandy Alcantara (21), Yoshinobu Yamamoto (21), Cristopher Sánchez (21), Cam Schlittler (20), and Michael Wacha (20). McLean is one of only two pitchers since 2015 to reach 19 quality starts in their rookie season, joining Shota Imanaga (19 in 2024). McLean also recorded his 20th start of six or more innings pitched this season, the second-most by a Met in a season since 2020, trailing only Wednesday’s opposing starter: Chris Bassitt (23 in 2022).
McLean recorded his 25th game with at least five strikeouts this season, the most by a Mets pitcher since Jacob deGrom (29) and Noah Syndergaard (27) in 2019.
Aaron Nola made his 33rd career start against the Mets, tied for 25th all-time against the franchise and tied with Randy Wolf and Tim Hudson for second-most since 2000, behind fellow longtime Phillies pitcher Cole Hamels (34). It was his 16th start as a visiting player at Citi Field, moving him into second place behind Gio Gonzalez (18) for most opposing starts in the ballpark’s history.
Nola recorded his seventh scoreless start against the Mets, tying him for the sixth-most all-time behind Rick Reuschel (11), Greg Maddux (10), Juan Marichal (9), Claude Osteen (9), and Jim Bunning (8).
The Mets suffered their 15th shutout loss of the season, tied with the Angels, Guardians, and Pirates for the second-most in MLB behind the Reds (17).
FRIDAY
Juan Soto reached base three times for the 324th time in his career, tying Mike Trout for the fourth-most such games by a player before turning 28 years old. Soto trails only Jimmie Foxx (348), Mickey Mantle (344), and Mel Ott (341).
Soto ripped two extra-base hits with an exit velocity of 108 mph or higher in the same game. In the statcast era (since 2015), a Mets left-handed hitter has accomplished that feat only 12 times: Robinson Cano, Lucas Duda, and Daniel Vogelbach each did it once, Brandon Nimmo did it twice, Michael Conforto did it three times, and Juan Soto has now done it four times in just two seasons.
Zac Thornton recorded his eighth quality start through 14 career games, marking the third-most by a Mets left-handed pitcher behind Steven Matz (10) and Sid Fernandez (9).
SATURDAY
Carson Benge’s eighth-inning single marked his 156th hit of the season, passing Pete Alonso to set the franchise’s new rookie hits record.
Benge recorded his 12th three-hit game of the season, marking another record for a Mets rookie, while notching three hits and a homer against the Phillies. The Mets outfielder with the most such games against the Phillies? Carlos Beltrán (7 times), who had his number retired in a pregame ceremony on Saturday.
The Mets scored 10 or more runs for the 18th time this season, tied with 1997 for the third-most such games in a season in franchise history. The 2000 (24) and 1999 (20) teams are the only ones in franchise history with more double-digit scoring performances.
SUNDAY
Francisco Alvarez’s second-inning single was his 23rd batted ball at 108 mph or higher this season, tied with Juan Soto for the most on the team.
The Mets scored two or fewer runs through nine innings for the 62nd time this season. That’s the most such games for the Mets in a season since 2013 (63), and their second-most in the Wild Card Era (since 1995).
The Mets finished the season with a losing record (3-4) against the Phillies at Citi Field for the first time since 2019, when they went 4-5.
The Mets finished the season with a 36-45 record at Citi Field, their worst in a full season since 2013, when they went 33-48.
Miscellaneous Mets stat of the week:
Here is a list of every player to record 99+ homers and 99+ stolen bases with multiple franchises:
Barry Bonds (Pirates and Giants)
Alex Rodriguez (Mariners and Yankees)
Carlos Beltrán (Royals and Mets)
Francisco Lindor (Guardians and Mets)
Beltrán’s 70.0 career bWAR ranks second all-time among players born in Puerto Rico, trailing only that of Roberto Clemente (95.0). Beltrán won the Roberto Clemente Award in 2013, and Francisco Lindor (who ranks fifth on the leaderboard with 57.2 bWAR) was named the Mets’ 2026 nominee last Monday.
Bonus Stat: There are 32 entries in this edition of Monday Stat Party — one for each year of Mets baseball that Howie Rose has called from the broadcast booth.

tracked_people.status: 2-time MVP with NYY, key piece of the 2009 title team.

It may not have received the same fanfare as the Polar Bear’s blast, but Adeiny Hecchavarría accomplished the feat with the Braves off Paul Sewald on September 29, 2019 — exactly one day after Alonso set a new MLB rookie record with his 53rd home run of the season. Hechavarría’s homer set up Dom Smith’s memorable walk-off homer on the final pitch of the regular season.
Alonso’s homer snapped Kodai Senga’s streak of seven consecutive saves successfully converted, the fourth-most by a Met to begin their career behind Tug McGraw (15), Anthony Young (12), and Hisanori Takahashi (8).
A.J. Ewing’s second-inning single marked the 100th hit of his career. Ewing and Carson Benge are just the third pair of Mets rookies to record 100 hits in the same season, joining Steve Henderson and Lee Mazzilli in 1977 and Jason Phillips and Ty Wigginton in 2003.
Since 2015, there have been four extra-inning inside-the-park homers in MLB. Three of those four have been hit by an opposing player at Citi Field: Blake Swihart of the Red Sox on August 28, 2015, Daylen Lile of the Nationals on September 20, 2025, and now Coby Mayo of the Orioles on September 15, 2026. The only other extra-inning inside-the-park homer in that span was hit by another Oriole, Austin Hays, on August 11, 2020, at Citizens Bank Park.
Mayo’s inside-the-park homer was a wind-prevented traditional homer, marking the first time a wind-prevented traditional homer has resulted in an inside-the-parker since…Daylen Lile’s on September 20, 2025, at Citi Field. (source: Sarah Langs on X, per Weather Applied Metrics)
The Mets played their 18th extra-inning game of the season, marking the fourth-most in the majors behind the Angels (20), Cubs (19) and Cardinals (19). It’s the most extra-inning games the Mets have played in a season since 2018 (18).
WEDNESDAY
With his 24th stolen base of the season, A.J. Ewing tied Mookie Wilson’s 1981 record for the most stolen bases by a rookie in franchise history.
By allowing homers to Pete Alonso, Christian Encarnacion-Strand, and Jeremiah Jackson, the Mets allowed homers to the same three players in back-to-back games for the first time in franchise history.
The Orioles hit three homers at 106+ mph against the Mets for the second day in a row. Prior to this series, the Mets hadn’t allowed three such homers in a game since April 4, 2023, during a 9-0 loss in Milwaukee.
Chris Bassitt completed six innings at Citi Field for the 16th time since 2022. He is tied with David Peterson for the most six-inning outings at Citi Field during that span, despite the fact that Bassitt played just one season as a Met.
Alonso hit his 125th homer at Citi Field. No other player has more than 80 (Francisco Lindor). It was also Alonso’s 58th homer of a Statcast-projected 410+ feet at Citi Field. No other player has more than 23 (Michael Conforto).
The Mets have now lost five games in a row against the Orioles, and nine of their last 12.
THURSDAY
Nolan McLean has a 0.71 ERA over his first four career starts against the Phillies. That’s tied with Chuck Taylor for the fourth-lowest ERA in a pitcher’s first four starts against the Phillies since the mound was lowered in 1969 (min. 20 IP), behind Rick Honeycutt (0.38), Bob Sykes (0.42), and Hiroki Kuroda (0.68).
McLean recorded his 19th quality start this season, tied with Sonny Gray and Chris Sale for sixth-most in the majors behind Sandy Alcantara (21), Yoshinobu Yamamoto (21), Cristopher Sánchez (21), Cam Schlittler (20), and Michael Wacha (20). McLean is one of only two pitchers since 2015 to reach 19 quality starts in their rookie season, joining Shota Imanaga (19 in 2024). McLean also recorded his 20th start of six or more innings pitched this season, the second-most by a Met in a season since 2020, trailing only Wednesday’s opposing starter: Chris Bassitt (23 in 2022).
McLean recorded his 25th game with at least five strikeouts this season, the most by a Mets pitcher since Jacob deGrom (29) and Noah Syndergaard (27) in 2019.
Aaron Nola made his 33rd career start against the Mets, tied for 25th all-time against the franchise and tied with Randy Wolf and Tim Hudson for second-most since 2000, behind fellow longtime Phillies pitcher Cole Hamels (34). It was his 16th start as a visiting player at Citi Field, moving him into second place behind Gio Gonzalez (18) for most opposing starts in the ballpark’s history.
Nola recorded his seventh scoreless start against the Mets, tying him for the sixth-most all-time behind Rick Reuschel (11), Greg Maddux (10), Juan Marichal (9), Claude Osteen (9), and Jim Bunning (8).
The Mets suffered their 15th shutout loss of the season, tied with the Angels, Guardians, and Pirates for the second-most in MLB behind the Reds (17).
FRIDAY
Juan Soto reached base three times for the 324th time in his career, tying Mike Trout for the fourth-most such games by a player before turning 28 years old. Soto trails only Jimmie Foxx (348), Mickey Mantle (344), and Mel Ott (341).
Soto ripped two extra-base hits with an exit velocity of 108 mph or higher in the same game. In the statcast era (since 2015), a Mets left-handed hitter has accomplished that feat only 12 times: Robinson Cano, Lucas Duda, and Daniel Vogelbach each did it once, Brandon Nimmo did it twice, Michael Conforto did it three times, and Juan Soto has now done it four times in just two seasons.
Zac Thornton recorded his eighth quality start through 14 career games, marking the third-most by a Mets left-handed pitcher behind Steven Matz (10) and Sid Fernandez (9).
SATURDAY
Carson Benge’s eighth-inning single marked his 156th hit of the season, passing Pete Alonso to set the franchise’s new rookie hits record.
Benge recorded his 12th three-hit game of the season, marking another record for a Mets rookie, while notching three hits and a homer against the Phillies. The Mets outfielder with the most such games against the Phillies? Carlos Beltrán (7 times), who had his number retired in a pregame ceremony on Saturday.
The Mets scored 10 or more runs for the 18th time this season, tied with 1997 for the third-most such games in a season in franchise history. The 2000 (24) and 1999 (20) teams are the only ones in franchise history with more double-digit scoring performances.
SUNDAY
Francisco Alvarez’s second-inning single was his 23rd batted ball at 108 mph or higher this season, tied with Juan Soto for the most on the team.
The Mets scored two or fewer runs through nine innings for the 62nd time this season. That’s the most such games for the Mets in a season since 2013 (63), and their second-most in the Wild Card Era (since 1995).
The Mets finished the season with a losing record (3-4) against the Phillies at Citi Field for the first time since 2019, when they went 4-5.
The Mets finished the season with a 36-45 record at Citi Field, their worst in a full season since 2013, when they went 33-48.
Miscellaneous Mets stat of the week:
Here is a list of every player to record 99+ homers and 99+ stolen bases with multiple franchises:
Barry Bonds (Pirates and Giants)
Alex Rodriguez (Mariners and Yankees)
Carlos Beltrán (Royals and Mets)
Francisco Lindor (Guardians and Mets)
Beltrán’s 70.0 career bWAR ranks second all-time among players born in Puerto Rico, trailing only that of Roberto Clemente (95.0). Beltrán won the Roberto Clemente Award in 2013, and Francisco Lindor (who ranks fifth on the leaderboard with 57.2 bWAR) was named the Mets’ 2026 nominee last Monday.
Bonus Stat: There are 32 entries in this edition of Monday Stat Party — one for each year of Mets baseball that Howie Rose has called from the broadcast booth.

title: Pave Ruth
author: Joshua Hunt
body:
A gut punching series loss at the hands of the Miami Marlins not only had the Diamondbacks lose more ground in the NL Wild Card race to the 3 teams ahead of them, it also seemed to take all the hopium that remained in our systems and replace it with either copium or just straight up despair as the D’Backs would go from 2 losing series against 2 sub .500 teams to welcoming the New York Yankees into town for the final home series of the 2026 season.
The Yankees may have already secured their spot in October before their trip to the desert but with a chance at the AL East title still a possibility, along with having Gerrit Cole and the probable AL Cy Young winner in Cam Schlittler taking the bump, this would be no cake walk of a series and the Diamondbacks would need to at least win this series if they want any sliver of hope going into their final 6 games in Colorado and San Diego. With the 25th anniversary of the 2001 World Series winning team being celebrated this series, maybe they would be able to have some of that magic rub off onto this 2026 ballclub and use it as the fuel they need to propel them towards postseason baseball.
Ed-Rough-do Start-Riguez
Eduardo Rodriguez has undoubtedly been the best starter in the Diamondbacks rotation for all of 2026 as he leads the starters in wins (15), ERA (2.89), IP (183.2) and K’s (140), but the issue that has been rearing its head all season for Rodriguez has been his struggles out of the gate and we got more of the same in Friday night’s series opener with the Yankees putting up a 5 spot before the Diamondbacks even had the chance to swing the lumber.
The three of us looked at ERod’s numbers from the 1st inning of his starts compared to the rest of the game and it was as night and day as it could get with his first inning ERA this season sitting at 7.84, a WHIP of 1.77 and an opposing slash of .302/.389/579. From the 2nd inning and beyond he evolves into a completely different pitcher with his 1.89 ERA, 1.12 WHIP and opposing hitter slashing just .222/.279/.326. This isn’t even necessarily just an issue he’s had in 2026 either as his career ERA in the 1st inning (4.51) compared to the rest of his innings (3.92) shows that he’s always had struggles early in games for most of his career.
Cravin for Pavin?
With the demoralizing 9-2 loss on Friday night the Diamondbacks and all snakes fans in attendance would hope that the vibes would be turned around as Saturday would be the big 25th anniversary celebration of the greatest world series of all time (yes I’m biased) with so many legends from that squad like Randy Johnson, Luis Gonzalez, Tony Womack, Miguel Batista, Damien Miller and more in the building for the festivities.
Both the Yankees and Diamondbacks had clutch pitching and hitting at times throughout this game as the score was knotted at 3 a piece going into the bottom of the 9th inning with the Snakes in desperate need of a win to keep their playoff hopes from lowering even further, and that’s when the infamous Pavin Smith stepped in the box as a pinch hitter with a runner on 1st and 1 out. The baseball gods must like reruns because they decided that a Diamondbacks walk-off of the Yankees on the night of the 2001 WS celebration would be the most fitting outcome, and Pavin delivered just that with a 2-R home run into the sea of Yankee fans in right field.
All 3 of us have been very vocal in our frustrations with Smith’s struggles in his career here in the desert and the front office seeming to refuse to move on from a player that has accumulated 0.1 bWAR in his time as a major leaguer, and we all still feel that he should not be on this roster at the beginning of the 2027 season (if we have one that is) in any capacity, but we did admit that it was nice to see Pavin summon his inner Luis Gonzalez and send the fans into a frenzy with a walk-off over the Yankees.
Unc-enado Still Got It
The fireworks might have been after the game on Friday night, but Sunday’s final home game of the 2026 regular season had plenty of leftovers as it felt like baseballs were flying out left and right. Most of them came for the Yankees off of Corbin Burnes in the 4th inning, but the biggest one was in the Diamondbacks favor with Nolan Arenado hitting a go ahead (and potential season saving) grand slam in the 5th inning, his 3rd in 2026 and the 9th of his career.
The fellas and I discussed how nice of a surprise this offensive resurgence has been from Arenado as he is putting up some of the best numbers at the dish we have seen since his MVP caliber season as a Cardinal in 2022 while also pondering the likelihood that Nolan can get to 30 home runs on the season (27 currently) with 3 of the final 6 games being played in his old stomping grounds of Coors Field where Arenado has 139 dingers in his career in the mile high city.
Colorado Cookin
Setting off for the final road trip of the regular season the Snakes will be heading to Coors Field to take on the Colorado Rockies as they continue to battle for their lives in an attempt to make miracles happen and sneak into the playoffs.
The last few weeks have seen us and other fans throw the term “must-win games” around a bunch but these 3 in Colorado are all truly must win games if the Diamondbacks want to have any real chance at making the final series in San Diego mean anything as a Diamondbacks loss+Padres win, 2 D’Backs losses or 2 Padres wins would put the final nail in the coffin of the Diamondbacks playoff hopes.
Gabe, Brandon and I all felt disgusted that we would have to actually root for the Los Angeles Dodgers to win baseball games (just typing that out makes me want to puke) but that is the reality we are in as a Dodgers sweep of the Padres with the Diamondbacks sweeping the Rockies would set us up for what could most likely feel like its own wild card series against the Padres in San Diego to decide who gets in and who goes to Cancun.

title: Why the Yankees can overcome concerning Aaron Judge development in the MLB playoffs
author: Miracle Dimwesh
body:
Aaron Judge’s latest injury has created another major question for the New York Yankees heading into the MLB playoffs.
Judge landed on the 10-day injured list Saturday with a right calf strain after returning from a lengthy absence earlier this month. The Yankees have not provided a timetable for his return, leaving his availability for October unclear.
There is no replacing Judge’s presence in the lineup. Still, New York has one major reason to believe it can survive without its captain: a starting rotation capable of controlling games in October.
Yankees can lean on their starting rotation
The Yankees’ pitching staff has given the team a foundation strong enough to withstand another stretch without Judge.
Cam Schlittler has emerged as the biggest reason for that confidence. The second-year right-hander entered his final regular-season starts with a 14-6 record and a 1.95 ERA, establishing himself as the Yankees’ top postseason pitching option.
Max Fried has also been excellent, carrying a 2.63 ERA through 19 starts. Gerrit Cole has provided another experienced arm with a 3.63 ERA and 123 strikeouts in 21 starts.
Carlos Rodón gives New York another left-handed option. He has also pitched well since returning from his elbow injury, allowing two runs over six innings in his most recent start against Minnesota.
That combination matters in the postseason. If the Yankees can consistently get quality starts, they do not need their offense to produce at the same level every night.
Mark DeRosa sees a path without Judge
MLB Network analyst Mark DeRosa made a similar point when discussing Judge’s injury and the Yankees’ postseason outlook.
“Concern level for Aaron Judge’s injury and the Yankees? Can they overcome it? Yes. They’re built on the strength of their starting rotation,” DeRosa said.
DeRosa also acknowledged the obvious issue. The Yankees need Judge’s presence in the lineup when October arrives, but their pitching gives them another way to win games.
That was already evident during Judge’s earlier absence. He missed more than three months with a rib injury, yet New York still reached the postseason.
The Yankees have already secured a playoff spot, but they still have important games remaining against Tampa Bay. Their final week will help determine their postseason position.
Judge’s return would obviously change the Yankees’ ceiling. But if he cannot make it back in time, New York has something many teams would want in October: multiple starting pitchers capable of taking control of a playoff game.
For the Yankees, that could be the difference between simply surviving Judge’s absence and remaining a serious postseason threat.

title: Justin Verlander is retiring. With a work stoppage on the horizon, how many others might join him? - WINDFM - 92.5 Gainesville 95.5 Ocala
author: Schristian
body:
By NOAH TRISTER AP Baseball Writer
Justin Verlander and Max Scherzer were together on some memorable Detroit teams before moving on and winning championships elsewhere.
Will they eventually enter the Hall of Fame as part of the same class?
The first question is whether both will retire after this season. The 43-year-old Verlander has already announced this is his final year. He’s made only one start in a reunion season with the Tigers, although Detroit fans are hoping he can return for another this coming week.
Scherzer’s future is less clear. The 42-year-old right-hander is slated to start Tuesday at Baltimore as the Blue Jays try to keep their flickering playoff hopes alive, but Scherzer has posted ERAs over 5.00 both this season and last. He’s on a one-year contract with Toronto.
Some other prominent players may also have made — or might be making — their last appearances in the major leagues. Trey Mancini signed a one-day contract to retire with the Orioles and was celebrated this past weekend in Baltimore. Andrew McCutchen and Carlos Santana, both 39, were released last month. Craig Kimbrel, now 38, has pitched for 10 different big league teams in the last six seasons.
Paul Goldschmidt is 39, but his team — the New York Yankees — is heading to the playoffs. And he may be more important than expected if Aaron Judge is out.
With a lockout possible after this season, there could be some retirements we don’t anticipate. Rick Sutcliffe, Bo Jackson and Hall of Famer Goose Gossage, for example, never played again after the 1994 strike but didn’t actually retire until the following year.
Trivia time
Who is the most recent player voted into the Hall of Fame by the BBWAA whose primary team was the Tigers? (The drought is likely to end soon with Miguel Cabrera and then Verlander.)
Performance of the week
Angel Martínez homered from both sides of the plate and had four hits in Cleveland’s 12-6 win over the Athletics on Saturday night. The Guardians have won five straight and are closing in on a postseason spot. They have a one-game lead over the Chicago White Sox atop the AL Central, and it’s another three games back from the White Sox to Toronto and Houston in the race for the last wild card.
In the National League, Philadelphia leads Arizona by four games for the final wild card, so anyone rooting for chaos this coming week may be disappointed.
Comeback of the week
Detroit was down 8-2 in the fifth inning Friday night before scoring nine unanswered runs to win 11-8 over the White Sox. Kevin McGonigle hit a three-run triple, and both Hao-Yu Lee and Riley Greene added two-run homers during the comeback. Detroit’s win probability was down to 3.2% in the fourth inning according to Baseball Savant.
That’s the only game the Tigers have won out of their last five. They’ve been eliminated from the playoff race, the end of a frustrating season in which nothing seemed to go as planned.
Team of the week
The Los Angeles Dodgers and San Diego Padres both went 6-1, with the Dodgers posting the superior run differential. A three-game sweep of San Francisco leaves the Dodgers four games ahead of Atlanta for the second bye in the National League as they try for a third consecutive World Series title.
There are still health concerns for the Dodgers, with Shohei Ohtani on the injured list and Blake Snell having left his last start after one inning.
Los Angeles did get Edwin Diaz back, and he threw scoreless innings on back-to-back days Friday and Saturday.
Trivia answer
Al Kaline, who was inducted in 1980.
George Kell, Hal Newhouser, Jim Bunning, Sparky Anderson, Jack Morris and Alan Trammell have been elected since then with the Tigers as their primary team, but they weren’t voted in by the BBWAA.
