title: Aaron Judge Cuenta Con El Apoyo De Un Miembro Del Salón De La Fama, Mientras Que El Debate Sobre Si Schlittler Es El MVP Divide A Los Yankees
author: Inna Zeyger
body:
NUEVA YORK — La respuesta de Aaron Judge ante los cada vez más sólidos argumentos a favor de Cam Schlittler como MVP ha llamado la atención en las filas de los Yankees. Ahora, un lanzador del Salón de la Fama se ha sumado al debate… y está de acuerdo con Judge.
El exas de los Atlanta Braves, John Smoltz, defendió el razonamiento que hay detrás de los comentarios de Judge durante su aparición en el podcast «Flippin’ Bats» de Ben Verlander, sumando así otra voz destacada a un debate que ha acompañado a Schlittler a lo largo de su dominante mes de septiembre.
«Entiendo lo que dice Aaron», dijo Smoltz.
El capitán de los Yankees desató el debate después de que Schlittler arrollara a los Mets el 13 de septiembre en el Yankee Stadium. Cuando le preguntaron si su compañero merecía ser tenido en cuenta para el premio al Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Americana, el tres veces MVP elogió a Schlittler, pero dejó clara la diferencia entre los dos principales premios individuales de la liga.
«Sin duda está lanzando como un MVP, pero el Premio Cy Young existe por algo: es para el mejor lanzador de la liga», dijo Judge. «Así que tiene mi voto, sin duda, para el Cy Young».
La respuesta llamó la atención porque otros Yankees habían llegado más lejos.
El entrenador de los Yankees, Aaron Boone, dijo que Schlittler «también podría ser el MVP», mientras que Cody Bellinger mencionó la temporada de Clayton Kershaw en 2014, cuando fue nombrado MVP de la Liga Nacional, como prueba de que un lanzador excepcional puede entrar en esa discusión.
Judge no criticó a Schlittler. De hecho, dijo explícitamente que el lanzador diestro estaba lanzando a un nivel digno de un MVP.
Pero su comentario de que el Premio Cy Young existe para reconocer al mejor lanzador del béisbol desató un debate más amplio sobre si los lanzadores deberían ser considerados seriamente para el MVP.
Smoltz explica por qué la postura de Judge le parece lógica
La defensa de Smoltz se centró menos en las estadísticas y más en el papel diferente que desempeña un jugador de campo a lo largo de una temporada.
El miembro del Salón de la Fama argumentó que los lanzadores, por lo general, no pueden liderar un equipo exactamente de la misma manera día a día, ya que los titulares suben al montículo una vez cada cinco días. Smoltz señaló que sus equipos de los Braves eran una excepción porque Greg Maddux, Tom Glavine y él mismo aportaban colectivamente a Atlanta un liderazgo significativo desde la rotación de lanzadores.
Lo que quería decir, en definitiva, es que los equipos campeones suelen necesitar a un jugador de campo que esté presente todos los días y que pueda convertirse en la voz principal de la plantilla.
Esa distinción ayudó a Smoltz a entender por qué el capitán de los Yankees, Judge, podía considerar a Schlittler el mejor lanzador del béisbol sin por ello situarlo necesariamente en lo más alto de una votación para el MVP.
Eso no quiere decir que los lanzadores no puedan ganar el MVP.
Kershaw se llevó tanto el premio Cy Young de la Liga Nacional como el de MVP en 2014 tras terminar con un balance de 21-3 y una efectividad de 1,77. Justin Verlander logró el mismo doblete en la Liga Americana en 2011.
La opinión de Judge, en cambio, parece reflejar una distinción filosófica sobre cómo deberían funcionar ambos premios.
Eso es lo que hace que su respuesta sea especialmente interesante.
Pocos jugadores tienen más autoridad en un debate sobre el MVP que Judge, que ya ha ganado el premio tres veces. Y pocos lanzadores entienden mejor el valor de un abridor de élite que Smoltz, ganador del Cy Young y uno de los lanzadores de postemporada más destacados de su generación.
Schlittler sigue haciendo que el debate sobre el MVP sea difícil de ignorar
Schlittler no ha hecho gran cosa en el montículo para acallar los rumores.
El jugador de 25 años llegó al domingo con un balance de 14-6 y una efectividad de 1,94 —la mejor de la Liga Americana— en 190 2/3 entradas. También tiene un WHIP de 0,91 y 234 ponches, mientras que sus rivales solo le están bateando .184.
Lidera la Liga Americana en ERA e entradas lanzadas, y figura entre los mejores en varias otras categorías importantes de pitcheo.
Incluso la irregular derrota de los Yankees del sábado ante Arizona reforzó en parte sus argumentos.
Schlittler cedió tres carreras en seis entradas, pero solo una fue limpia. Permitió tres hits, dio tres bases por bolas y ponchó a seis, bajando su ERA de 1,95 a 1,94 a pesar de no obtener la decisión en la derrota por 5-3 de Nueva York en la última entrada.
Esta actuación prolongó una racha impresionante en la que los rivales han tenido dificultades para generar una ofensiva significativa contra él.
Esto nos deja con dos cuestiones distintas ahora que la temporada regular llega a su última semana.
La primera es si Schlittler, de los Yankees, ha sido el mejor lanzador de la Liga Americana. Sus estadísticas hacen que cada vez sea más difícil rebatir esa afirmación.
La segunda es si un lanzador que tiene una temporada así debería compararse con los bateadores habituales a la hora de decidir el MVP.
Judge ha dejado bastante clara su postura.
Ahora, Smoltz le ha dado al capitán de los Yankees el apoyo de una de las figuras más destacadas del béisbol en el mundo del pitcheo.
Así que la polémica en torno a Schlittler quizá tenga menos que ver con si su temporada es extraordinaria y más con lo que los votantes creen que debería significar la palabra «valioso».
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

La primera es si Schlittler, de los Yankees, ha sido el mejor lanzador de la Liga Americana. Sus estadísticas hacen que cada vez sea más difícil rebatir esa afirmación.
La segunda es si un lanzador que tiene una temporada así debería compararse con los bateadores habituales a la hora de decidir el MVP.
Judge ha dejado bastante clara su postura.
Ahora, Smoltz le ha dado al capitán de los Yankees el apoyo de una de las figuras más destacadas del béisbol en el mundo del pitcheo.
Así que la polémica en torno a Schlittler quizá tenga menos que ver con si su temporada es extraordinaria y más con lo que los votantes creen que debería significar la palabra «valioso».
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

title: Yankees' three-homer day somehow made the standings uglier
author: Alexander Wilson
body:
The Yankees hit three homers in Arizona on Saturday and still walked away with an 8-4 loss. Heliot Ramos, Spencer Jones and George Lombard Jr. all went deep, which should have been plenty of oxygen for a club trying to chase Tampa Bay.
Instead, Will Warren gave up four earned runs in 4 1/3 innings, John Schreiber gave up two more in the eighth, and the Yankees fell to 89-66. They are six games behind the Rays with a four-game series against Tampa Bay packed into three days starting Tuesday. It is a brutal spot after a game with three home runs on the board.
The Yankees cannot live on solo shots
The frustrating part is not that the Yankees lost a road game in September. It is that they got the type of offensive noise that normally buys a team room to breathe, then gave it all back before the night was over.
Ramos has been a useful part of this group, and Jones brought the kind of power that keeps making the October roster debate complicated. Lombard’s homer was another reminder that the young infield is not going to sit quietly just because the calendar got serious.
None of that changes the larger issue. Three solo shots are not a plan when the pitching staff is handing the other side too many extra chances. The Yankees needed cleaner innings from Warren, and they needed the bullpen to keep the game from turning into a chase.
Tampa Bay is waiting for a mistake
The Rays do not need to make a speech about this series. They have a six-game cushion, while the Yankees have four direct opportunities to cut into it. A six-game gap supplies plenty of urgency on its own.
I am not pretending one series erases everything that came before it. But it can change the temperature fast. A split leaves New York scrambling for help elsewhere, while a big run gives the final week a pulse.
Saturday felt like the kind of game that gets brushed off in July. On September 20, with Tampa Bay next, it landed much harder.
More about:New York Yankees

title: Una Foto De Mickey Mantle Encontrada En Un Mercadillo, Escondida En Un Libro Viejo, Se Convierte En Un Chollo De 20.000 Dólares En Una Subasta
author: Esteban Quiñones
body:
NUEVA YORK — Una de las imágenes más emblemáticas de Mickey Mantle pasó parte de su vida en uno de los lugares menos glamurosos que te puedas imaginar.
Dentro de un libro sobre béisbol en un mercadillo.
Según Heritage Auctions, una pareja que estaba hojeando un libro de gran formato de Topps sobre cromos de béisbol descubrió una foto del joven y legendario jugador de los Yankees metida dentro. En otra foto del libro aparecía Joe DiMaggio.
Lo que al principio parecía un regalo inesperado dentro de un libro de segunda mano acabó teniendo mucho más valor.
La foto de Mantle fue autenticada por PSA/DNA como una impresión de Tipo 2 y se vendió a través de Heritage Auctions por 20 740 dólares el 20 de diciembre de 2025. La insólita historia detrás del hallazgo volvió a ser noticia el lunes en un nuevo reportaje sobre este objeto de colección.
El precio es impresionante.
Los detalles que se esconden en la foto son aún mejores.
La foto muestra a Mantle antes de que los Yankees adoptaran el emblemático número 7
Mantle es casi inseparable del número 7 en la historia de los Yankees.
Pero ese no es el número que se ve en esta foto.
Mantle lleva el número 6, el que lució brevemente al principio de su temporada de novato antes de acabar adoptando el número que le acompañaría hasta el Monument Park.
La imagen muestra a Mantle durante los entrenamientos de primavera, en un momento en el que aún no se había convertido en «The Mick», ni en tres veces MVP, ni en ganador de la Triple Corona, ni en uno de los jugadores más emblemáticos de la historia de los Yankees.
Hay otra pequeña pista que te da una idea de lo antigua que es la foto.
El bate que se ve sobre el hombro derecho de Mantle no era suyo.
Heritage lo identificó como el del primera base de los Yankees, Joe Collins. Según la casa de subastas, Mantle aún no había firmado su propio contrato de bates con Hillerich & Bradsby.
Incluso el uniforme cuenta parte de la historia.
Heritage señaló la manga remangada de Mantle como otro detalle que recuerda que aquel novato de 19 años aún no había alcanzado el prestigio que más tarde le permitiría decidir hasta los más mínimos detalles de su uniforme de los Yankees.
Esos elementos aparentemente insignificantes convierten la fotografía en una instantánea de Mantle antes de que la mitología que le rodeaba se hubiera consolidado del todo.
Una foto de un mercadillo pasó a formar parte de la historia de las tarjetas de béisbol
Su importancia va mucho más allá de mostrar a un Mantle joven.
Esa foto sirvió para crear la tarjeta de novato de Mantle de la colección Bowman de 1951, reconocida oficialmente como su primera edición.
Bowman transformó la fotografía en el aspecto ilustrado tan característico de la tarjeta. También se utilizaron variaciones de la misma imagen en la tarjeta de Mantle de Berk Ross de 1952 y en su tarjeta de Topps de 1953.
Esa conexión hace que la foto esté directamente relacionada con una de las piezas más importantes de la historia de las tarjetas de béisbol de la posguerra.
La Bowman de 1951 suele quedar a la sombra de la famosa tarjeta Topps de Mantle de 1952, pero la Bowman fue la primera. Muestra a la futura superestrella de los Yankees en la postura de bateo capturada por la fotografía que, de alguna manera, acabó más tarde dentro de ese libro de un mercadillo.
La foto que se encontró no estaba en perfecto estado.
Heritage informó de desgaste en la superficie, grietas horizontales en el acabado brillante, zonas en las que faltaba papel alrededor del borde blanco y un pequeño desgarro a lo largo del lado derecho.
Además, alguien había escrito «Mickey Mantle» en el reverso.
Nada de eso impidió que la fotografía de Tipo 2 alcanzara un precio de cinco cifras cuando salió a subasta.
Otra versión demuestra lo valiosa que puede llegar a ser esta imagen
El resultado de 20 740 dólares ni siquiera representa el límite superior del mercado para esta imagen concreta de Mantle.
Una versión de primera generación del Tipo 1, procedente de la colección del exlanzador de los Yankees Jack Kramer, se vendió a través de Heritage por la extraordinaria cifra de 843 750 dólares el 7 de abril de 2024.
Esa foto la hizo Bob Olen, el fotógrafo oficial de los Yankees , y había estado guardada entre los recuerdos de Kramer durante décadas.
Heritage afirmó que, en el momento de la subasta, PSA solo tenía constancia de cuatro ejemplares originales de la famosa imagen. La venta por 843.750 dólares estableció lo que Heritage describió como un récord para una fotografía deportiva de Tipo 1.
La enorme diferencia entre ambos precios refleja una distinción importante para los coleccionistas.
La foto de la venta de garaje recibió la designación de Tipo 2, en lugar de la clasificación de Tipo 1, más valiosa, que se otorga a una foto original de primera generación producida poco después de que se tomara la imagen.
Sin embargo, su relación con la tarjeta de novato de Mantle seguía siendo innegable.
Eso es, en definitiva, lo que hace que la historia de la venta de garaje sea tan extraordinaria.
Los coleccionistas se gastan fortunas buscando piezas relacionadas con Mantle. Sus cromos, uniformes, bates y fotos suelen alcanzar precios astronómicos.
Esta pieza en concreto no salió de una colección famosa ni de una caja fuerte sofisticada.
Estaba dentro de un libro de béisbol en una venta de garaje.
Y escondida entre esas páginas había una foto de un Yankee adolescente con el número 6, que había cogido prestado el bate de Joe Collins y se encontraba justo antes de comenzar una de las carreras más célebres de la historia del béisbol.

title: Yankees rooting for front office exec who lived out lifelong ‘Survivor’ dream
author: Gary Phillips
body:
For the last several months, Brian Cashman has kept a close eye on his assistant director of baseball operations. Any lavish purchase — a luxury car, a swanky penthouse, fancy new clothes — would be an indication that Mike Pinsky had come into life-changing money, the Yankees’ general manager figured.
“If he’s driving a Lamborghini, then I know he won,” Cashman said, referring to Pinsky’s casting on Season 51 of “Survivor.”
The 33-year-old will make his debut on the CBS reality show on Wednesday. It is a “lifelong dream” come true for Pinsky, who grew up a superfan of the franchise before traveling to Fiji’s Mamanuca Islands to film between April and May this year.
“I spend all day, every day, sort of evaluating players from the comfort of a stadium seat or my desk chair, and inside of me is this burning passion to actually be the one competing myself,” said Pinsky, who began watching “Survivor” when he was 8, created his own version of the game with his friends, and even worked one of the show’s catchphrases into his marriage proposal. “I long to actually be the one playing the game, and so this was a really interesting opportunity to actually get to be the player instead of the evaluator, and actually see what I’m made of.”
Pinsky added that he brought the Yankees’ championship-or-bust mindset with him to Fiji.
“Anytime you’re playing a game, anytime you’re competing, you play to win,” he said. “So I don’t do anything for second place.”
As per his agreement with CBS, Pinsky could not disclose how he fared on the show, or much of anything that happened during filming. That has not stopped Cashman and the rest of the Yankees’ baseball ops department from trying to find out, though.
“We’ve been peppering him and teasing him and trying to steal information,” Cashman said. “He’s like Fort Knox.”
Pinsky did say that Cashman, Yankees owner Hal Steinbrenner and the rest of his colleagues were “incredibly gracious” and supportive of him being on the show.
Filming required Pinsky to be away from the Yankees and cut off from the outside world for an unspecified period of time at the beginning of the season, so he needed permission to leave his job. Luckily for him, that “was probably the most opportune time,” Cashman said, as Pinsky is not involved in draft operations, and teams typically don’t make major moves during that early in the season.
Pinsky was also fortunate that Cashman is a proponent of chasing one’s dreams and leaping at unique opportunities.
“Ultimately, life is too short, and we gotta live it to the max. Literally, just live every day as if it’s your last day. Don’t put things off if you have a chance to do something special,” said Cashman, who has repelled skyscrapers, swam with sharks and jumped out of a plane. “We all should be living our lives to the best of our abilities and challenging ourselves on a daily basis so there’s no regrets on the back end.”
Plus, with Pinsky fighting just 20 other contestants for “Survivor’s” $1 million grand prize, Cashman couldn’t deny him those odds.
“He would have a 1-in-21 chance of winning that, which is a hell of a lot better than when you’re playing Powerball and Mega Millions,” Cashman said.
Understanding how much this could mean to Pinsky on multiple levels, Cashman took the conversation to Steinbrenner. He signed off before Pinsky was officially cast on the show.
Pinsky, who also applied to be on Season 49, then kept the Yankees updated as he advanced through the casting process. As he got closer to the final cut, he and his superiors laid out a plan for how the front office would manage his absence.
“It was an extremely strange experience missing parts of the year,” Pinsky said.

title: Aaron Judge injury explained: What is Yankees star facing? Surgeon talks possible return, risk
author: Randy Miller
body:
NEW YORK — The Yankees surely were in a somber mood during Sunday night's cross-country flight from Phoenix to New York. The AL East race is all but over and Aaron Judge is hurt again, this time potentially for the season.
The Diamondbacks prevailed 5-3 on Saturday night and 8-4 on Sunday afternoon, costing the Yankees two more games in the standings and leaving them six games behind with seven games remaining in the regular season.
Following Monday's off day, the first-place Rays will be in the Bronx for four games in three days at Yankee Stadium, which will probably lead to champagne corks popping in the visiting clubhouse. The Rays need just one win to clinch the AL East.
At this point, the Yankees will inevitably face the Red Sox a week from Tuesday in Game 1 of a Wild Card Series.
The mystery is whether Judge will be back for this best-of-three.
Here's what we know:
1. The three-time MVP is back on the injured list with a right calf strain less than two weeks after returning from a fractured rib that sidelined him for 88 games.
2. The strain is in the soleus muscle.
3. He's eligible to be activated for next Sunday's regular-season finale, game 162.
How bad is it? What did the MRI reveal?
As usual, the Yankees and Judge have remained guarded/secretive about revealing his injury and rehab details.
"It doesn't matter what the grade is," manager Aaron Boone said last Friday in Phoenix. "We're going to get him back or we're not. That's what we're going to work to do and we'll see.''
Judge basically said the same thing to Yankees media on Saturday, while adding, "I'd like to be back for the playoffs. That's definitely the plan."
What can we unpack from what little we know?
NJ.com consulted with an NYU Langone Health sports orthopedic surgeon to provide a clearer picture of what Judge is facing without knowing if the strain is a Grade 1 (mild), Grade 2 (moderate partial tear) or Grade 3 (severe complete rupture).
"If it's a Grade 1, in two weeks you could see Judge doing baseball activities again and then three weeks back playing," Dr. Spencer Stein said. "It's a calf muscle strain and they're annoying injuries."
Judge was injured during last Wednesday's game in Minnesota, so three weeks would be Oct. 7. If the Yankees win their Wild Card Series, that would be Game 3 of their best-of-five Division Series with the Rays.
"But that's really best-case scenario," Dr. Stein said. "That would be the fastest."
Yankees designated hitter Giancarlo Stanton went on the IL in April with a Grade 1 calf strain and still hasn't returned. He had a setback in June, and then while rehabbing, he strained his other calf in August.
If Judge rushes back, he'd also be risking a setback, the doctor warned.
"I've seen studies there's up to 50% chance of re-injury in these muscular injuries — hamstring injuries, calf muscle injuries," Dr. Stein said. "There's a high rate of retear, so it's definitely a balance of not going back too quickly on them."
Rushing back might be why Judge is hurt again. When he was out with his rib injury, he was shut down from baseball activities from June 1 until Aug. 19. Less than three weeks later, Judge was back from the IL and playing right field for the Yankees with no rehab games and a few live batting-practice at-bats packed into a workout the day before his first game back.
"Well, I would say that there should always be a stepwise return to sports where you build things up and that takes time," Dr. Stein said. "When you're under a time constraint because it's end of season and the playoffs are around the corner, sometimes you have to take a risk and go a little faster. But with a risk, you can end up with another injury."
The location of his calf strain is problematic.
"The gastrocnemius, plantaris and soleus muscles comprise the calf, and the soleus muscle is a push-off muscle and part of the Achilles tendon," Dr. Stein said. "There's just a lot of force in that area, a lot of strain and stress, especially when you're swinging a baseball bat."
If Judge returns, he'd be much better off DHing instead of playing right field, Dr. Stein added.
"No question," he said. "The soleus muscle constantly is engaged during simple standing and walking."
That's another risk the Yankees would have to take.
Judge would have to play right field rather than be the designated hitter. Ben Rice, who has 39 home runs and 95 RBI, is entrenched at DH, while Luis Garcia Jr. and Paul Goldschmidt form a potent first base first-base platoon
Here is Dr. Stein's advice for Judge:
"Follow the instructions and take it day-by-day. Work with the therapists and trainers. Make sure your strength is there. You don't want to rush it too much. You don't want a long-term injury that keeps happening.
"You want to be able to come back, and we get that, but you do want to meet the criteria: Good strength with a good amount of flexibility in the knee and ankle area."

title: Yankees playoff roster prediction: Who makes the cut with division dreams dwindling ahead of Rays series?
author: Gary Phillips
body:
Shortly after getting walked-off by the Diamondbacks on Saturday night, the Yankees acknowledged their reality.
“Mathematically, [it’s] probably pretty tough, but you never know,” Cody Bellinger said of winning the American League East.
Unable to bounce back with an 8-4 loss in Sunday’s series finale against Arizona, the second-place Yankees are now six games back of the division-leading Rays with seven games left in the regular season. The rivals will play four of those games against each other at Yankee Stadium this week, starting with a doubleheader on Tuesday.
Aaron Boone acknowledged that his team will probably have to sweep the Rays just for a crack at the division crown, as FanGraphs gave the Yankees a measly 2.7% chance of winning the AL East before Sunday’s game.
“There’s still a chance,” Cam Schlittler said, “but we gotta play our asses off a little bit.”
While the Yankees still technically have a shot to defy the odds, the far likelier scenario is that their postseason begins on Sept. 29 at home against Boston in the Wild Card round for the second straight year.
With that in mind, let’s try to predict what the club’s roster could look like for that series.
Hitters (15): Ben Rice, Heliot Ramos, Spencer Jones, Trent Grisham, Cody Bellinger, Ryan McMahon, George Lombard Jr., Paul Goldschmidt, Luis García Jr., Jazz Chisholm Jr., José Caballero, Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez, Anthony Volpe, Amed Rosario
With the Yankees providing minimal info on Aaron Judge’s calf strain, it can’t be assumed he’ll be available.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. could return from a sprained thumb as soon as Tuesday. Meanwhile, Trent Grisham is still in play as a playoff option as he recovers from a hamstring strain, but Boone said that activating him before the end of the regular season is “complicated,” partly due to roster logistics.
With Max Schuemann presumably the corresponding move for Chisholm, the Yankees would have to option someone else if they activated Grisham before the playoffs. That someone wouldn’t be able to be recalled for 10 days barring a new injury; it seems like Jasson Domínguez is being protected from that window in case he’s needed for the Wild Card roster.
Grisham has been doing baseball activities and is “pretty deep into his running progression,” Boone said. If he is on the Wild Card roster, the Yankees will have an interesting decision to make between him and Spencer Jones in center field.
Third base could also be a conundrum, as Ryan McMahon and José Caballero don’t offer much offensively, and Amed Rosario is a poor defender. He’s only on the roster as an option against lefties, even though he hasn’t been great against them.
Another idea would be to use Volpe, who has been playing second, at third against lefties since he played a few games there in the minors this season. However, he doesn’t have a strong arm, and he hasn’t been working at third base since being recalled. Volpe said that the Yankees have not talked to him about manning the hot corner before the regular season ends.
“We’ll see,” Boone said. “First things first, getting Jazz back, and then we’ll figure out as the week unfolds how I want to play it.”
Volpe can also play second over Chisholm against lefties.

title: Boone Retira Su Controvertida Declaración Sobre Los Yankees Tras La Fea Derrota Ante Arizona Y Lanza Una Advertencia A Los Rays
author: Inna Zeyger
body:
PHOENIX — Los Yankees se fueron del Chase Field con el tipo de derrota que cambia el panorama de la última semana.
El domingo, Nueva York tuvo a Corbin Burnes contra las cuerdas, remontó un déficit inicial y se puso con una ventaja de 4-1 gracias a tres jonrones en la tercera entrada. Heliot Ramos empató el partido con un jonrón solitario. George Lombard Jr. sumó un jonrón de dos carreras, y Spencer Jones conectó otro justo después de él. Burnes se fue del partido tras 2 2/3 entradas.
La ventaja inicial no duró mucho. Will Warren llenó las bases con un out en la quinta entrada, y el bullpen de los Yankees no pudo evitar que Arizona le diera la vuelta al partido. Brent Headrick ponchó a Geraldo Perdomo y luego concedió una base por bolas a Corbin Carroll con las bases llenas. Nolan Arenado siguió con un grand slam ante una bola rápida de cuatro costuras a 94,2 mph, dando la vuelta a un marcador de 4-2 y poniendo a los Diamondbacks por delante 6-4. Arizona sumó dos carreras más en la séptima y ganó 8-4.
Los Yankees perdieron dos de tres partidos en Arizona y ahora tienen un balance de 89-66. Tampa Bay mejoró su balance a 95-60, lo que deja a Nueva York a seis partidos de distancia en la División Este de la Liga Americana, cuando quedan siete partidos por disputar. Los Rays llegan al Yankee Stadium para una serie de cuatro partidos que empieza el martes con una doble jornada dividida. Una sola victoria de Tampa Bay en la serie dejaría a los Yankees fuera de la lucha por el título de la división.
Ese contexto hizo que las declaraciones del entrenador tras el partido tuvieran más peso que un simple intento de pasar página. Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero el club tiene que encontrar el equilibrio entre una lucha por el título de división que se va desvaneciendo y proteger a un cuerpo de lanzadores muy castigado, además de preparar una plantilla plagada de lesiones para octubre.
La afirmación de Boone choca con la clasificación
A Aaron Boone le preguntaron cómo se enfrentarían los Yankees a Tampa Bay y si el hecho de que la lucha por el título de división se esté desvaneciendo podría cambiar su forma de gestionar los minutos de juego. Su respuesta incluyó una amplia defensa de cómo ha respondido su equipo durante una temporada llena de lesiones y una importante racha negativa este verano.
«Y hemos estado a la altura en casi todas las ocasiones», dijo Boone.
Esa es la parte que llama la atención del mensaje de Boone. Aaron Judge estuvo más de tres meses de baja por una lesión en las costillas, volvió el 8 de septiembre y luego volvió a entrar en la lista de lesionados por una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha. Además, Nueva York sufrió una racha de siete derrotas seguidas durante un tramo de 4 victorias y 14 derrotas, antes de recuperarse y asegurarse una plaza en la postemporada.
El final del partido en Arizona fue el contrapunto. Los Yankees llegaron a la quinta entrada con una ventaja de tres carreras y la terminaron perdiendo por dos. No anotaron nada después de la tercera y encadenaron dos derrotas seguidas tras ganar el primer partido del viernes por 9-2.
Las cifras cuentan dos historias diferentes sobre los Yankees
La clasificación de la MLB a fecha de 21 de septiembre muestra por qué Boone puede hablar de una temporada sólida, mientras que la tabla de la División Este de la Liga Americana presenta un panorama más sombrío.
Los Yankees han marcado 137 carreras más que sus rivales, frente a la diferencia de +83 de Tampa Bay. Según las previsiones de la MLB, Nueva York debería tener un balance de 92-63, tres victorias más que su balance real. Sin embargo, los Rays llevan una ventaja de seis partidos.
Nueva York tiene un balance de 33-32 contra equipos con un porcentaje de victorias igual o superior al 50 %. Tampa Bay tiene un balance de 37-25 en esos partidos. La capacidad de los Yankees para anotar y evitar carreras sugiere que son un equipo más fuerte de lo que indica su segunda posición en la clasificación, pero los Rays han sabido convertir los partidos difíciles en victorias con mayor consistencia.
Ese contraste es lo que le da tensión a la afirmación de Boone. Los Yankees se han recuperado de rachas perjudiciales, pero no con la frecuencia suficiente como para controlar la división de cara a la última semana.
Boone lanza un mensaje contundente a los Rays
Boone también dejó claro que no ve el martes como una puesta a punto inmediata de cara a la postemporada. Dijo que las decisiones sobre el descanso pueden dejarse para más adelante, una vez que los Yankees se enfrenten por primera vez al equipo al que llevan meses persiguiendo.
«Pero lo primero es lo primero: el martes vamos a salir al campo e intentar darles una buena paliza. Así de sencillo. Y lo mantendremos así de sencillo», dijo Boone.
A Tampa Bay le falta una victoria contra los Yankees para asegurarse el título de la División Este de la Liga Americana. Nueva York tiene que ganar los cuatro partidos para mantener vivas sus opciones de cara al último fin de semana.
Eso hace que Boone tenga que gestionar dos frentes a la vez. A los Yankees aún les queda una posibilidad matemática de ganar la división, pero la plantilla para la postemporada, la carga de trabajo del bullpen y los jugadores lesionados se están convirtiendo en las preocupaciones más prácticas de octubre. Nueva York también empieza la semana ocupando el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana.
La carga de trabajo de Headrick añade urgencia a la decisión de Boone
La 79.ª salida de Headrick el domingo fue la segunda más alta de las Grandes Ligas. La velocidad media de su bola rápida fue inferior a la de esta temporada, aunque él lo achacó a la ejecución más que al cansancio.
Los Yankees han confiado en Headrick durante toda la temporada. El domingo quedó claro lo rápido que esa fortaleza puede convertirse en un motivo de preocupación en octubre. Se encontró con las bases llenas, estuvo a un out de salir del apuro, pero luego concedió la base por bolas y encajó el golpe decisivo de Arenado.
Boone dijo tras la derrota que el descanso podría formar parte del plan una vez que se decida el campeón de la división. Eso podría pasar ya el martes.
Hasta entonces, su postura pública está clara. Los Yankees no van a ceder la serie ante Tampa Bay, ni siquiera después de que el colapso de Arizona haya dejado la clasificación prácticamente decidida. La gran afirmación de Boone es ahora lo que los Yankees deben demostrar en el campo: tras decir que han sabido hacer frente a la adversidad en casi todas las ocasiones, su próxima prueba llega con los Rays en posición de celebrar la victoria en el Yankee Stadium.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

Tampa Bay mejoró su balance a 95-60, lo que deja a Nueva York a seis partidos de distancia en la División Este de la Liga Americana, cuando quedan siete partidos por disputar. Los Rays llegan al Yankee Stadium para una serie de cuatro partidos que empieza el martes con una doble jornada dividida. Una sola victoria de Tampa Bay en la serie dejaría a los Yankees fuera de la lucha por el título de la división.
Ese contexto hizo que las declaraciones del entrenador tras el partido tuvieran más peso que un simple intento de pasar página. Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero el club tiene que encontrar el equilibrio entre una lucha por el título de división que se va desvaneciendo y proteger a un cuerpo de lanzadores muy castigado, además de preparar una plantilla plagada de lesiones para octubre.
La afirmación de Boone choca con la clasificación
A Aaron Boone le preguntaron cómo se enfrentarían los Yankees a Tampa Bay y si el hecho de que la lucha por el título de división se esté desvaneciendo podría cambiar su forma de gestionar los minutos de juego. Su respuesta incluyó una amplia defensa de cómo ha respondido su equipo durante una temporada llena de lesiones y una importante racha negativa este verano.
«Y hemos estado a la altura en casi todas las ocasiones», dijo Boone.
Esa es la parte que llama la atención del mensaje de Boone. Aaron Judge estuvo más de tres meses de baja por una lesión en las costillas, volvió el 8 de septiembre y luego volvió a entrar en la lista de lesionados por una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha. Además, Nueva York sufrió una racha de siete derrotas seguidas durante un tramo de 4 victorias y 14 derrotas, antes de recuperarse y asegurarse una plaza en la postemporada.
El final del partido en Arizona fue el contrapunto. Los Yankees llegaron a la quinta entrada con una ventaja de tres carreras y la terminaron perdiendo por dos. No anotaron nada después de la tercera y encadenaron dos derrotas seguidas tras ganar el primer partido del viernes por 9-2.
Las cifras cuentan dos historias diferentes sobre los Yankees
La clasificación de la MLB a fecha de 21 de septiembre muestra por qué Boone puede hablar de una temporada sólida, mientras que la tabla de la División Este de la Liga Americana presenta un panorama más sombrío.
Los Yankees han marcado 137 carreras más que sus rivales, frente a la diferencia de +83 de Tampa Bay. Según las previsiones de la MLB, Nueva York debería tener un balance de 92-63, tres victorias más que su balance real. Sin embargo, los Rays llevan una ventaja de seis partidos.
Nueva York tiene un balance de 33-32 contra equipos con un porcentaje de victorias igual o superior al 50 %. Tampa Bay tiene un balance de 37-25 en esos partidos. La capacidad de los Yankees para anotar y evitar carreras sugiere que son un equipo más fuerte de lo que indica su segunda posición en la clasificación, pero los Rays han sabido convertir los partidos difíciles en victorias con mayor consistencia.
Ese contraste es lo que le da tensión a la afirmación de Boone. Los Yankees se han recuperado de rachas perjudiciales, pero no con la frecuencia suficiente como para controlar la división de cara a la última semana.
Boone lanza un mensaje contundente a los Rays
Boone también dejó claro que no ve el martes como una puesta a punto inmediata de cara a la postemporada. Dijo que las decisiones sobre el descanso pueden dejarse para más adelante, una vez que los Yankees se enfrenten por primera vez al equipo al que llevan meses persiguiendo.
«Pero lo primero es lo primero: el martes vamos a salir al campo e intentar darles una buena paliza. Así de sencillo. Y lo mantendremos así de sencillo», dijo Boone.
A Tampa Bay le falta una victoria contra los Yankees para asegurarse el título de la División Este de la Liga Americana. Nueva York tiene que ganar los cuatro partidos para mantener vivas sus opciones de cara al último fin de semana.
Eso hace que Boone tenga que gestionar dos frentes a la vez. A los Yankees aún les queda una posibilidad matemática de ganar la división, pero la plantilla para la postemporada, la carga de trabajo del bullpen y los jugadores lesionados se están convirtiendo en las preocupaciones más prácticas de octubre. Nueva York también empieza la semana ocupando el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana.
La carga de trabajo de Headrick añade urgencia a la decisión de Boone
La 79.ª salida de Headrick el domingo fue la segunda más alta de las Grandes Ligas. La velocidad media de su bola rápida fue inferior a la de esta temporada, aunque él lo achacó a la ejecución más que al cansancio.
Los Yankees han confiado en Headrick durante toda la temporada. El domingo quedó claro lo rápido que esa fortaleza puede convertirse en un motivo de preocupación en octubre. Se encontró con las bases llenas, estuvo a un out de salir del apuro, pero luego concedió la base por bolas y encajó el golpe decisivo de Arenado.
Boone dijo tras la derrota que el descanso podría formar parte del plan una vez que se decida el campeón de la división. Eso podría pasar ya el martes.
Hasta entonces, su postura pública está clara. Los Yankees no van a ceder la serie ante Tampa Bay, ni siquiera después de que el colapso de Arizona haya dejado la clasificación prácticamente decidida. La gran afirmación de Boone es ahora lo que los Yankees deben demostrar en el campo: tras decir que han sabido hacer frente a la adversidad en casi todas las ocasiones, su próxima prueba llega con los Rays en posición de celebrar la victoria en el Yankee Stadium.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

title: Yankees’ Aaron Boone Drops Honest Take After Loss to Diamondbacks
author: Keith Watkins
body:
The New York Yankees led 4-1 after three innings on Sunday in Arizona. Three home runs off Corbin Burnes had knocked the Diamondbacks starter out of the game and given the lineup exactly the kind of start it needed.
None of it held. A five-run fifth inning turned a comfortable lead into a deficit, and the Yankees fell 8-4 at Chase Field to drop two of three in the series. New York is 89-66 and now sits six games behind the Rays in the American League East with seven to play.
After the game, manager Aaron Boone met with the media and offered an honest assessment of how it all fell apart.
Boone on Warren’s Start
Will Warren carried a 4-1 lead into the fifth inning before things unraveled. Warren allowed three consecutive baserunners in the fifth, loading the bases with one out, and Boone pulled him for Brent Headrick.
Boone’s evaluation was measured. He saw a pitcher whose stuff was there but whose command slipped at the wrong time.
“Early on he was in the strike zone really well and getting a lot of first pitch strikes ahead,” Boone said. “His stuff was again good. I feel like it’s been in a good place for the last three or four weeks now, but just started falling behind a little bit there in the latter part of the game.”
Warren had retired hitters efficiently through four innings, but back-to-back frames in which he fell behind multiple hitters proved costly. The stuff did not abandon him. The execution did.
The Offense Went Quiet
The Yankees scored all four of their runs in the third inning. Spencer Jones, Heliot Ramos, and George Lombard Jr. all connected off Burnes to build what felt like a comfortable lead.
After that, nothing. The Diamondbacks’ bullpen shut the door, and the lineup could not find a way to respond after the fifth-inning collapse.
“They’ve got a good relief corps. Obviously a lot of big arms,” Boone said. “I thought we had some decent at-bats along the way, but just obviously weren’t able to build on the lead or crawl our way back in.”
A Late Concern Emerges for the Yankees
Boone also provided an update on Clarke Schmidt at the end of his postgame session.
“He felt some cramping in his bicep when he was warming up, so obviously he didn’t want to take any chances there,” Boone said. “He checked out pretty well afterwards and all the strength tests. And so I’m hoping it’s not a big deal. But enough to have him not go into the game.”
Final Word for the Yankees
The Yankees blew a three-run lead and dropped a series they needed. The division is slipping away. The bullpen showed cracks on a day where the workload caught up with one of its most reliable arms.
Boone was honest about all of it. Warren’s stuff was good but the execution faltered. The offense disappeared after the third inning.
The Rays come to the Bronx on Tuesday for a doubleheader. The margin for error is gone.

title: Why Rushing Aaron Judge Back Isn't Worth It for the Yankees
author: Joe Najarian; Unknown
body:
Despite landing on the injured list, Aaron Judge is still eager to contribute to the Yankees in the postseason.
Judge, who chose to forgo a rehab assignment in favor of rejoining the team earlier in the month, told the media that he wanted to recover from his right calf strain by the start of postseason play. The American League Wild Card Series, which the Yankees would play in if the season ended today, is slated to begin on Sept. 29, just 10 days from now.
On Saturday, Judge offered a simple "we'll see" when asked if he'd be back in time for the playoff action (h/t Brendan Kuty).
So if Judge were to return before then, his stay on the injured list would effectively last a minimum of 10 days. Unfortunately, it's highly unlikely that he fully recovers by then—and from a team perspective, it's not worth it for the Yankees to rush him back.
The Yankees' best lineup needs Judge in the outfield
Judge's injury will effectively prevent him from playing in right field and limit him to designated hitter duties. However, the Yankees' best lineup needs him playing in right field, as sticking him at DH with the roster currently constructed will force another one of the team's best hitters onto the bench.
After spending the first half of the season as the Yankees' starting first baseman, Ben Rice became the everyday DH when the team traded for Luis Garcia Jr., who subsequently took over at first. Garcia plays much better defense at first than Rice does, but Rice has been more productive overall (h/t Yankees) at the plate.
Regardless, both are among the Yankees' best hitters and will be integral to their postseason run.
By having Judge at DH, either Garcia or Rice would come out of the lineup. If Rice is playing first, the Yankees lose access to Garcia's strong glove at the position as well as a threat for extra bases in the heart of the order. If Garcia is at first, the team loses access to Rice's elite power and outstanding poise in clutch situations.
If one of them is called upon to pinch-hit at any point, then one will take over for the other for the rest of the game.
Having Judge in right field instead of the DH spot allows the Yankees to play both Garcia and Rice. But putting Judge in the field with a bad calf is a recipe for disaster.
The Yankees can't afford a career-altering injury to Judge
Calf strains are notorious for being easy to re-injure; look no further than Giancarlo Stanton, who essentially missed the entire season due to calf strains in both legs, including a re-injury to the original strain when rehabbing.
The calf also leads into the Achilles tendon, which becomes vulnerable to tears if the calf is already injured. Achilles tears are not only season-ending in any sport, but the long-term effects are devastating. In a baseball example, former Phillies first baseman Ryan Howard was one of the game's premier sluggers before an Achilles tear during the 2011 postseason, and he was never the same hitter after.
The Yankees don't want that for Judge, and neither does he (h/t Gary Phillips).
If Judge were to reaggravate the calf or tear his Achilles, he risks missing even more time during the 2027 season. The Yankees already saw how dramatically the offense struggles when he's out long-term, and they simply can't risk that happening again next year, especially for a player approaching his mid-30s. Neither Judge nor the Yankees even know the grade of the calf strain right now, which is further reason not to chance anything and shut him down.
Obviously, Judge still wants to play during the postseason because that's when the games matter the most. But given the nature of his injury—which is to the soleus muscle, a crucial part of his ability to hit and run—playing through it isn't an option.
The only option is for the rest of the team to step up in Judge's absence and make a deep postseason run, and perhaps the Yankees can get their captain back if he's feeling 100% by the AL Championship Series or World Series.
Joe Najarian is a writer for Yankees On SI, having previously covered the Yankees both for SI and additional sites since 2023. He also served as Deputy Editor for the Yankees, Mets and Orioles On SI sites, and additionally contributes to Athlon Sports and Men’s Journal covering Major League Baseball and other trending sports news. Joe is a graduate of Rutgers University in 2022, earning a bachelor’s degree in Journalism and Media Studies.

title: Los Yankees Desperdician El Espectáculo De Poderío De Sus Novatos Al Ver Cómo Una Ventaja De 4-1 Se Convierte En Una Costosa Derrota Por 8-4
author: Esteban Quiñones
body:
PHOENIX — Una sola entrada convirtió una serie fuera de casa que los Yankees parecían dispuestos a salvar en una derrota que les acompañó hasta su regreso al Bronx.
El domingo, en el Chase Field, Nueva York llegaba a la parte baja de la quinta con una ventaja de tres carreras. Para cuando terminó la entrada, Nolan Arenado ya había dado la vuelta a las bases, Arizona había anotado cinco veces y los Yankees se habían quedado atrás para siempre, acabando por perder 8-4 ante los Diamondbacks.
Con esta derrota, los Yankees quedan con un balance de 89-66 y a seis partidos de los Tampa Bay Rays, cuando solo quedan siete partidos por jugar. Además, esto puso fin a una gira por Arizona con un balance de 1-2, después de que Nueva York empezara la serie con una victoria por 9-2 y luego perdiera dos veces en partidos que se decidieron en los últimos compases.
Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada y siguen ocupando el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana. Pero la última semana tiene ahora un carácter de urgencia diferente. Tampa Bay puede hacerse con el título de la División Este de la Liga Americana con una sola victoria en la serie de cuatro partidos que empieza el martes en el Yankee Stadium.
El domingo también se prolongó el drástico cambio de rumbo tras el partido inaugural del viernes. El sábado terminó con un jonrón decisivo de Pavin Smith contra Michael Fulmer. El último partido trajo consigo otro fallo del bullpen, pero el mismo perjuicio en la clasificación.
Una entrada de cuatro carreras debería haber cambiado el rumbo de la tarde
Arizona se adelantó en el marcador gracias a un sencillo impulsador de Geraldo Perdomo en la primera entrada. A partir de ahí, Will Warren se asentó en el montículo, impidiendo que los Diamondbacks ampliaran su ventaja hasta la cuarta entrada y dando tiempo a la alineación para atacar a Corbin Burnes.
Ese ataque llegó de repente en la tercera entrada.
Heliot Ramos empató el partido con su decimotercer jonrón. George Lombard Jr. le siguió más adelante en la entrada con un jonrón de dos carreras, el quinto de la temporada.
El batazo de Lombard recorrió, según las estimaciones de Statcast, 424 pies, el jonrón más largo de su carrera en las Grandes Ligas.
Spencer Jones conectó un jonrón justo después, su undécimo. A continuación, lanzó una bola que se calculó que recorrió 448 pies. Los dos jonrones de los novatos sumaron un total de 872 pies.
Los Yankees habían pasado de ir perdiendo 1-0 a ponerse 4-1 por delante y habían obligado a Burnes a abandonar el partido tras solo 2 2/3 entradas. Parecía el tipo de remontada de los jóvenes que podría sacar adelante a una alineación en la que faltaban los titulares lesionados.
En cambio, esas cuatro carreras fueron toda la producción ofensiva de los Yankees.
Diecinueve outs demuestran lo mucho que ha dado un giro el partido
Cinco relevos de los Diamondbacks sumaron entre todos 6 1/3 entradas sin encajar carreras tras la salida de Burnes. Los Yankees solo consiguieron tres hits contra ese grupo y no anotaron en las últimas 19 eliminaciones.
Justin Martínez lanzó una quinta entrada sin permitir carreras y se llevó la victoria, mejorando su balance a 3-0. Brent Headrick cargó con la derrota, quedando con un balance de 7-4. No se concedió ningún salvamento.
Los Yankees terminaron el día con 216 jonrones, liderando la Liga Americana, pero su poderío no pudo compensar el colapso que vino después.
Warren y Headrick pierden el quinto
Warren llegó a la quinta entrada defendiendo la ventaja de 4-1. Lars Nootbaar conectó un doble, Ketel Marte un sencillo y Gabriel Moreno recibió una base por bolas, llenando las bases con un out. Aaron Boone recurrió a Brent Headrick, uno de los lanzadores del bullpen más utilizados por los Yankees.
Headrick ponchó a Perdomo y luego concedió una base por bolas a Corbin Carroll con las bases llenas, dejando el marcador en 4-2. Arenado mandó una bola rápida justo fuera por la línea del jardín izquierdo antes de conectar con fuerza el siguiente lanzamiento para un grand slam, dando a Arizona una ventaja de 6-4.
Headrick disputaba su 79.ª salida, la segunda cifra más alta de las Grandes Ligas, y, según se informó, la velocidad media de su bola rápida estaba aproximadamente 1,3 mph por debajo de su media de la temporada.
Headrick dijo que el problema era la precisión, no el cansancio.
«Me sentí bien, pero me faltó precisión y me quedé atrás respecto a los bateadores», dijo Headrick.
Warren se fue del partido con cuatro carreras encajadas, seis hits y tres bases por bolas en 4 1/3 entradas. Boone ha dicho que Warren hará una salida más como titular en la temporada regular contra Baltimore antes de pasar al bullpen en octubre.
Warren apoyó al relevo que se hizo cargo de la situación complicada que él había dejado.
«Nos ha dado un montón de problemas todo el año», dijo Warren. «Es un rollo, pero está claro que contamos con él, y nos ha ido muy bien con él todo el año, y va a seguir haciéndolo bien».
Arizona sigue sumando mientras el bullpen de los Yankees flaquea
Perdomo impulsó una carrera con un triple ante John Schreiber en la séptima entrada, y Carroll le siguió con un sencillo impulsor que dejó el marcador final en 8-4. Arizona terminó con siete carreras sin respuesta y se aseguró su 47.ª victoria tras remontada, la mejor marca de la MLB.
Los Yankees también se quedaron sin poder ver a Clarke Schmidt en el bullpen, como tenían previsto. El lanzador diestro tuvo que dejar de calentar por unos calambres cerca del brazo que se le había operado. Las primeras pruebas de fuerza fueron alentadoras, y se esperaba que Schmidt fuera examinado una vez que el equipo volviera a Nueva York.
Por qué esta podría ser la derrota más cara de los Yankees en 2026
Tras dos derrotas seguidas en Arizona, los Yankees vuelven al Yankee Stadium con Tampa Bay en condiciones de zanjar la lucha por el título de la División Este de la Liga Americana en el campo de Nueva York.
El daño va más allá de haber desperdiciado una ventaja. El Tampa Bay llega ahora al Bronx y solo necesita una victoria en la doble jornada del martes para asegurarse el título de la División Este de la Liga Americana, ya que esa victoria también le garantizaría el desempate en la serie de la temporada.
Eso da lugar a la consecuencia más incómoda del colapso de Arizona: los Yankees podrían verse obligados a ver cómo los Rays celebran el título de división en el Yankee Stadium, en el mismo campo donde Nueva York esperaba mantener viva la lucha hasta la última semana.
¿Qué le parece? Deje su comentario a continuación.

title: MLB roundup: Braves clinch NL East with win over Astros
body:
Field Level Media
                
21 Sep 2026, 11:49 GMT+10
            
(Photo credit: Erik Williams)
Mike Yastrzemski capped a four-run sixth inning with a three-run homer, and the visiting Atlanta Braves clinched the National League East with a 4-2 victory over the Houston Astros on Sunday.
The Braves swept the three-game interleague series and claimed their seventh division pennant over the last nine seasons. Yastrzemski was the last of four batters to reach safely against Astros left-handed reliever Bryan King (3-6), who didn't record a single out and exited after allowing Yastrzemski's 12th homer of the season.
Jose Altuve and Yainer Diaz homered for the spiraling Astros, who will enter the final week of the regular season one game behind the Texas Rangers in the American League West.
Astros starter Hunter Brown allowed just three singles and two walks over five shutout innings. Braves starter Martin Perez navigated traffic, allowing just one run on six hits and two walks in 4 1/3 innings.
Rays 5, Red Sox 1
Tampa Bay's Jonny DeLuca and Chandler Simpson drove in two runs apiece during a four-run first inning, Victor Mesa Jr. homered and the Rays defeated visiting Boston in St. Petersburg, Fla.
With the win, the Rays completed their final regular-season homestand with an 8-1 record and wrapped their home schedule with a major league-best 55-26 mark.
Trevor Story homered, and Roman Anthony and Caleb Durbin each went 2-for-4 for the Red Sox, who managed just six hits while losing their second straight game.
Pirates 4, Royals 3
Rafael Flores Jr. belted a go-ahead two-run homer in the eighth inning to cap Pittsburgh's three-game sweep over visiting Kansas City. With the win, the Pirates improved to 14-6 in their last 20 games.
Oneil Cruz went deep to lead off the fourth inning and Spencer Horwitz had an RBI single in the sixth for Pittsburgh. Carmen Mlodzinski earned the win after allowing two runs on three hits in three innings.
Vinnie Pasquantino had a pinch-hit two-run homer for the Royals, who have lost four in a row and seven of their past eight games.
Phillies 7, Mets 2
Cristopher Sanchez tossed 6 1/3 solid innings and earned the victory for visiting Philadelphia, which earned a much-needed win over New York.
Luis Arraez was 1-for-4 with two RBIs for the Phillies. Justin Crawford provided insurance in the eighth with a bases-clearing triple off Kodai Senga. Sanchez (18-6) gave up two runs on six hits. Philadelphia sits four games ahead of the Arizona Diamondbacks in the race for the final National League wild card.
Bo Bichette homered for the Mets, who dropped their home finale for the third time in four years, while Brett Baty had a pinch-hit run-scoring single in the seventh. Francisco Alvarez and A.J. Ewing each singled twice.
Cubs 9, Reds 1
Pete Crow-Armstrong tied the major league lead with his 45th home run, and David Peterson held host Cincinnati to one run on three hits in six innings in Chicago's win.
Crow-Armstrong was 3-for-5 with two RBIs, three runs, his 30th double and his 38th stolen base. He matched Philadelphia's Kyle Schwarber at 45 homers, and he became the first center fielder in history with 40 home runs, 30 doubles and 30 steals in a season.
Michael Conforto and Seiya Suzuki also homered for the Cubs. JJ Bleday hit a home run for the Reds, who have dropped three of four.
Cardinals 5, Nationals 3
Leo Bernal's two-run home run capped a three-run eighth inning, and St. Louis rallied for a win against visiting Washington to salvage the finale of the three-game series.
Ivan Herrera tied it 3-3 with one out when he hit his second solo homer of the day. Luis Gastelum (5-3) pitched a scoreless inning for the win. Jose Fermin had two hits for the Cardinals, who had lost four straight.
CJ Abrams homered, and Daylen Lile had a double and a single for Washington, which had won six of seven.
Mariners 2, Rockies 1
Kade Anderson threw seven scoreless innings, allowing just three hits in the longest outing of his rookie season, and visiting Seattle stayed alive in the postseason race with a win over Colorado in Denver.
Dominic Canzone had two hits and two RBIs for Seattle, which gained a game on the Texas Rangers in the AL West. Closer Andres Munoz left the game in the ninth with an apparent right arm injury.
Hunter Goodman's 39th home run of the season couldn't prevent Colorado from moving within one loss of its fourth consecutive 100-loss season.
Blue Jays 7, Rangers 2
Nathan Lukes and Charles McAdoo each had two RBIs to lead Toronto to a win over Texas in Arlington, Texas.
Kazuma Okamoto broke a 2-2 deadlock with an RBI single in the fifth and gave the Blue Jays a lead they would never relinquish as they remained three games back of the final AL wild-card spot. Spencer Arrighetti (9-9) picked up the win, allowing two runs in 2 1/3 innings during a bullpen game.
Jake Burger delivered the Rangers' lone runs on a game-tying two-run homer in the fourth. Jacob deGrom (11-10) had a shaky outing, giving up three runs with five hits in 4 1/3 innings for Texas, which maintained its one-game lead in the AL West despite the defeat.
Brewers 3, Orioles 0
Jacob Misiorowski set the tone with three shutout innings and Milwaukee blanked host Baltimore for the second game in a row to complete a three-game sweep and set a franchise record for regular-season victories.
William Contreras homered, and Cooper Pratt provided two run-scoring singles with two outs. Milwaukee is two games ahead of the Los Angeles Dodgers for the best record in the National League. Misiorowski's ERA dipped to 1.86.
The Orioles further damaged their fading playoff hopes, losing the first three games of the homestand to fall five games back of the Chicago White Sox for the final American League wild-card spot. Colton Cowser had two of Baltimore's four hits. Orioles starter Brandon Young (9-5) was charged with two runs in six innings.
Diamondbacks 8, Yankees 4
Nolan Arenado hit his third grand slam of the season to cap a five-run fifth and Arizona kept its slim National League wild-card chances alive with a victory over New York in Phoenix.
Geraldo Perdomo had two hits and two RBIs and five Arizona relievers limited the Yankees to three hits in 6 1/3 scoreless innings. The D-backs remained five games behind NL wild-card leaders Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres and four behind the Philadelphia Phillies with six to play.
Heliot Ramos, George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones homered for the Yankees, who fell six games behind Tampa Bay in the AL East. The Yankees lead the American League with 216 homers. Lombard had two hits.
Twins 8, Angels 0
Dean Kremer allowed one hit over six innings and Alan Roden went 3-for-5 with a home run and four RBIs as Minnesota earned a split of its four-game series with Los Angeles in Anaheim, Calif.
Josh Bell had three hits, a walk, two RBIs and a run while Brooks Lee also had three hits and scored three times for Minnesota, which finished with 13 hits. Kremer (4-5) allowed just a fourth-inning leadoff single to Vaughn Grissom.
Ryan Johnson (5-9) suffered the loss for Los Angeles, which finished the 2026 season with a 34-47 home record.
Guardians 1, Athletics 0
Gavin Williams threw seven shutout innings to lift Cleveland past the visiting Athletics.
Williams (14-8) gave up only three hits while throwing 63 of 89 pitches for strikes. Steven Kwan had three hits and Cade Smith earned his 39th save as the Guardians swept the series and remain atop the American League Central.
A's starter Jack Perkins (3-12) gave up five hits and one run in six innings. Zack Gelof had two of the team's six hits as the Athletics suffered their sixth straight loss
Dodgers 3, Giants 1
Emmet Sheehan pitched brilliantly in long relief, Enrique Hernandez broke a seventh-inning tie with a run-scoring double and Los Angeles completed a three-game sweep of visiting San Francisco.
Tommy Edman homered for the Dodgers, who trailed 1-0 after one inning before Sheehan took over to start the second and held the Giants to just one hit with nine strikeouts over the next 5 1/3 scoreless innings.
Jung Hoo Lee and Victor Bericoto singled for the only hits for the Giants, who completed their road schedule with a 28-53 record. Sam Hentges (1-7) allowed a pair of one-out singles in the seventh before Hernandez's double for a 2-1 edge.
Padres 7, Marlins 3
Jake Cronenworth homered twice and knocked in a season-high five runs while Fernando Tatis Jr. also homered as host San Diego polished off a three-game sweep and finished 6-0 against Miami this season.
The Padres won their fifth straight game and are 13-1 in their last 14 games. Walker Buehler (9-6) worked 6 2/3 innings, allowing three hits and three runs.
Sandy Alcantara (13-11) absorbed the loss for the Marlins after permitting eight hits and four runs over six innings. Alcantara is winless in his last eight starts.
White Sox 8, Tigers 1
Chase Meidroth hit a two-run homer for Chicago and Sam Antonacci's two-run double highlighted a 2-for-4 performance as the White Sox waited through a rain delay of nearly four hours and played in wet, blustery conditions to beat Detroit.
Five pitchers held the Tigers to six hits and five walks as Detroit was limited to a single run for the third time in the series. title: Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player
author: James Riggenbach
body:
The Colorado Rockies are 57–99.
Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player
An absurd rule for absurd times: if the worst team in baseball could steal one player from a playoff club, who should the Rockies take?
One more loss will give them their fourth consecutive 100-loss season, and they are almost certainly going to finish with the worst record in baseball.
These are absurd times for the Rockies, so I have devised an appropriately absurd rule to help them out.
The team with the worst record in baseball gets to steal one player from a playoff team.
There are, naturally, some restrictions. We’re freezing the playoff field as it stood before games on Sunday, September 20. The player has to come from one of those 12 teams, cannot be a pending free agent, and you cannot take the player who leads his team in FanGraphs WAR. The Rockies also inherit the player’s existing contract.
No, one player is not suddenly turning the Rockies into a contender. But could one poached superstar at least keep this thing from becoming five consecutive 100-loss seasons?
Here’s the board:
| Team | Off limits: fWAR leader | Highest available fWAR | Other players worth considering | 
| Rays | Junior Caminero (5.2) | Drew Rasmussen (4.7) | Jonathan Aranda (3) | 
| Guardians | Parker Messick (4.6) | Steven Kwan (3.4) | Gavin Williams (3.4), Brayan Rocchio (3.3), José Ramírez (2.2) | 
| Rangers | Ezequiel Duran (4.6) | Jacob deGrom (4.2) | Josh Jung (2.9), Wyatt Langford (2.8) | 
| Yankees | Cam Schlittler (6.1) | Ben Rice (4) | Cody Bellinger (3.9), Aaron Judge (2) | 
| Red Sox | Willson Contreras (4.1) | Payton Tolle (4) | Ceddanne Rafaela (3.9), Ranger Suárez (3.7) | 
| White Sox | Miguel Vargas (5) | Chase Meidroth (4) | Tristan Peters (3.9), Sean Burke (3.1) | 
| Brewers | Jacob Misiorowski (6.3) | Brice Turang (5.4) | Jackson Chourio (4), Jake Bauers (3.6) | 
| Dodgers | Shohei Ohtani (6.7) | Yoshinobu Yamamoto (4.7) | Max Muncy (4.3), Andy Pages (3.9) | 
| Braves | Chris Sale (5.7) | Michael Harris II (4) | Matt Olson (4), Drake Baldwin (3.1) | 
| Cubs | Pete Crow-Armstrong (10.2) | Alex Bregman (5) | Dansby Swanson (3.6) | 
| Padres | Fernando Tatis Jr. (5) | Jackson Merrill (4) | Ty France (3.8), Mason Miller (3.7) | 
| Phillies | Cristopher Sánchez (5.8) | Jesús Luzardo (5.6) | Zack Wheeler (3.5), Bryce Harper (3.4) | 
For me, the choice comes down to Brice Turang, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Aaron Judge.
Turang is probably the sensible choice.
At 5.4 fWAR, he would easily lead the Rockies, giving them a legitimate top-end player while immediately solving second base for the foreseeable future. He’s 26, hitting .266/.367/.441 with an .808 OPS, and brings value on both sides of the ball with elite range, strong baserunning and a 95th-percentile walk rate.
It would be a very easy way to make the roster better.
But the Rockies really need starting pitching.
Enter Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He’s 14–8 with a 2.51 ERA, 178 strikeouts and a 0.87 WHIP over 179 innings. His Statcast profile is just as impressive: 100th-percentile pitching run value, 99th-percentile fastball run value, 95th-percentile offspeed run value and a 91st-percentile xERA.
Pitchers are risky, and Yamamoto comes with a lot of money attached. But it’s hard to argue with either the profile or the results, and the addition of the Penner family makes absorbing that contract a lot easier to imagine.
Speaking of high-priced items...
Aaron Judge.
Judge being available is basically a loophole created by our own stupid rule. Injuries have limited him to just 285 plate appearances, which is why he sits at only 2 fWAR, but he’s still hitting .241/.360/.511 with 15 home runs.
And the underlying numbers are still very much Judge: a .396 xwOBA, .569 xSLG, 94.0 mph average exit velocity and a 57.5% hard-hit rate.
It is very hard to look at that and say, “No thanks.”
After all, Aaron Judge is the type of hitter that, if he were playing 81 games a year at Coors Field, I might take out a small loan for season tickets.
So who are you stealing?

So who are you stealing?

title: SWB RAILRIDERS: End of an era for franchise’s nickname
author: Scott Walsh
body:
MOOSIC — Edinson Duran became the unlikely answer to a trivia question.
Sunday’s season finale between the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders and Jacksonville Jumbo Shrimp at PNC Field was canceled due to rain and wet grounds. That meant Saturday night’s game was the last one featuring the RailRiders nickname. The team is rebranding and expected to announce the new identity in November.
So when people ask who was the winning pitcher in the final game of the RailRiders era, it isn’t a top prospect like Elmer Rodriguez or an ace like Brendan Beck. It is Duran, a catcher who spent more time on the development list this season than the active roster.
Whenever the RailRiders would need to use a position player to save arms in the bullpen, they would go to Duran. He’s done it eight times in the past two seasons, including six this season.
In the top of the 10th inning Saturday night, Justin Topa struck out the first two batters with the automatic runner on second base. However, with the count 2-1 to Logan Driscoll, Topa reached his pitch limit. With no other options, manager Shelley Duncan called upon Duran. The 24-year old from Venezuela walked Driscoll, then walked Gage Miller to load the bases, but got Johnny Olmstead to fly out to center fielder Duke Ellis to end the inning. The RailRiders won in the bottom of the 10th, 6-5, when automatic runner Yanquiel Fernandez scored from third base on a wild pitch, making Duran the winning pitcher.
“It was really exciting for Duran to come in and do what he did,” RailRiders reliever Eric Reyzelman said. “It’s fun, kind of reminds you why you play this game. Technically, we had nothing on the line playoff-wise. But we did not want to leave this place without a win.”
And so the RailRiders’ final ride has pulled into the station. The team finished 78-68 overall (37-37 first half, 41-31 second half). Its all-time record wound up 1,028 wins and 834 losses.
From the first pitch by Vidal Nuño to Pawtucket’s Brock Holt on April 4, 2013, to the last one Saturday night — Jacksonville’s Stephen Jones’ wild pitch with Kenedy Corona batting — a lot of memorable moments happened in between.
Six times the RailRiders made the playoffs. Three times they lost in the International League championship series (2017, 2018, 2025). But in 2016, they defeated the Gwinnett Braves in four games to capture the IL title, then beat the Pacific Coast League champion El Paso Chihuahuas to claim the Triple-A national championship.
Many notable players have worn a RailRiders uniform.
Hall of Famer Derek Jeter spent seven games on a rehab assignment in early July 2013 while recovering from a broken ankle. During his time here, it became a daily game to see where he was spotted in downtown Scranton.
Later that month, Alex Rodriguez played three games here while coming back from offseason hip surgery. He hit a two-run home run in the second at-bat of his first game.
Curtis Granderson and D.J. LeMahieu were other notable Yankees who rehabbed here over the years. This season, pitchers Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodon and outfielder Cody Bellinger had rehab stints.
Current Yankees slugger Aaron Judge played 154 games with the RailRiders in 2015 and 2016 and five more games on a rehab assignment in 2019. He totaled 28 home runs and 95 RBIs. Prospects such as Gary Sanchez, Anthony Volpe and George Lombard Jr. spent time here.
“A lot of great players have played for the RailRiders,” said Beck, who wound up leading the International League in earned-run average (2.93), strikeouts (151), innings (135.1), WHIP (1.06) and opponents’ batting average (.210). “To be the last ones to do it is fun. The future is exciting as well. Looking forward to starting something new next year. But to be the team to end the RailRiders dynasty on a comeback win with a good crowd at home is a lot of fun. Definitely a fun day at the office.”
When Duncan played in Scranton/Wilkes-Barre from 2007-09, the team was known as the Yankees. But in his four seasons as manager, the term “RailRiders” has come to mean a lot to him.
“I just always think about the character of every team that I’ve had,” said Duncan, whose record as RailRiders manager is 327-195. “I’ve been lucky to be a part of some good groups that fought all the way to the end. Some good memories and some good relationships. Each year has been a different team and each year has been very special.”
Clint Frazier was a top prospect who played 213 games for the RailRiders from 2016-19 before a severe concussion and lingering symptoms ultimately sidetracked his career. Because of his frequent shuttling between the minors and the majors, he proclaimed himself a “RailRider for Life.”
He made an appearance at Saturday night’s game, signing autographs for fans and throwing out the ceremonial first pitch.
“It was me being a little facetious,” Frazier said. “I think it started around the time I got optioned to the minor leagues in 2019. I was doing relatively well at the big-league level. When I came down here, there was something in the media about September roster expansion and the Yankees were kind of vague on whether I going to be coming back. I remember parking in a parking garage and seeing this sign that said ‘Scranton Life’ and I was like, ‘Dude, I don’t want to be a Yankee. I want to be a RailRider for Life.’ It was a facetious comment and I ended up running with it because it was kind of funny. People obviously took notice to it because I put it on my Twitter bio and it’s been there for like 10 years.”
Frazier was a little surprised and a bit disappointed when he heard the team was rebranding and retiring the RailRiders nickname.
“I’m not a part of the Yankees anymore and I’m not here in Scranton,” Frazier said. “So if they want to rebrand or it’s something the fans want, you give them it. But other than that, I was kind of like, ‘Damn, I guess I won’t be a RailRider anymore. I’ll be whatever they are.’ But I’ll still be a RailRider at heart.”
The nickname has not only meant something to players.
Kristina Knight has been with the team for 20 seasons. She started as an intern with the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre Red Barons, then worked in tickets sales and group sales, sponsor servicing and currently is senior director of partnership management and marketing.
“I think it was extra special because it was a community-thought name,” Knight said. “We surveyed the community and did the poll of submitting your ideas. So I like to think it was the community’s name, which was extra special within itself. The reason we went away from the Yankees name was to give the area more ownership of the team here. I think it did that for sure.
“When we were the Yankees, it was very nice and obviously nice to be included in the Yankees family. But the RailRiders was our very own name and gave our own identity in the minor-league baseball world.”
When the new nickname is announced in November, Knight believes that the community will accept it as well.
“I think it will be as well-received and special to the community,” Knight said. “We are trying to make sure it reflects everything in this area that we find very special and attractive about our area and try to make it a highlight to the nation.”

title: Top 9 things at stake in the final week
author: Brent Maguire
body:
The final week of the 2026 regular season has arrived and there is still much to be determined.
While six teams have clinched playoff spots and a few others are close, multiple playoff positions are still up for grabs. And from an individual perspective, there are awards that could be determined in the coming days.
Here’s what is at stake in the final week of the season.
Who will win the AL West and Central?
There’s no telling who will win these two divisions in the American League. The Rays have just about wrapped up the AL East, but the White Sox and Guardians are still battling for the AL Central, while the Rangers and Astros are battling for the West.
This is where things stand. The Rangers lead the Astros by one game in the AL West but Houston won the pivotal tiebreaker against Texas. That means if the two clubs end the season with the same record, the division would go to the Astros.
In the AL Central, the Guardians hold a one-game lead over the White Sox, but Chicago holds the tiebreaker advantage. Any tie between the two clubs means the White Sox would win the division.
Who gets the last AL Wild Card spot?
The AL West and Central battles are directly linked to what’s happening for the final Wild Card spot. It’s very likely that one of those four aforementioned teams will grab the last AL Wild Card spot, unless the Blue Jays have something to say about it. Right now, the White Sox have a fairly comfortable three-game lead over the Blue Jays and Astros.
Could Yordan still win the Triple Crown?
For a while, Yordan Alvarez looked like he might win the MLB Triple Crown, leading the Majors in average, home runs and RBIs. Now, the lefty slugger and presumptive AL MVP winner might merely finish first or second in average, home runs and RBIs. Heading into the final week, Alvarez has a slight edge in average (.313) over Chandler Simpson (.309) and is second in home runs (40) behind Junior Caminero (41) and second in RBIs (99) behind Pete Alonso (105). Alvarez could still snag the AL Triple Crown, but it’ll take a monstrous final week.
Simpson’s unique season and quest for an unusual batting title
Back to Simpson for a second, though. The Rays outfielder is having an excellent season, hitting for average, swiping bases and playing solid outfield defense. What he hasn’t done, though, is hit a single home run. The last hitter to win a batting title without hitting a home run was Rod Carew in 1972. Even if he doesn’t win, he could be the first qualified hitter to bat .300 without a home run since Luis Castillo in 1999.
Will Misiorowski win the ERA title?
It's been a remarkable season for Jacob Misiorowski, who has a 1.86 ERA and 247 strikeouts after Sunday's outing against the Orioles. Assuming he's in line for one more start next weekend -- even if it's abbreviated like his three-inning outing on Sunday -- Misiorowski is in line to join some impressive company. If he can hold his ERA edge over Cam Schlittler's 1.94 mark, he'd join 2021 Corbin Burnes (2.43 ERA in 2021) as the only Brewers to win an ERA title.
If Misiorowski keeps his ERA under two and gets to 250 strikeouts, there's some other fun company he'll join. He'd be just the 13th pitcher (15th instance) since earned runs became official in 1913 to finish a season with a sub-2 ERA and 250-plus strikeouts. The last to do so was Jacob deGrom in 2018.

Kyle Schwarber led the National League with 56 home runs last year. As hard as it is to believe, though, Schwarber has never led the Majors in home runs. That could change this year, as the Phillies’ slugger is tied for the MLB lead with 45 homers. The last Phillie to pull that off was Ryan Howard in 2008, when he hit 48 homers and helped lead Philly to a World Series title.
Schwarber, though, has Pete Crow-Armstrong tied with him at the top. The surefire NL MVP has completely taken off this season with 45 homers, 38 stolen bases (more on this shortly), a .949 OPS and his usual excellent center field defense, which has led to an MLB-best 10.5 WAR, per FanGraphs. If PCA surpasses Schwarber, he’d be the first Cub to lead the NL in homers since Sammy Sosa’s 49 homers in 2002 and the first to lead the Majors in long balls since Sosa hit 50 in 2000.
Does PCA get to 40-40?
Crow-Armstrong is making all sorts of history this season. Reaching 10 WAR puts PCA in rarified territory and it seems very likely that the Cubs’ superstar center fielder will be a unanimous MVP winner, something no Cub has ever achieved. Crow-Armstrong is also a mere two stolen bases away from a 40-40 season, something no Cub has done and only six other MLB players have achieved.
Burleson vying to join impressive Cardinals history
Alec Burleson leads the Majors with 111 RBIs, putting him in line for some impressive Cardinals history. He’s looking to become the first Cardinal to lead the National League since Albert Pujols in 2010 and the first to lead the Majors in the category since Joe Torre drove in 137 runs in 1971. His stiffest competition is Cincinnati’s Sal Stewart, who sits at 110 RBIs entering the final week.
How does Verlander's final start go?
Justin Verlander returned to the Tigers for the 2026 season, which will be his final before retiring. Unfortunately, he only made one start in April and hasn't pitched since that point. The good news is he's lined up to pitch on Saturday at Detroit's Comerica Park, which will surely be a feel good moment and send off for the likely future Hall of Famer. Verlander can also add a few more strikeouts to his career total of 3,554.
