title: Yankees Social Media Spotlight: Merry Clinchmas
author: John Griffin
body:
It’s Sunday once more, and you know what that means — it’s time for our weekly social media roundup! This weekend has been yet another veritable whirlwind in the Bronx, as the team celebrated a postseason appearance, bid farewell to a fan favorite, closed an era of minor league baseball, and watched as their Captain hit the shelf once more. With so much in store, let’s get started!
Another Celebration in Minnesota
It was deja vu all over again! For what feels like the fifty millionth time, the Yankees celebrated in Minnesota, as they clinched a postseason berth earlier this week with a victory over their favorite AL Central punching bag.
The Roberto Clemente Award
This week, the New York Yankees named Carlos Rodón their nominee for the 2026 Roberto Clemente Award. The team honored the Rodón Foundation, which sets out to help families suffering with fertility issues.
In Service
Yankees reliever Brent Headrick welcomed Henry Ledlowe from his hometown in Illinois to the Bronx, courtesy of the National Down Syndrome Society. Unfortunately, the Instagram post cannot be embedded, but can be found here.
The Jazz Chisholm Jr. Foundation, meanwhile, marked the 25th anniversary of 9/11.
Where’s Oswaldo? Unfortunately, Cincy.
This week, the Yankees designated fan favorite Oswaldo Cabrera for assignment in order to make room on the 40-man roster for Clarke Schmidt. Unfortunately, he was claimed off waivers by the Cincinnati Reds, and while we’re all excited to see him (hopefully) get some regular playing time — as he was very much blocked in the Bronx — it will be sad to see the human golden retriever, well-loved by the fans and players alike, in a different uniform.
A testament to his popularity is the fact that the Yankees, RailRiders, Patriots, and YES Network all posted farewells to him on their social media accounts. David Cone also came back to Twitter briefly in order to wish him well.
Farewell to the RailRiders
Starting next year, the Yankees’ Triple-A affiliate will undergo its second rebrand since joining the Yankees family, abandoning the RailRider moniker in exchange for a new nickname which has yet to be revealed. To honor the end of the era, Clint Frazier — who self-identifies as a Scranton RailRider more than anyone else in baseball — threw out the ceremonial first pitch prior to their final game.
Road Trip Nonsense
Meredith Marakovitz, Suzyn Waldman, and Dave Simms always have fun on the road trips, and this one is no different!
The Knicks are Back
This week, the Yankees will be hosting Josh Hart bobblehead night, celebrating the 2026 NBA Champion (and 2016 NCAA Champion!) who is related to Yankees legend Elston Howard. Fun fact — this has been scheduled since last year, so it actually predates the Knicks’ championship; what fantastic luck for the marketing team!
Celebrating Howie
Last Sunday, Mets broadcaster Howie Rose called his last game at Yankee Stadium. The Yankees set out to make the day special, and many of his friends and coworkers in the Yankees broadcast teams celebrated his career with him.
Official Videos
First, the latest episode of Behind the NY gives us a behind-the scenes look at the 25th anniversary of 9/11.
Then, we got a behind-the-scenes look of David Bednar entering the game on Sunday.
Last, but not least, we have Cody Bellinger talking about his story.
We’ve got a special edition of this week’s Question of the Day, as we not only have the Yankees answering questions, we’ve got the Somerset Patriots reading Thank You Cards as they wrap up their season.

title: Cristopher Sánchez, annoyed at early pull, gets back on track in win against Mets
author: Destiny Lugardo
body:
Cristopher Sánchez turned his back as Don Mattingly walked to the mound. Sánchez, with his pitch count at 98 in the seventh inning, had a runner on first and one out. But Mattingly wanted to go to rookie Alex McFarlane, his most trusted high leverage arm outside of Jhoan Duran.
Sánchez stared into center field. He eventually looked over his shoulder and gave the ball to Mattingly. He screamed as he walked back to the dugout and shook his head as he watched the remainder of the inning from the dugout.
McFarlane, with two outs and two runners on, blew three fastballs right by Juan Soto for the final out of the inning. He may have gone back out for the eighth, but the Phillies scored three runs in the top half of the inning. Mattingly instead went to Chase Shugart in the eighth and José Alvarado in the ninth. Both relievers threw scoreless innings. All three helped preserve Sánchez’s league-leading 18th win of the season and a 7-2 Phillies win over the New York Mets on a rainy Sunday afternoon at Citi Field.
Sánchez may have been perturbed by what he perceived to be an early pull, but he pitched well when he was in the game. That’s all that really matters for the Phillies, who desperately need the best version of Sánchez to show up next week in the wild card round.
After allowing 18 hits in his last two starts, Sánchez bounced back. After doing a deep dive on his recent mechanical issues, Sánchez limited traffic on the bases and had his signature changeup going.
His next scheduled start is Saturday at home against the Tampa Bay Rays. He’ll have to pitch if the Phillies haven’t clinched yet. With the win, the Phillies’ magic number to make the postseason is 3. Seeding, and an opportunity to host the wild card series, could be on the line.
If they do clinch in the next few days, the Phillies could opt to rest him and get him ready for the postseason. The Phillies could also move his start up a day to Friday with the off day on Monday and have him pitch on regular rest for Game 2 of a potential wild card series. How the Phillies manage their rotation over the last weekend will be interesting. Both Sánchez and Zack Wheeler are lined up to pitch the final two games of the year. They will have to find someone who can eat innings.
The Phillies broke the game wide open in the eighth on a bases-clearing triple by Justin Crawford. Prior to Crawford’s big hit, all of the Phillies offense came in the first three innings. They scored twice in the first on a Luis Arraez sacrifice fly and an RBI single from Alec Bohm. The two runs in the third broke an odd streak of five consecutive games in which the Phillies scored exactly three runs.
The Phillies will head back to Philadelphia for the start of the final homestand of the regular season on Tuesday against the Milwaukee Brewers. Pending the results of the Diamondbacks vs. Yankees game, the Phillies could clinch at home as early as Tuesday night. Wheeler will get the start for the Phillies in the opening game.

rss_title: Cristopher Sánchez, annoyed at early pull, gets back on track in win against Mets
rss_body:
Cristopher Sánchez turned his back as Don Mattingly walked to the mound. Sánchez, with his pitch count at 98 in the seventh inning, had a runner on first and one out. But Mattingly wanted to go to rookie Alex McFarlane, his most trusted high leverage arm outside of Jhoan Duran.
Sánchez stared into center field. He eventually looked over his shoulder and gave the ball to Mattingly. He screamed as he walked back to the dugout and shook his head as he watched the remainder of the inning from the dugout.
McFarlane, with two outs and two runners on, blew three fastballs right by Juan Soto for the final out of the inning. He may have gone back out for the eighth, but the Phillies scored three runs in the top half of the inning. Mattingly instead went to Chase Shugart in the eighth and José Alvarado in the ninth. Both relievers threw scoreless innings. All three helped preserve Sánchez’s league-leading 18th win of the season and a 7-2 Phillies win over the New York Mets on a rainy Sunday afternoon at Citi Field.
Sánchez may have been perturbed by what he perceived to be an early pull, but he pitched well when he was in the game. That’s all that really matters for the Phillies, who desperately need the best version of Sánchez to show up next week in the wild card round.
After allowing 18 hits in his last two starts, Sánchez bounced back. After doing a deep dive on his recent mechanical issues, Sánchez limited traffic on the bases and had his signature changeup going.

body:

Looking at Jazz Chisholm Jr.
Chisholm has been on the injured list with a right thumb strain since Sept. 10.

Looking at Trent Grisham
Grisham has been on the injured list with a right hamstring strain since Sept. 5.
This season, Grisham has hit .211/.308/.395 with 18 home runs and 59 RBI over 121 games. He is set to be a free agent at the end of the season.
New York Yankees Right Now
The Yankees have already clinched a postseason berth. They hold a 5 1/2 game lead over the Boston Red Sox for the top AL Wild Card spot with an 89-65 record.
Meanwhile, New York is five games behind the Tampa Bay Rays for first place in the American League East.
After the Diamondbacks series, the Yankees will host the Rays for a four-game set and then the Baltimore Orioles for three games to finish the regular season.

title: New York Yankees Quickly Announce Jose Caballero Change
author: Ben Stinar
body:
On Sunday, the New York Yankees and Arizona Diamondbacks will finish their series at Chase Field in Phoenix.
The two teams are tied up at 1-1, so whoever wins on Sunday will take the series.
Most recently, the Yankees lost by a score of 5-3 on Saturday.
Jose Caballero (who started in center field) finished with two hits and one walk.
Yankees Announce Caballero Change
For Sunday’s game, the Yankees have announced their starting lineup.
Underdog MLB wrote: “Yankees 9/20 B. Rice DH C. Bellinger LF H. Ramos RF L. García Jr. 1B G. Lombard Jr. SS S. Jones CF A. Volpe 2B A. Wells C J. Caballero 3B W. Warren SP”
Caballero (who is hitting 9th) has been moved to 3rd base on Sunday.
He comes into the day batting .238 with 94 hits, 14 home runs, 51 RBIs, 49 runs and 32 stolen bases in 130 games.
The 30-year-old is in the middle of his second season playing for the Yankees.
Social Media Reacts To Lineup On Sunday
Here’s what people were saying about the team’s lineup on Sunday:
@MyGSDog_HavoK: “How will you embarrass yourselves today?? The Hal Steinbrenner goal has been met. A wildcard and make 800 million in revenue…”
@Yankees44Giants: “This might actually be the best lineup we can send out right now 🙄”
@bryant_cleary: “Debating the order is fine but…. Currently the best 9 guys they can put out there.”

@NYYPinstripes27: “WIN THE SERIES. Will Warren toes the slab for the Yanks as they look to take the series from the Arizona Diamondbacks. First pitch is set for 4:10 PM ET. LET’S GO YANKS!!”

title: NY Yankees, Aaron Boone hope to have Trent Grisham for playoffs
author: Matías Persuh
body:
The New York Yankees are one of the teams that will compete in the 2026 MLB playoffs, and they are looking to have as many players as possible at full strength. According to insider Bryan Hoch on X, Aaron Boone said that Trent Grisham isn’t expected to be activated before the end of the regular season, but the Yanks hope to have him on their playoff roster.
The manager also provided an update on other injured players. Jazz Chisholm Jr. is “in play, potentially” to be activated on Tuesday, and the Pinstripes are also hopeful of having him back for the Wild Card round.
With little time remaining in the regular season, it would seem wise for the Bronx Bombers not to rush any player back. On the other hand, having already clinched a playoff spot could be beneficial for giving Grisham some playing time on the field.
What happened to Trent Grisham?
Trent Grisham is back on the shelf after tweaking his right hamstring again during a stolen base attempt against San Diego on September 4th. The Yankees officially placed him on the 10-day injured list on September 5th with a moderate Grade 2 strain, making this his second IL stint for the same hamstring issue this season after missing roughly three weeks back in June and July.
Xander Bogaerts #2 of the San Diego Padres tags out Trent Grisham #12 of the New York Yankees.
He’s been sidelined since then, putting his status up in the air as the regular season winds down and leaving the Yanks hoping he can heal up in time to be a factor in the postseason.
The Yankees’ final stretch
Aaron Boone and the Yankees are heading into the final stretch of the regular season, closing things out with a huge six-game homestand at the Stadium against two division foes: three against the Tampa Bay Rays followed by three with the Baltimore Orioles.
They’re coming off a long road swing that had a bit of everything—sweeping a short two-game set against the Minnesota Twins, but dropping two out of three in Phoenix against the Arizona Diamondbacks. Having already clinched their playoff ticket, these final home games are all about locking up seeding, dialing in the bullpen, and sharpening the bats before the October pressure cooker begins.

title: Yankees news: Why Cam Schlittler was pissed at himself after NY's loss to Diamondbacks
author: Richard Pereira; ClutchPoints
body:
Yankees news: Why Cam Schlittler was pissed at himself after NY's loss to Diamondbacks appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Cam Schlittler wasn't happy with his performance on the mound after the New York Yankees' 5-3 loss to the Arizona Diamondbacks on Saturday night.
Schlittler is going through the second season of his career in the majors with the Yankees. He has quickly broken out as one of the best young pitchers, helping New York be firm in the playoff picture this year.
Schlittler started on the mound as he lasted six innings, striking out six batters while conceding three hits and one earned run. New York lost on Pavin Smith's pinch-hit, two-run homer in the ninth inning, resulting in Arizona's victory. He blamed himself for those mistakes after the game.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"I mean, I wouldn't say I really gave them a chance,'' Schlittler said. "That one's kind of on me, so I'll take the blame for that. Made an error there, let up two runs."
"I mean, there's still a chance,'' Schlittler said, "but we got to play our (butts) off a little bit.'
How Cam Schlittler, Yankees played against Diamondbacks
Cam Schlittler and the Yankees have preparation for the postseason. These last games of the regular season will decide their place in the AL bracket, needing every win they can get.
The game was scoreless throughout the first four innings, seeing both teams finally get on the board in the fifth frame. However, Arizona dealt more blows as New York was unable to muster up more big plays to rally back against the hosts.
New York fell to an 89-65 record on the season, sitting at second place in the AL East Division standings. They are above the Boston Red Sox and the Toronto Blue Jays while trailing the Tampa Bay Rays.
The Yankees will look to bounce back in their series finale against the Diamondbacks. That contest commences on Sept. 20 at 4:10 p.m. ET.

title: Yankees' Aaron Judge injury updates from Judge, Aaron Boone feel purposely vague
author: Adam Weinrib
body:
Eagle-eyed New York Yankees beat writers stalked the field for any signs of Aaron Judge's post-injury workouts on Sunday, in the same way that both Cody Bellinger and Trent Grisham were back on the grass testing their agility shortly after coming up lame. No such luck with Judge; the Yankees kept him in the shadows instead. That shouldn't be surprising.
Judge kept his timeline under lock and key throughout his entire rib injury rehab process (though somehow the Rockies series managed to emerge as an accurate target along the way). His reinjury just one week after returning to the lineup has thrown both his rehab plan and playoff availability into question, with detectives looking to ding him retroactively for his process and dig into the future simultaneously.
It's no wonder that information about Judge's new injury has come in drips and drabs. The only thing Judge has been willing to give the media so far is the information that it's the soleus muscle that he hurt, which makes baseball motions difficult and could lead to a more progressive and harrowing injury down the line under the wrong circumstances.
But what grade is it? Is a 2-3 week timeline typical, or is it something much worse? Judge won't say, only betraying that he'd like to be back for the postseason.
Get it? If he never admits the grade, he doesn't remove himself from consideration for the Wild Card series outright. Very clever. Not reassuring.
Aaron Boone doesn't help Yankees fans learn more about Aaron Judge calf strain
If you were hoping to ply the information Judge has refused to give out of Aaron Boone, you weren't any luckier by choosing that path. Instead of cheeky optimism, though, you would've received frustrated bluster.
If Judge says he wants to be back for October, then Boone will neither refute nor endorse that notion. Instead, he'll give you the curt half-truth.
He'll be back. Or he won't. The only two options.
The Yankees and Judge will never say it, both to betray their competitive advantage and their beloved captain, but a return in the Wild Card series feels somewhere between foolish and impossible. A return during the postseason will depend on many factors, most of them related to how far this team is able to push without Judge's star power and added gravity. If you're looking for clarity here, maybe you can find it in between the Yankees' public statements.

title: New York Yankees @ Arizona Diamondbacks: Will Warren vs. Corbin Burnes
author: Michael Zeno
body:
The final road game of the 2026 regular season is upon us, as the Yankees will conclude it with a seven-game homestand before likely hosting the Red Sox for the Wild Card Series. If the season ends there, this is the end of the line for the gray uniforms for 2026, but obviously, we all hope we'll see them next in Tampa (and more) in early October.
Looking to end a road slate that has been very generous to the Yankees on a high note is Will Warren, who's finishing his sophomore season strong after his great start to the campaign unraveled into a bit of a mess over the summer. Rotation reinforcements that threatened to throw him in the bullpen never came with the recurring injuries, so he'll finish 2026 with 30 starts for the second straight season. This is No. 29, as he enters with a 3.89 ERA (108 ERA+) and 4.07 FIP in 148 innings. No matter what happens from here, Warren has had a successful year in solidifying himself as a true MLB-caliber rotation arm.
Opposing him will be a former Cy Young winner trying to round into form off Tommy John surgery in Corbin Burnes, whom Yankees fans remember well from his lone season in Baltimore in 2024. Returning from a 16-month absence on September 8 to help with the playoff push, Burnes has allowed five runs across 7.2 innings with six strikeouts to two walks against the Royals and Marlins. He isn't totally built up, having thrown 75 pitches in his last start, so expect him to settle around 80-85 today. He's always befuddled the Yankees, pitching to a 1.93 ERA across 23.1 innings in his career, but he doesn't have a win in any of those four starts.
Ben Rice will once again lead off, followed by Cody Bellinger, Heliot Ramos, and Luis García Jr. We've seen better ABs and swings from George Lombard Jr. lately, who'll bat fifth. Spencer Jones is back after a one-day absence due to a sore foot and will bat in front of Anthony Volpe, Austin Wells, and José Caballero.
Lars Nootbaar will also be a repeat leadoff hitter for the D-backs, followed by Ketel Marte, Gabriel Moreno, and Geraldo Perdomo. Corbin Carroll is batting fifth, Nolan Arenado will bat sixth, and former Blue Jay Jesús Sánchez bats seventh ahead of last night's hero Pavin Smith and Tim Tawa.
How to watch
Location: Chase Field, Phoenix, AZ
First pitch: 4:10 pm ET
TV broadcast: YES, DBACKS.TV
Radio broadcast: WFAN 660/101.9 FM, WADO 1280 (NYY), ESPN 620 AM, La Campesina 101.9 FM & 860 AM (AZ)

title: Rangers put pitcher Quantrill on IL due to right lat tightness
author: ESPN Staff
body:
ARLINGTON, Texas -- The American League West-leading Texas Rangers put versatile right-hander Cal Quantrill on the 15-day injured list Sunday, a day after he exited following four batters and 12 pitches because of right lat tightness.
Hard-throwing right-hander Winston Santos was recalled from Triple-A Round Rock and joined the Rangers before the finale of their three-game series against the Toronto Blue Jays.
About an hour before the game, the Rangers said right fielder Brandon Nimmo was being scratched from the starting lineup because of illness.
Before the IL move was announced, manager Skip Schumaker said the Rangers knew going into Saturday night’s game that Quantrill’s velocity was lower.
Quantrill (9-5) was showing no signs of pain when Schumaker, pitching coach Jordan Tiegs and head trainer Matt Lucero went to the mound in the second inning and he came out of the game. Quantrill has a 2.86 ERA in 32 games (15 starts) after going to spring training with the Rangers on a minor league deal.
He left his previous start after six innings and 70 pitches at Arizona last Sunday with back soreness.
Quantrill, 31, has a 1.75 ERA (11 earned runs in 56⅔ innings) over his past 11 appearances (10 starts). Cam Schlittler of the New York Yankees at 1.64 is the only qualified pitcher with a better ERA over that span.
Santos is beginning his third stint with the Rangers, though his only appearance in the first two was his big league debut July 1 at Cleveland, where he allowed two runs in two innings. He has 103 strikeouts in 83⅓ innings in the minor leagues this season.

title: 7x MLB All-Star Will Be A New York Yankees Free Agent This Winter
author: Ben Stinar
body:
On Sunday, the New York Yankees will finish their series with the Arizona Diamondbacks.
The Yankees won the first game by a score of 9-2 (on Friday).
Paul Goldschmidt had one hit, one walk and two runs.
He was not in the lineup for Saturday’s 5-3 loss.
Goldschmidt also remains out of the lineup on Sunday.
7x MLB All-Star Will Be A Yankees Free Agent
With the season nearly over, it’s worth noting that Goldschmidt will become a free agent who is available to sign with any team in the MLB this winter.
He is being paid $4 million for the 2026 season.
If Goldschmidt wants to keep playing, it’s hard to imagine a world where the Yankees would not want him.
It’s also fair to wonder if any other teams would have interest.
In addition to being an incredible veteran in the clubhouse, the 39-year-old is still a very productive player.
Goldschmidt is batting .253 with 85 hits, 18 home runs, 50 RBIs, 44 runs and one stolen base in 102 games this year.
Looking At The Rest Of Goldschmidt’s Career
Goldschmidt was picked in the 8th round of the 2009 MLB Draft.
He spent the first eight years of his career with the Diamondbacks.
From 2013-18, Goldschmidt made five straight trips to the All-Star Game.
Following Arizona, Goldschmidt had another strong run with the St. Louis Cardinals (2019-24).
He made another trip to the All-Star Game (and won the 2022 National League MVP Award).
Looking At New York Right Now
The Yankees are the second-place team in the American League East with an 89-65 record in 154 games.
They have won seven out of their last ten games.

title: Iván Herrera y José Caballero destacan al bate; Cardinals y Yankees pierden en la MLB
author: Eric Conte
body:
Los panameños Iván Herrera y José Caballero tuvieron una jornada destacada en las Grandes Ligas, con buenas producciones al bate, aunque sus equipos, Cardenales de San Luis y Yankees de Nueva York, terminaron perdiendo sus respectivos partidos el sábado 19 de septiembre.
Iván Herrera, de 5-3 con doblete en la derrota de San Luis
Herrera fue uno de los más activos en la ofensiva de los Cardenales: se fue de 5-3 con un doblete y un ponche. A pesar de su aporte, San Luis cayó 8-5 ante los Nacionales de Washington en el Busch Stadium. En el mismo encuentro, el también panameño Leonardo Bernal conectó de 6-1, anotó una carrera y registró dos ponches.
José Caballero, perfecto al plato en la caída de los Yankees
José Caballero, conocido como “Chema” o “Cabby”, tuvo una noche perfecta al plato: se fue de 2-2 y además recibió un pasaporte en la derrota de los Yankees 5-3 frente a los Diamondbacks de Arizona en el Chase Field. Con esta actuación, Caballero mantiene un promedio de .238, con 14 cuadrangulares, 51 empujadas, 49 carreras anotadas y 32 bases robadas en la temporada.

title: Yankees sueñan con Aaron Judge en playoffs
author: Emmanuel Campa
body:
Los Yankees de Nueva York mantienen viva la esperanza de recuperar a Aaron Judge para los playoffs, aunque el regreso de su capitán dependerá de cómo evolucione durante los últimos días de la temporada regular. 
Judge fue colocado nuevamente en la lista de lesionados de 10 días después de que una resonancia magnética reveló una distensión en el músculo sóleo, ubicado en la parte baja de la pantorrilla. La lesión afecta principalmente su capacidad para correr y, por ahora, el poderoso bateador no tiene una fecha definida para volver a la alineación.  
“Me gustaría estar de vuelta para la postemporada”, reconoció Judge, seleccionado ocho veces al Juego de Estrellas, quien aseguró que continuará realizando todos los entrenamientos posibles con la intención de estar disponible en octubre. 
El escenario todavía permite cierto optimismo para los Yankees. Judge podrá ser reactivado para el último partido de la temporada regular, programado para el 27 de septiembre, aunque eso no significa que necesariamente estará listo para jugar ese día.  
La nueva lesión llegó apenas una semana después de que Judge regresó de una fractura de costilla que lo mantuvo fuera de actividad durante más de tres meses. Desde su vuelta acumuló cuatro hits en 23 turnos, con 13 ponches y un extrabase en siete partidos. En toda la temporada únicamente ha participado en 66 encuentros.  
La ausencia del capitán ha acompañado a Nueva York durante buena parte de la campaña. Los Yankees presentan marca de 41-25 en los partidos en los que Judge estuvo disponible, mientras que tienen récord de 48-39 cuando el toletero no formó parte de la alineación.  
Aaron Boone, mánager de los Yankees, evitó ponerle una fecha al regreso de su estrella y señaló que la decisión dependerá exclusivamente de la respuesta de su cuerpo durante la recuperación. 
Judge, por su parte, admitió la frustración que representa volver a quedar fuera después de una ausencia tan prolongada, especialmente porque su intención era disputar algunos encuentros antes del inicio de la postemporada. 
Para los Yankees, el tiempo comienza a convertirse en el principal rival. La temporada regular entra en sus últimos días y el objetivo ahora es conseguir que Judge pueda estar disponible cuando llegue octubre, incluso si eso significa hacerlo sin demasiados partidos de preparación. 
Nueva York ya piensa en los playoffs. Y una parte importante de sus aspiraciones pasa por volver a colocar a Aaron Judge en el corazón de su alineación.

title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Tom Tresh
author: Andrew Mearns
body:
Although a familiar name to scholars of Yankees history (for lack of a better term), Tom Tresh did not have a long big-league career due to injuries and treatment of the time. Nonetheless, he was among the Bombers’ finest players of the 1960s and one of the last gasps of greatness from their vaunted farm system. As the team around him declined, Tresh continued to perform at a high level at multiple positions, making him a fan favorite and a valued final connection to those terrific teams of old.
Thomas Michael Tresh
Born: September 20, 1938 (Detroit, MI)
Died: October 14, 2008 (Venice, FL)
Yankees Tenure: 1961-69
September 1938 was a big month for the Tresh family, as patriarch Mike made his MLB debut with the Chicago White Sox on September 4th, and son Tom was born on September 20th. Mike Tresh spent 11 years catching for the South Siders, playing in over 1,000 games in the majors until ending his career in 1949 with Cleveland. He was named an All-Star by the Associated Press in 1945, the only year of the 20th century in which the Midsummer Classic wasn’t held (after the creation of the All-Star Game in 1933).
Tom Tresh spent some time living with his parents in an apartment in Chicago, but he went to school in Michigan, as his father’s career was over by then. At Allen Park High School in Detroit, he lettered in baseball, football, and basketball, and he later went to Central Michigan University in Mount Pleasant. His father’s prestigious job allowed him to gain some first-hand perspective on how clubhouses operated and what big-league living was like. He was even allowed to become a bat boy when his father briefly managed at Daytona Beach and Wausau, Wisconsin in 1951 and 1952, respectively.
MLB teams knew just how talented the younger Tresh was, and they kept a close scouting eye on him growing up. Mike and Doris Tresh wanted their son to go to college, but after a year at shortstop in Central Michigan, Tresh felt that he could not turn down a $30,000 offer from the New York Yankees. It was a lot of money for the time, the Yankees were baseball’s marquee team, and like many boys in the ’50s, Mickey Mantle was his idol. He recalled going to Tiger Stadium when the Yankees came to town and watching him intently from the upper deck in center field. Mike had even taught Tom how to switch-hit like Mantle.
Ultimately, Tresh was able to convince his parents to let him sign with the Yankees at age 19, assuring them that he would go back and finish his degree. He was on his way to joining his hero at Yankee Stadium.
Tresh was quick to impress in his first exposure to pro ball in 1958, as he hit .316/.435/.445 for the St. Petersburg Saints in 126 games of Class D ball. His pace slowed down upon a late-season promotion to the Double-A New Orleans Pelicans (no, not them), where the average player was seven years his senior.
It was around this time that Tresh met his idol for the first time, down in spring training. It was recalled in Jane Leavy’s book on Mantle, The Last Boy:
The first time he saw Mantle up close, Tresh was in an elevator during rookie camp in St. Pete--the doors opened and there he was. Though they stood eye to eye, Mantle seemed a thousand steps higher--a feeling Tresh never got over. “I never could see him as just one step higher than I was.”
After batting .246/.363/.415 in 133 games with the Binghamton Triplets in A-ball in 1960, the Yankees tested him at the minors’ highest level. There was no pressure to promote the young prospect, as the big-league club was in the midst of one of their greatest seasons in history, a 109-win romp to the World Series powered by Mantle and Roger Maris. Tresh had a superb year in his own right, hitting .315/.380/.428 in 141 games at shortstop with Richmond and taking home International League MVP honors.
As a reward of sorts, Tresh was tabbed for his MLB debut as a September call-up in ‘61. With another Rookie of the Year-turned-regular in Tony Kubek at shortstop ahead of him, it was hard to find time. Tresh did make it into nine games though, debuting on September 3rd as a pinch-runner and taking his first at-bat on September 16th in his hometown at Tiger Stadium. Tresh notched his first big-league hit in the first game of a doubleheader on September 26th against the Orioles. The huge story that day was Maris tying Babe Ruth with his 60th homer of the season, but Tresh played his part as well, singling to right field off Jack Fisher in the middle of a rally that put the Yankees in front.
Tresh was only technically part of a championship team in ‘61, but the next year, he truly earned his ring. An opportunity arose, as Kubek was recalled to the U.S. Army Reserve. Manager Ralph Houk entrusted the starting role at shortstop to Tresh over fellow infielder Phil Linz. It was the right call, as Tresh went on to an All-Star rookie campaign. He capably fielded the position in Kubek’s absence while hitting well from both sides of the plate. Tresh racked up 20 homers and a .286/.359/.441 triple slash, good for a 119 wRC+, Rookie of the Year honors, and even a 12th-place finish for MVP.
There was the potential for an awkward situation to arise when Kubek returned from the service in August, and Houk tasked Tresh with playing alongside Mantle in left field. In 573 minor-league games, Tresh had never manned the outfield, but he handled it with aplomb. Having previously made that same transition, Mantle even gave Tresh his glove, choosing to befriend and praise his potential future replacement rather than ignoring him, as Joe DiMaggio did to Mantle. Tresh knew Mantle had his flaws, but he loved him anyway and eventually nicknamed his son “Mickey” for him in 1964. (“What the fuck did you do that for?” Mantle later asked. He knew he was no idol.)
The Yankees won the pennant and played the San Francisco Giants in the World Series. Tresh had only just turned 24 and yet he didn’t appear to be fazed at all. He hit .321/.345/.464 in the seven-game series, leading the Yankees in hits and average. It wasn’t garbage time participation either, as his three-run homer in the eighth off Jack Sanford gave the Yankees a Game 5 victory,
Mike Tresh was in the stands at Yankee Stadium when Tresh hit that homer to win Game 5, crying tears of joy. His son had definitely made it.
A terrific one-handed catch by Tresh on a seventh-inning Willie Mays drive in Game 7 likely saved a run with the red-hot Willie McCovey on deck. The Yankees edged the Giants 1-0 to bring home their 20th championship.
Rather than suffering a sophomore slump in ‘63, Tresh had an outstanding year. He was on fire, hitting .269/.371/.487 with 25 dingers and a career-best 141 wRC+. Tresh was an All-Star for the second year in a row and again earned down-ballot MVP votes as the Yankees ran away with the AL pennant thanks to 104 victories. Tresh spent the year in the outfield and even manned center while Mantle missed a few months due to injury. Unfortunately, they had no answer for the overwhelming Los Angeles Dodgers pitching staff in the World Series. Tresh managed to take the seemingly untouchable Sandy Koufax deep late in Game 1, but like most of his team, he was otherwise quiet. They swept the Yankees away.
Houk moved up to the front office in 1964 and the popular Yogi Berra took over in the dugout. The Yankees won their fifth straight pennant, but it was as tough a climb to the top as the team of that era ever endured. They battled injuries and ineffectiveness from several positions, including Kubek at shortstop. Tresh remained a solid player, though he also saw his numbers slip. The Yankees faced a tough competitor in the Cardinals, and it was a tight seven-game series. Tresh slugged .636 and homered twice, including a game-tying blast off World Series MVP Bob Gibson in the ninth inning of Game 5.
It wasn’t enough, as the Cardinals prevailed and Berra was stunningly fired.
The Yankees pulled off a classic “if you can’t beat him, sign him” move for ‘65 by hiring Johnny Keane, who just beat them in the World Series. Kubek played poorly at shortstop and missed a lot of time, but Keane kept Tresh in the outfield, alternating him between relieving Mantle in center and playing left (there was even some right mixed in). To some extent, it paid off, as Tresh finished in the top 10 for AL MVP, won a Gold Glove, and showed no sign of ill-effect at the plate with a 136 wRC+. To another extent, it didn’t, as the team around him was not good; the Yankees fell below .500 for the first time in 40 years.
Despite the increasing effects of a pitching-heavy era, Tresh pulled off a career-high in home runs in ‘66, smacking 27 dingers in 151 games. That was one of the few highlights for the Yankees though, who were abysmal and dropped all the way to last place. Keane was fired and replaced by Houk in May, who moved Tresh to third base since he wanted to give a young Roy White time in the outfield. Tresh ended up splitting time between left and the hot corner. The Yankees appreciated his athleticism and Zobristian ability to handle basically any position, but it still mystified Tresh to a certain degree:
“I win Rookie of the Year as a shortstop and they move me to the outfield. Then I win a Gold Glove Award there in 1965 and they move me to third. I couldn’t figure out what position I was supposed to prove I could play.“
Although Tresh was only 28 entering the 1967 campaign, the second game of spring training was the beginning of the end. He popped his right knee while firing a throw across his body from left field to the cutoff man. Tresh was in serious pain and could barely walk; it was later revealed to be torn cartilage. Inexplicably, the Yankees told him that he should try to play on it rather than undergo surgery.
It was a disaster. Through some miracle, Tresh kept his numbers above league-average with a 106 wRC+, but his OPS dipped below .700 and he was a shadow of the defender he once was in left field. Tresh later recalled that his knee “gave out five more times” that year, undoubtedly affecting his future. He had surgery to repair the damage in the offseason (why he wasn’t simply shut down on a 90-loss team is a mystery), but the damage was done. Tresh was mostly a hobbling shortstop in ‘68 and his play only worsened in ‘69.
By then, the only other position players aside from Tresh remaining from the Yankees’ early ’60s glory were Joe Pepitone and catcher Jake Gibbs. Mantle, Maris, Berra, Kubek, Elston Howard, and Bobby Richardson were all gone. Tresh was miserable. The team was middling at best, and he could barely hit, let alone play shortstop. So he asked if the Yankees would trade him to the Tigers, where he could at least be close to home, not to mention play for the defending World Series champions. The Yankees acquiesced, and Tresh was dealt to Detroit on June 14th. The very next person to wear number 15 for the Yankees was a worthy heir: Thurman Munson.
Tresh remained primarily a shortstop and appeared in 94 games for the Tigers, batting .224/.305/.387 with 13 homers, a .692 OPS that was amusingly still good for a 92 wRC+ in the league-wide offensive malaise. While Detroit was a better team, there was still no competing with the 109-win juggernaut Orioles, who ran away with the AL East in the first year of divisional play.
Tresh had gone through another surgery on his knee in hopes of playing again in 1970. However, the Tigers told him that he would need to rehab in the minors, and Tresh had no intention of living that kind of life again, particularly with a wife and four kids at home. So Tom Tresh retired having played just eight games after his 31st birthday. His story was a warning sign about the dangers of dismissing injuries, but he had no regrets.
Even though Tresh was so talented before his injury that the Red Sox briefly considered a swap of him for Carl Yastrzemski, one can’t blame Tresh for his overall happiness about his career. He was a beloved teammate, a World Series champion, an All-Star, and an MVP candidate for baseball’s greatest franchise. At the time of his retirement, he was even in the Yankees’ all-time top 20 in homers at 140 (the recent offensive spike pushed him back to a tie for 34th as of 2026). Tresh had a fine life post-retirement too, as he did fulfill that college promise to his parents, even after his father’s passing in 1966.
Tresh earned his degree in physical education from Central Michigan in 1969, where he later served as an assistant baseball coach for 15 years and helped innovate a training tool for sliding and diving called the Slide-Rite. His son Mickey inherited the baseball gene, playing at Miami University of Ohio before going through four years in the minors as well with New York and Detroit. The younger Tresh even got a glimpse of the ascendance of one of the great successors to Tresh and Mantle in center: his 1988 Prince William Yankees teammate, 19-year-old Bernie Williams.
The bond between the Mantles and Treshes remained strong—the two Yankees were at a card show in Nashville when Mickey Tresh called to inform his father that he just had a boy of his own, who he named Tommy. Mantle celebrated with Tresh by ordering a $150 bottle of Dom Perignon, raising a toast to the lad, and later writing “Happy birthday Tommy, we had one for you. Mickey Mantle.” on the bottle.
That bottle could have sold for something valuable, as the glove Mantle gave to Tresh in 1962 was enough by itself to put a down payment on a cottage. Tom Tresh never sold it though; it meant too much to him, and he grieved as much as any of his teammates on the day Mantle passed away from liver cancer in 1995. Thirteen years later, Tresh suddenly left the world as well, as he died of a heart attack on October 14, 2008, not even a month after turning 70.
At least Tresh got to see the old Yankee Stadium one last time before it closed for good, as he was in attendance at the final Old-Timers’ Day. As always, the crowd gave him an ovation before he stepped to foul line one last time. Number 15 will always mean Thurman Munson, but it will also always be connected to Tommy Tresh, another fantastic Yankee.

Kubek played poorly at shortstop and missed a lot of time, but Keane kept Tresh in the outfield, alternating him between relieving Mantle in center and playing left (there was even some right mixed in). To some extent, it paid off, as Tresh finished in the top 10 for AL MVP, won a Gold Glove, and showed no sign of ill-effect at the plate with a 136 wRC+. To another extent, it didn’t, as the team around him was not good; the Yankees fell below .500 for the first time in 40 years.

That was one of the few highlights for the Yankees though, who were abysmal and dropped all the way to last place. Tresh ended up splitting time between left and the hot corner. “I win Rookie of the Year as a shortstop and they move me to the outfield. Then I win a Gold Glove Award there in 1965 and they move me to third. I couldn’t figure out what position I was supposed to prove I could play.“

Inexplicably, the Yankees told him that he should try to play on it rather than undergo surgery.

Mantle, Maris, Berra, Kubek, Elston Howard, and Bobby Richardson were all gone. Tresh was miserable. The team was middling at best, and he could barely hit, let alone play shortstop. So he asked if the Yankees would trade him to the Tigers, where he could at least be close to home, not to mention play for the defending World Series champions. The Yankees acquiesced, and Tresh was dealt to Detroit on June 14th. The very next person to wear number 15 for the Yankees was a worthy heir: Thurman Munson.
Tresh remained primarily a shortstop and appeared in 94 games for the Tigers, batting .224/.305/.387 with 13 homers, a .692 OPS that was amusingly still good for a 92 wRC+ in the league-wide offensive malaise. While Detroit was a better team, there was still no competing with the 109-win juggernaut Orioles, who ran away with the AL East in the first year of divisional play.
Tresh had gone through another surgery on his knee in hopes of playing again in 1970. However, the Tigers told him that he would need to rehab in the minors, and Tresh had no intention of living that kind of life again, particularly with a wife and four kids at home. So Tom Tresh retired having played just eight games after his 31st birthday. His story was a warning sign about the dangers of dismissing injuries, but he had no regrets.
Even though Tresh was so talented before his injury that the Red Sox briefly considered a swap of him for Carl Yastrzemski, one can’t blame Tresh for his overall happiness about his career. He was a beloved teammate, a World Series champion, an All-Star, and an MVP candidate for baseball’s greatest franchise. At the time of his retirement, he was even in the Yankees’ all-time top 20 in homers at 140 (the recent offensive spike pushed him back to a tie for 34th as of 2026). Tresh had a fine life post-retirement too, as he did fulfill that college promise to his parents, even after his father’s passing in 1966.
Tresh earned his degree in physical education from Central Michigan in 1969, where he later served as an assistant baseball coach for 15 years and helped innovate a training tool for sliding and diving called the Slide-Rite. The bond between the Mantles and Treshes remained strong—the two Yankees were at a card show in Nashville when Mickey Tresh called to inform his father that he just had a boy of his own, who he named Tommy. Mantle celebrated with Tresh by ordering a $150 bottle of Dom Perignon, raising a toast to the lad, and later writing “Happy birthday Tommy, we had one for you. Mickey Mantle.” on the bottle.
That bottle could have sold for something valuable, as the glove Mantle gave to Tresh in 1962 was enough by itself to put a down payment on a cottage. Tom Tresh never sold it though; it meant too much to him, and he grieved as much as any of his teammates on the day Mantle passed away from liver cancer in 1995. Thirteen years later, Tresh suddenly left the world as well, as he died of a heart attack on October 14, 2008, not even a month after turning 70.

As always, the crowd gave him an ovation before he stepped to foul line one last time. Number 15 will always mean Thurman Munson, but it will also always be connected to Tommy Tresh, another fantastic Yankee.
rss_title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Tom Tresh
rss_body:
Although a familiar name to scholars of Yankees history (for lack of a better term), Tom Tresh did not have a long big-league career due to injuries and treatment of the time. Nonetheless, he was among the Bombers’ finest players of the 1960s and one of the last gasps of greatness from their vaunted farm system. As the team around him declined, Tresh continued to perform at a high level at multiple positions, making him a fan favorite and a valued final connection to those terrific teams of old.
Thomas Michael Tresh
Born: September 20, 1938 (Detroit, MI)
Died: October 14, 2008 (Venice, FL)
Yankees Tenure: 1961-69
September 1938 was a big month for the Tresh family, as patriarch Mike made his MLB debut with the Chicago White Sox on September 4th, and son Tom was born on September 20th. Mike Tresh spent 11 years catching for the South Siders, playing in over 1,000 games in the majors until ending his career in 1949 with Cleveland. He was named an All-Star by the Associated Press in 1945, the only year of the 20th century in which the Midsummer Classic wasn’t held (after the creation of the All-Star Game in 1933).
Tom Tresh spent some time living with his parents in an apartment in Chicago, but he went to school in Michigan, as his father’s career was over by then. At Allen Park High School in Detroit, he lettered in baseball, football, and basketball, and he later went to Central Michigan University in Mount Pleasant. His father’s prestigious job allowed him to gain some first-hand perspective on how clubhouses operated and what big-league living was like. He was even allowed to become a bat boy when his father briefly managed at Daytona Beach and Wausau, Wisconsin in 1951 and 1952, respectively.
MLB teams knew just how talented the younger Tresh was, and they kept a close scouting eye on him growing up. Mike and Doris Tresh wanted their son to go to college, but after a year at shortstop in Central Michigan, Tresh felt that he could not turn down a $30,000 offer from the New York Yankees. It was a lot of money for the time, the Yankees were baseball’s marquee team, and like many boys in the ’50s, Mickey Mantle was his idol. He recalled going to Tiger Stadium when the Yankees came to town and watching him intently from the upper deck in center field. Mike had even taught Tom how to switch-hit like Mantle.
Ultimately, Tresh was able to convince his parents to let him sign with the Yankees at age 19, assuring them that he would go back and finish his degree. He was on his way to joining his hero at Yankee Stadium.
Tresh was quick to impress in his first exposure to pro ball in 1958, as he hit .316/.435/.445 for the St. Petersburg Saints in 126 games of Class D ball. His pace slowed down upon a late-season promotion to the Double-A New Orleans Pelicans (no, not them), where the average player was seven years his senior.
It was around this time that Tresh met his idol for the first time, down in spring training. It was recalled in Jane Leavy’s book on Mantle, The Last Boy:
The first time he saw Mantle up close, Tresh was in an elevator during rookie camp in St. Pete--the doors opened and there he was. Though they stood eye to eye, Mantle seemed a thousand steps higher--a feeling Tresh never got over. “I never could see him as just one step higher than I was.”
After batting .246/.363/.415 in 133 games with the Binghamton Triplets in A-ball in 1960, the Yankees tested him at the minors’ highest level. There was no pressure to promote the young prospect, as the big-league club was in the midst of one of their greatest seasons in history, a 109-win romp to the World Series powered by Mantle and Roger Maris. Tresh had a superb year in his own right, hitting .315/.380/.428 in 141 games at shortstop with Richmond and taking home International League MVP honors.
As a reward of sorts, Tresh was tabbed for his MLB debut as a September call-up in ‘61. With another Rookie of the Year-turned-regular in Tony Kubek at shortstop ahead of him, it was hard to find time. Tresh did make it into nine games though, debuting on September 3rd as a pinch-runner and taking his first at-bat on September 16th in his hometown at Tiger Stadium. Tresh notched his first big-league hit in the first game of a doubleheader on September 26th against the Orioles. The huge story that day was Maris tying Babe Ruth with his 60th homer of the season, but Tresh played his part as well, singling to right field off Jack Fisher in the middle of a rally that put the Yankees in front.
Tresh was only technically part of a championship team in ‘61, but the next year, he truly earned his ring. An opportunity arose, as Kubek was recalled to the U.S. Army Reserve. Manager Ralph Houk entrusted the starting role at shortstop to Tresh over fellow infielder Phil Linz. It was the right call, as Tresh went on to an All-Star rookie campaign. He capably fielded the position in Kubek’s absence while hitting well from both sides of the plate. Tresh racked up 20 homers and a .286/.359/.441 triple slash, good for a 119 wRC+, Rookie of the Year honors, and even a 12th-place finish for MVP.
There was the potential for an awkward situation to arise when Kubek returned from the service in August, and Houk tasked Tresh with playing alongside Mantle in left field. In 573 minor-league games, Tresh had never manned the outfield, but he handled it with aplomb. Having previously made that same transition, Mantle even gave Tresh his glove, choosing to befriend and praise his potential future replacement rather than ignoring him, as Joe DiMaggio did to Mantle. Tresh knew Mantle had his flaws, but he loved him anyway and eventually nicknamed his son “Mickey” for him in 1964. (“What the fuck did you do that for?” Mantle later asked. He knew he was no idol.)
The Yankees won the pennant and played the San Francisco Giants in the World Series. Tresh had only just turned 24 and yet he didn’t appear to be fazed at all. He hit .321/.345/.464 in the seven-game series, leading the Yankees in hits and average. It wasn’t garbage time participation either, as his three-run homer in the eighth off Jack Sanford gave the Yankees a Game 5 victory,
Mike Tresh was in the stands at Yankee Stadium when Tresh hit that homer to win Game 5, crying tears of joy. His son had definitely made it.

title: 2026 Cubs Heroes and Goats: Michael Busch is the Superhero vs. the Reds
author: Thomas Smith
body:
There just haven’t been enough games like Saturday’s for the Cubs this year. It wasn’t easy. It never is with this team if they aren’t scoring 10 plus runs. But the pitching was really good save for one rough inning in the fifth that probably wasn’t as bad as it looked, aided by a weird, bad throw from Dansby Swanson on a relay play. That led to one of the two runs that the Cubs did allow in this one to being unearned. Daniel Palencia followed and was terrific. Aaron Civale was a little shaky. Ryan Zeferjahn is really tough to watch despite clearly immense talent. I’ve not followed his career and haven’t dug into it, but without doing so, I can confidently say that every coach he’s ever has dreamed of a fully unlocked Zeferjahn who might be a truly elite pitcher. Ryan Rolison faced one batter, doing his job and recording a save.
Fun fact, this team has allowed exactly two runs 34 times this year. They are 26-8 (.765) when they do so. I was surprised it was so many games, given the struggles of this pitching staff. They’ve allowed two or fewer 50 times. They have a record of 42-8 in those games. If you mentally shed a tear for this team not having a healthy dose of 2024 Justin Steele, 2025 Cade Horton or 2026 Ben Brown, this is why. I heard it said on the Marquee pregame Saturday that this position player group should have led to a 100-plus win team. It felt so bold. But it’s totally true. With reasonable pitching, this is a 100-plus win team. And that’s why the postseason is not completely hopeless. If they get some pitching, they can win.
On the other side of the ball, the Cubs turned eight hits and three walks and a hit batter into five runs. So slightly less traffic than the night before, but one more run. Two homers and not one. A double to go with it. But more than anything, it was just clustering things together a little better. For the second straight night, the Cubs got largely nothing out of the duo of Pete Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman, who have led the way for this team, particularly in the second half. The rest of the lineup was pretty balanced and the offense was a team effort.
It’s been a week now since the last double-digit offensive game. It’s probably not worth a lot of mention, but it seems like the Cubs get one of those every week or 10 days. So that’s probably coming somewhere in the near term. It would be nice to get one of those easier ones and not to have to sweat every inning as this team closes in on clinching a playoff spot and tries to secure the top Wild Card. Regardless, the Cubs will have a chance to win a third straight series on Sunday afternoon and that’s what you want to see. It’s been a welcome bounceback after the nightmare in Milwaukee. As I said following that last game there, this team is very professional. They’ll bounce back and this won’t linger. It was a really good time to be right.
With any luck, this team will just keep on winning series as the season winds down. Win Sunday afternoon, get home and take a series from a Marlins team that is fighting down to the wire despite being eliminated. The Marlins are in San Diego and we’ll catch them coming back east after playing there and in Arizona. That’s a tough trip. Especially when the clock strikes midnight on your season mid trip. Nine-game trips are always hard. But three good teams, a couple of different time zones (that are both different from their home time zone), different styles of play. It’s a lot. Then the Cubs get a Red Sox team that is pretty squarely locked into the second Wild Card spot. They’ll want to be lining up pitching for their Wild Card series which very likely will be against the Yankees. Of course, the Cubs will be getting theirs set too. But the gap between one and six for Cub starters just isn’t massive (which is damning with faint praise).
Anyway, it was a good night in Cincinnati. Seiya Suzuki seems to be coming out of a slump a little bit. Three singles in the last two games. Only one really hit hard, but using the field and having some success. Michael Busch hit a monster homer. Dansby Swanson had his rehab washed out, but save for the weird throw, he looked like he’s ready to contribute. He had a single and a homer of his own. Good to get Dansby back. It’s his defense that provides most of his value. But, Dansby has the mind and approach of a superstar. He doesn’t shy from the biggest moments. That’s not a bad bat to have down at eight or nine in your lineup. This team is better with Dansby on the field. Just as it usually is with Ian Happ on the field. A player need not be a Superstar to produce consistent positive value for a team.
Three Positives:
- Daniel Palencia faced six batters in the sixth and seventh inning. That sixth inning was huge with just a one-run lead and the 2-3-4 hitters due up for the Reds. He was fairly efficient and got a second inning of work. He’s looked better the last couple of times and is maybe re-finding himself just in time.
- Dansby Swanson had a single and a homer, scored twice.
- Michael Busch had a single, a homer and was hit by a pitch. He scored once. He had a really nice homestand before this trip (.316/.417/.526). He hasn’t really hit a groove all year long. Maybe he too is hitting his peak at just the right time?
Game 155, September 19: Cubs 5, Reds 2 (86-69)
Reminder: Heroes and Goats are determined by WPA scores and are in no way subjective.
THREE HEROES:
- Superhero: Michael Busch (.208). 2-3, HR, HBP, RBI, R
- Hero: Daniel Palencia (.197). 2 IP, 6 BF, 3K
- Sidekick: Seiya Suzuki (.128). 2-3, BB, RBI
THREE GOATS:
- Billy Goat: Tyrone Taylor (-.125). 0-3
- Goat: Carson Kelly (-.094). 0-4
- Kid: Pete Crow-Armstrong (-.082). 0-5
WPA Play of the Game: Michael Busch hit a solo homer with one out in the sixth to give the Cubs a one run lead. (.167)
Reds Play of the Game: JJ Bleday singled with a runner on first and one outs, the Reds down two in the fifth. This is the play where Dansby Swanson threw it past Alex Bregman at third, allowing a run to score. (.149)
Cubs Player of the Game:
Game 154 Winner: Carson Kelly received just 17 of 43 votes, but with very divided voting, that was enough to win.
Rizzo Award Standings: (Top 5/Bottom 5)
The award is named for Anthony Rizzo, who finished first in this category three of the first four years it was in existence and four times overall. He also recorded the highest season total ever at +65.5. The point scale is three points for a Superhero down to negative three points for a Billy Goat.
- Alex Bregman +25
- Pete Crow-Armstrong +22.5
- Carson Kelly +17.5
- Shōta Imanaga +15
- Ben Brown +13.5
- Jameson Taillon -13
- Nico Hoerner -16
- Dansby Swanson -17
- Seiya Suzuki -17
- Caleb Thielbar -17.5
Scoreboard Watching: The Phillies lost for the second straight night. They fall one game behind the Cubs, while the Padres won and are tied with the Cubs. The Cubs hold tiebreakers over both teams. The Diamondbacks won a game started by Cam Schlittler, finding some offense against him and then walking it off to win. The Arizona win delays the eventual Cub playoff clinch. That’s two this week as they try to keep their very narrow playoff hopes alive. Even with the win, they remain four games behind the Phillies for the last playoff spot.
Up Next: The Cubs finish the series with the Reds. David Peterson (8-8, 5.11) starts for the Cubs. David is 2-1 with a 4.31 over his last seven, including a win last time against the Braves, allowing a run on three hits and three walks over six innings. The general trend for Peterson is about four good starts to every bad one and they are very stratified. So once he gets it going, he usually delivers. Look to see if he can get locked in early in Cincy. Certainly a guy who likes to keep the ball down is a welcome choice in that park. He held the Reds to two runs over five at Wrigley at the end of August. But they also saw him twice as a Met and did quite well against him (nine runs in eight innings of work).
24-year-old Rhett Lowder (6-11, 5.79) has had a rough first full year as a starter (27 appearances, 24 starts). The strain of a long season may be weighing him down as the year draws towards a close. He’s 2-4 with a 7.13 over his last seven games. He’s allowed 45 hits and 12 walks in just 35.1 innings over those seven starts. The Cubs have seen him twice as a starter and once as a reliever. As a starter, he’s allowed six runs in just eight innings of work. The two relief innings were scoreless, though he issued two walks. He and Peterson faced each other in that game in August. Lowder won, despite allowing three runs over five innings. He did a good job that night staying in the strike zone, not walking anyone (the only time he’s done so since July). He hasn’t won since that start at the end of August, losing all three starts (Brewers, Dodgers, Dodgers, ouch).
Get the offense going early and see if you can post some crooked numbers and ride that to a win. Don’t let Lowder settle in and find some of what made him a 7th overall pick in 2023. He’ll probably eventually be a good starter. But how about not now?

title: Cam Schlittler Enters MLB History With Sandy Koufax, Bob Gibson During Cy Young Race
author: Justin Binkowski; Unknown
body:
New York Yankees right-hander Cam Schlittler has joined two Hall of Fame pitchers in the record books after what was likely his second-to-last start of the 2026 regular season.
Schlittler tossed six innings against the Arizona Diamondbacks on Saturday, giving up one earned run on three hits and three walks while striking out six. This was the 24th time this season the right-hander hasn't allowed more than one earned run in a start, tying Hall of Famers Bob Gibson and Sandy Koufax for the second-most such starts since 1920, according to MLB.com's Sarah Langs. Koufax is also at the top of that list with 25 starts in which he gave up no more than one earned run, so the Yankees hurler will have a chance to tie the Dodgers legend again in his final regular-season outing of the year.
This stat is just the latest example of how truly dominant Schlittler has been this season. In fact, some fans have been debating whether the hard-throwing righty could be a legitimate contender for the 2026 American League MVP. At the very least, the young pitcher has made a strong case for the 2026 AL Cy Young Award.
Has Cam Schlittler already done enough to claim the AL Cy Young?
With just one week left in the 2026 MLB regular season, the two pitchers with the best chance to win the American League Cy Young Award are Schlittler and Toronto Blue Jays right-hander Dylan Cease. Schlittler now has an AL-leading 1.94 ERA in 32 starts this year, racking up 234 strikeouts in 190 2/3 innings. Meanwhile, Cease leads the American League with 239 strikeouts and has a 2.40 ERA in 169 innings.
In Cease's most recent start on Friday, the 30-year-old threw just 2 2/3 innings and walked six batters. He had an MRI done on his shoulder Saturday night and is no longer expected to make his next scheduled start on Wednesday, according to The Athletic's Mitch Bannon. While the Toronto hurler could pitch again later in the week, this may impact his chances of making a late push for the 2026 AL Cy Young Award.
As things stand, Schlittler seems like the frontrunner for this year's AL Cy Young Award. But the final week of the regular season could play a last-minute role in the eventual outcome.
Justin Binkowski is a lifelong baseball fan returning to cover the sport he loves after spending nearly a decade writing about video games. Before his time as managing editor at Dot Esports, Binkowski attended King's College in Wilkes-Barre, PA, where he was also a relief pitcher on the school's baseball team. While in college, Binkowski was a media relations intern for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders during the 2014 season.

title: The only Yankees position without multiple Silver Slugger winners should send message to front office
author: Stephen Parello
body:
The New York Yankees aren't nicknamed the Bronx Bombers for no reason. For that reason, they've been well represented in the Louisville Slugger Silver Slugger Awards throughout the years. The Yankees have multiple representatives at every position except for one: shortstop.
This is in part because the award was first introduced in 1980, meaning that franchise greats and champions like Phil Rizzuto and Frank Crosetti missed the boat by a large margin. Another mitigating factor is that New York had one player dominate the position for much of the Silver Slugger era. That, of course, is Derek Jeter, who had a stranglehold on the position for the better part of two decades, taking home the award five times himself.
But while it seems like yesterday, Jeter's last big league season was in 2014. Since then, the position has looked pretty bleak. From 2015 through the present day, the Yankees have gotten a .715 OPS out of the position, which ranks 15th in the majors during that span.
That number includes the Didi Gregorius years, which included some very fine performances. Gregorius hit 97 homers in pinstripes over five seasons, while slashing .269/.313/.446. That's nothing to sneeze at, but he was never the AL's best hitter at the position during his time here.
Gregorius left following the 2019 season, and since then, things have been bleak. From 2020 onward, we have mostly been dealing with Isiah Kiner-Falefa and Anthony Volpe at short. In that time period, Yankees shortstops have produced a .668 OPS, ranking 26th in baseball.
The Yankees can't continue getting subpar offensive production out of the shortstop position
Right now, the hope for the future is George Lombard Jr. The club's top prospect got off to a hot start, but since then, he's cooled substantially. It's too early to write him off just yet, especially at just 21 years old. However, the Yankees can't afford to get into another Volpe-esque holding pattern where years go by and no material improvements are made.
That leaves the front office with an interesting conundrum. Shortstops who can hit and field don't grow on trees, and while Brian Cashman passed on a generational shortstop free-agent class to sign IKF to keep the seat warm for Volpe, he cannot afford to repeat the same lethargic approach to the position.
Ideally, Lombard Jr. snatches the job for the next 20 years with a strong finish to 2026, a postseason to remember, and a spring training that eliminates all doubt. Jeter met with the promising youngster to advise him on the responsibilities that lie ahead. Now we'll see if he took those lessons to heart.
But if we come to the conclusion of New York's 2026 campaign and haven't seen Lombard Jr. show signs that he can consistently rise to the occasion; the Yankees must be opportunistic when it comes to pursuing upgrades.
After being wrapped up in rumors at the trade deadline, it's thought that the Angels could revisit trade talks for Zach Neto in the offseason. Another possible scenario is that the Astros follow the Kyle Tucker path and trade Jeremy Peña this winter ahead of his final year of team control.
In an ideal situation, the Yankees could acquire a player like Neto or Peña while retaining Lombard Jr. to hedge their bets. Worst-case scenario: Lombard Jr. busts, and the team has a high-end veteran to man the position. Best-case scenario: they have to undertake some shuffling, but Lombard Jr. is a star, and the team is deeper and better for it.
What can't happen is the Yankees put all their eggs in the Lombard Jr. bucket, and then miss out on young stars in their prime and let the position languish for another half-decade. The time to wait and see is over, and the time to be bold is now.

rss_title: The only Yankees position without multiple Silver Slugger winners should send message to front office
rss_body:
The New York Yankees aren't nicknamed the Bronx Bombers for no reason. For that reason, they've been well represented in the Louisville Slugger Silver Slugger Awards throughout the years. The Yankees have multiple representatives at every position except for one: shortstop.
This is in part because the award was first introduced in 1980, meaning that franchise greats and champions like Phil Rizzuto and Frank Crosetti missed the boat by a large margin. Another mitigating factor is that New York had one player dominate the position for much of the Silver Slugger era. That, of course, is Derek Jeter, who had a stranglehold on the position for the better part of two decades, taking home the award five times himself.
But while it seems like yesterday, Jeter's last big league season was in 2014. Since then, the position has looked pretty bleak. From 2015 through the present day, the Yankees have gotten a .715 OPS out of the position, which ranks 15th in the majors during that span.
That number includes the Didi Gregorius years, which included some very fine performances. Gregorius hit 97 homers in pinstripes over five seasons, while slashing .269/.313/.446. That's nothing to sneeze at, but he was never the AL's best hitter at the position during his time here.
Gregorius left following the 2019 season, and since then, things have been bleak. From 2020 onward, we have mostly been dealing with Isiah Kiner-Falefa and Anthony Volpe at short. In that time period, Yankees shortstops have produced a .668 OPS, ranking 26th in baseball.
The Yankees can't continue getting subpar offensive production out of the shortstop position
Right now, the hope for the future is George Lombard Jr. The club's top prospect got off to a hot start, but since then, he's cooled substantially. It's too early to write him off just yet, especially at just 21 years old. However, the Yankees can't afford to get into another Volpe-esque holding pattern where years go by and no material improvements are made.
That leaves the front office with an interesting conundrum. Shortstops who can hit and field don't grow on trees, and while Brian Cashman passed on a generational shortstop free-agent class to sign IKF to keep the seat warm for Volpe, he cannot afford to repeat the same lethargic approach to the position.
Ideally, Lombard Jr. snatches the job for the next 20 years with a strong finish to 2026, a postseason to remember, and a spring training that eliminates all doubt. Jeter met with the promising youngster to advise him on the responsibilities that lie ahead. Now we'll see if he took those lessons to heart.
But if we come to the conclusion of New York's 2026 campaign and haven't seen Lombard Jr. show signs that he can consistently rise to the occasion; the Yankees must be opportunistic when it comes to pursuing upgrades.
After being wrapped up in rumors at the trade deadline, it's thought that the Angels could revisit trade talks for Zach Neto in the offseason. Another possible scenario is that the Astros follow the Kyle Tucker path and trade Jeremy Peña this winter ahead of his final year of team control.
In an ideal situation, the Yankees could acquire a player like Neto or Peña while retaining Lombard Jr. to hedge their bets. Worst-case scenario: Lombard Jr. busts, and the team has a high-end veteran to man the position. Best-case scenario: they have to undertake some shuffling, but Lombard Jr. is a star, and the team is deeper and better for it.
What can't happen is the Yankees put all their eggs in the Lombard Jr. bucket, and then miss out on young stars in their prime and let the position languish for another half-decade. The time to wait and see is over, and the time to be bold is now.

title: Cubs magic number ticks lower, but home-field advantage is far from locked up
author: Jake Misener
body:
On a night dedicated to the 2001 World Series champions, the Arizona Diamondbacks fittingly walked off the Aaron Judge-less New York Yankees. That win, paired with a Chicago Cubs victory over the Cincinnati Reds, has the Cubs' magic number to clinch a playoff spot at just 2 with a week to go in the regular season.
That means any combination of two Cubs' wins and Diamondbacks' losses punches the former's playoff ticket, sending Chicago back to the postseason for the second consecutive season. It would take a catastrophic turn of events for that to not happen at this point. But the Cubs have their sights set on a higher prize: the #4 seed and home-field advantage in the Wild Card Series.
Home-field advantage is critical for the three teams ahead of Arizona in the wild-card standings. The Cubs and Padres enter Sunday tied for the first spot at 86-69 and the Phillies are hot on their heels at 85-70. Wodering why getting that top spot is so important? Just look at each team's home record:
- Cubs: 45-33
- Padres: 48-29
- Phillies: 41-34
Home-field advantage is critical to Cubs' World Series aspirations
Last postseason, the Cubs went 4-1 at Wrigley Field, taking down the Padres in the Wild Card Series and winning both of the games against Milwaukee in Chicago, as well. What they don't want to do is have to go to Philly or San Diego as the road team. The Padres are cooking at Petco Park of late, winning 22 of 27.
The Cubs go for a series win over the Reds on Sunday afternoon, then have a scheduled off-day Monday before returning home for the final home series of the regular season - a three-game set against Miami. Chicago then heads to Boston to close out the year against the Red Sox.
Looking at the rest of the NL playoff picture, the Brewers already locked up a fourth consecutive NL Central title and the Dodgers have won the NL West. Atlanta is knocking on the door of a division crown in the National League East, so it'll be all eyes on the wild-card race as the 2026 regular season draws to a close.

title: New York Yankees Get Positive Injury Update on Spencer Jones During D-Backs Series
author: Cole Shelton
body:
The New York Yankees avoided a major injury to star outfielder Spencer Jones.
Jones didn't play on Saturday due to an injury; it isn't considered long-term
New York is coming off a 5-3 loss to the Arizona Diamondbacks on Saturday, as the Yankees will look for the series win on Sunday.
New York Yankees Get Injury Update on Spencer Jones
After Jones didn't play on Saturday due to an injury, there was some concern about him. New York is already without Aaron Judge, so losing Jones before the playoffs begin would be a blow.
Yet, the injury to Jones doesn't seem serious, according to the MLB.com injury report, as he was available off the bench.
"Jammed his heel during Twins series earlier in the week, Jones said Sept. 19. Could be available off the bench," the injury report read.
The hope for the Yankees is Jones could return to the lineup on Sunday, or Tuesday when they begin a series against the Tampa Bay Rays. They could opt to give Jones another day off on Sunday to give him three full days off to make sure his jammed heel is fully healthy.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone, meanwhile, confirmed Jones was available off the bench on Saturday if needed.
"He was available, like I would've… if a spot came up to hit or we needed to do something I would've gone to him," Boone said.
Jones also said the injury was no big deal and doesn't need an IL stint.
Jones is hitting .248 with 10 home runs and 38 RBIs with the Yankees this season in 80 games in his first MLB season.
New York Right Now
The Yankees will be a Wild Card team again this year but could be without star slugger Aaron Judge.
Judge is back on the IL due to a right calf strain and he said he hopes he can return for the playoffs.
"I'd like to be back by the postseason," Judge said. "That's definitely the plan. [It's the] 10-day IL, so the 10th day is probably the last game of the season. So we'll see. I've got really no answers for you on any timeline or anything like that."
Judge doesn't know the grade of the strain, but is confident he can return for the playoffs.
"I've dealt with strains before and kind of played through them, but this was kind of in a different spot where it made it a little bit more difficult," Judge said.
The Yankees are 89-65 and 5 games back of the Rays for the top spot in the AL East.

title: New York Yankees Reveal Aaron Judge Diagnosis Before Diamondbacks Series Finale
author: Maria Aldrich
body:
After watching star slugger Aaron Judge return to the plate, fans hoped he'd help the New York Yankees as they wrap up their regular season.
But now, he's back on the IL, and new details have emerged.
Yankees Provide Latest Aaron Judge Update
According to MLB analyst Jim Bowden of The Athletic, the 34-year-old outfielder has been diagnosed with a "soleus strain which is a strain of the deeper calf muscle underneath the gastrocnemius."
He added, "Typical recovery is 2-6 weeks. Soleus strains often times linger because it's the muscle that works every time you stand/walk etc. Yanks have not shared the grade."
Aaron Judge calf injury is a soleus strain which is a strain of the deeper calf muscle underneath the gastrocnemius. Typical recovery is 2-6 weeks. Soleus strains often times linger because it's the muscle that works every time you stand/walk etc. Yanks have not shared the grade.
— Jim Bowden⚾️ (@JimBowdenGM) September 20, 2026
Since returning to the plate on Sept. 8, he's appeared in seven games.
He played in two against the Colorado Rockies, three against the New York Mets and two against the Minnesota Twins.
His last appearance was on Sept. 16.

title: New York Yankees Star George Lombard Jr. Makes Honest Gerrit Cole Statement
author: Ben Stinar
body:
On Sunday, the New York Yankees will finish their series with the Arizona Diamondbacks in Phoenix.
They are coming off a 5-3 loss on Saturday night.
That said, the series is tied up at 1-1 heading into the finale.
George Lombard Jr. Makes Honest Gerrit Cole Statement
On Friday, Gerrit Cole got the start.
He allowed just two earned runs in 6.0 innings.
After the game, George Lombard Jr. was asked about Cole (via YES Network).
Reporter: “Gerrit won a Cy Young in 2023 when you graduated from high school. What’s it like for you to play behind him?”
Lombard Jr.: “It’s awesome. Yeah. I’ve watched him dominate on the mound for as long as I can remember. It’s really cool to be on the same field as him.”
Looking At Lombard Jr.
Lombard Jr. was picked in the 1st round of the 2023 MLB Draft.
He made his MLB debut last month.
The 21-year-old is currently batting .227 with 29 hits, four home runs, 15 RBIs, 19 runs and two stolen bases in 36 games.
Looking At Cole
Cole has been one of the best pitchers in the recent era of baseball.
The former Cy Young Award winner is in the middle of his 6th season pitching for New York.
He has also had stops with the Houston Astros and Pittsburgh Pirates.
Right now, Cole is 9-9 with a 3.63 ERA in 21 starts.
Looking At The Yankees Right Now
The Yankees are the second-place team in the American League East with an 89-65 record in 154 games.
They have won seven out of their last ten games (and are 47-33 in 80 games on the road).
On Tuesday, the Yankees will return home to host the Tampa Bay Rays in the Bronx.
