rss_title: Cam Schlittler Lanza Un Mensaje Contundente A Los Yankees Mientras La Derrota Ante Arizona Agrava Los Problemas En La División Este De La Liga Americana
rss_body:
PHOENIX — Cam Schlittler se fue del Chase Field con otra actuación como lanzador que se consideraría dominante en casi cualquier otro sitio. Para los Yankees, fue otro recordatorio de que un as solo puede compensar hasta cierto punto cuando el margen a su alrededor no deja de reducirse.
Schlittler limitó a Arizona a tres hits y una carrera limpia en seis entradas el sábado por la noche, ponchando a seis y concediendo tres bases por bolas. Aun así , los Yankees perdieron por 5-3 cuando Pavin Smith conectó un jonrón de dos carreras como bateador suplente ante Michael Fulmer en la novena entrada, lo que convirtió un partido empatado en la undécima derrota de Nueva York en la última entrada de la temporada.
Con esta derrota, los Yankees quedan con un balance de 89-65 y a cinco partidos del Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, cuando solo quedan ocho partidos por disputar. Nueva York ya se ha asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero el camino hacia el título de división pasa ahora por cuatro partidos contra los Rays en el Yankee Stadium y necesitará algo de ayuda más allá de esa serie.
La actuación de Schlittler hizo que el resultado fuera más difícil de pasar por alto como una simple derrota de septiembre. Su promedio de carreras limpias bajó hasta 1,94, el mejor de la Liga Americana, y sus estadísticas de la temporada quedaron en 14-6, con 234 strikeouts en 190 2/3 entradas. Terminó su gira con un promedio de carreras limpias de 1,16 en 17 partidos como titular.
Los Yankees le dieron una ventaja momentánea de 3-2 en la sexta entrada gracias a dos jonrones solitarios de Heliot Ramos y Austin Wells. Schlittler empezó entonces la parte baja de la entrada con ocho bolas seguidas, Geraldo Perdomo conectó un sencillo de toque y un fly de sacrificio de Corbin Carroll empató el partido. Antes, un error de Schlittler en la defensa ante un toque de Tim Tawa ayudó a que Jordan Lawlar conectara un triple de dos carreras.
Juan Morillo se llevó la victoria tras lanzar 1 1/3 entradas sin permitir ningún hit con Arizona. Fulmer se llevó la derrota después de que Ildemaro Vargas ganara una revisión de ABS por una base por bolas al primer bateador en la novena y Smith mandara un cutter a las gradas del campo derecho. No hubo salvamento.
Así pues, Schlittler había sumado seis entradas más de excelente control de carreras sin cambiar el problema general de los Yankees. Nueva York acabó con un balance de 20-12 en sus 32 salidas como titular, un balance poco habitual para un equipo que solo ha encajado una carrera limpia o menos en 24 de esas salidas.
La racha histórica de no encajar carreras sigue adentrándose en un terreno cada vez más excepcional
La derrota no frenó el ascenso de Schlittler en las estadísticas. Según la investigación histórica de Sarah Langs, Schlittler acumuló 24 salidas en las que no permitió más de una carrera limpia, lo que le sitúa empatado con Bob Gibson en 1968 y Sandy Koufax en 1966 en el segundo puesto de la «Era de la Bola Viva». Koufax llegó a 25 en 1963.
En la historia de la Liga Americana, solo Walter Johnson logró más salidas de este tipo en una temporada: 27 en 1913 y 26 en 1914. El promedio de carreras limpias permitidas (ERA) de Schlittler a domicilio, de 1,16, solo queda por detrás del 1,06 de Johnson en 1913 entre los lanzadores de la Liga Americana con al menos 15 salidas como visitante.
Su trayectoria profesional es casi igual de impresionante. En sus primeras 45 salidas como titular en las Grandes Ligas, antes del sábado, Schlittler sumaba 312 strikeouts y una ERA de 2,24. Según los datos históricos que nos han facilitado, se sitúa junto a José Fernández y Paul Skenes como los únicos lanzadores que han superado los 300 ponches sin superar una efectividad de 2,30 hasta ese momento.
Schlittler tiene ahora una media de carreras limpias permitidas (ERA) de 2,22 en su carrera, con 318 strikeouts en 46 partidos como titular. Además, está intentando unirse a Ron Guidry en 1978 y a Spud Chandler en 1943 como los únicos lanzadores titulares de los Yankees de la «era de la bola viva» que han terminado una temporada con una efectividad por debajo de 2,00.
Schlittler lanza un mensaje contundente
No fue hasta después del partido cuando Schlittler pasó de hablar de sus propias estadísticas de lanzamiento a hablar de la posición de los Yankees en la clasificación. Cuando le preguntaron por la diferencia de cinco partidos, hizo un análisis directo de una carrera en la que Nueva York ha tenido varias oportunidades de recortar distancias.
«Tenemos que encadenar una buena racha. Va a ser duro. Creo que hemos tenido oportunidades durante toda la temporada para ponernos por delante, y no las hemos aprovechado muy bien. Así que todavía hay posibilidades, pero tenemos que darlo todo».
El mensaje cobró aún más importancia porque Schlittler acababa de asumir la responsabilidad de la jugada que le había cambiado el comienzo del partido. No utilizó las dos carreras no ganadas como excusa para que los Yankees perdieran otro partido que necesitaban ganar.
«Bueno, no diría que les di una oportunidad de verdad», dijo Schlittler. «Eso es culpa mía, así que asumo la responsabilidad. Cometí un error ahí y les dejé marcar dos carreras».
Reiteró esa idea unos instantes después, en lugar de echarle la culpa a la defensa, al bullpen o a la alineación.
«Bueno, así es el béisbol, pero sí, esa la pago yo».
Una jugada maestra más podría decidir cómo empieza octubre
Un gráfico comparativo de la MLB publicado antes del sábado situaba la temporada de Schlittler al mismo nivel que la de Clayton Kershaw en 2014, cuando fue MVP, y la de Justin Verlander en 2011, también como MVP. Esa comparación refleja hasta qué punto su candidatura ha ido más allá de la típica discusión sobre el premio Cy Young, aunque la carrera por el MVP siga siendo otra historia.
Para los Yankees, lo más importante ahora mismo es octubre. Los Yankees pueden armar su rotación para la postemporada en torno a Schlittler, que está listo para encabezar esa rotación, y Nueva York puede alinearlo para una salida más en la temporada regular, posiblemente contra Tampa Bay durante la serie de cuatro partidos que empieza el martes.
Su valoración sin rodeos después de que Arizona demostrara más que nadie la urgencia del momento. Los Yankees siguen contando con su mejor lanzador, que está rindiendo a un nivel histórico. Lo que sigue siendo una incógnita es si le han dejado suficientes partidos para dar un giro a la lucha por el título de división.

title: A Beloved Species Of September Nears Extinction. How the Game Is Forcing Out Pinch-Runners. | Arkansas Democrat Gazette
author: Chad Jennings The Athletic
body:
Rudy Martin Jr. waited 12 years for an opportunity that lasted three days. And the shame of it is, he never really got to run.
Called up by the Toronto Blue Jays last Friday, Martin was wearing a big league uniform for the first time at age 30. He had been drafted in 2014 and played stints in Mexico and two independent leagues before the Blue Jays decided a guy with 45 stolen bases in 91 minor league games might help them make the MLB playoffs.
Martin pinch-ran last Friday, he played seven innings Saturday, and he went on the injured list with a strained hamstring Monday. He never went first to third, never scored on a sacrifice fly, never attempted to steal second base. There is little guarantee he will ever get another chance.
But 10 years ago, his chances would have been annual events.
Martin was, for one weekend, a throwback to a not-so-distant era when anonymous minor leaguers arrived every September and made big league names for themselves with their speed. Some of those September call-ups eventually established long careers, turning exciting moments as stretch-run pinch-runners into lasting big league paychecks.
Martin might have been one of those annual call-ups, but he did not reach Class AAA until 2019, the year before MLB limited September call-ups to two players per team, effectively condemning September pinch-runners to near extinction, and making it harder for anyone to run so fast that major league teams simply could not ignore them.
"Having speed and chasing the playoffs definitely had a big impact and gave me more opportunities than I would if I did not have this speed," Atlanta Braves first-base coach Antoan Richardson said.
Richardson got to the big leagues twice as a player, each time as a September call-up for a team in contention. He debuted with Atlanta in 2011, then he scored the winning run on Derek Jeter's final Yankee Stadium at-bat in 2014. Jeter's much-replayed walk-off single featured a player with only 20 career at-bats.
Under the old rules, players like Richardson arrived every September. But these days, having one tool is no longer enough for such specialized, game-changing players to get a foot in the door.
"Call-ups in September have changed completely," said Tim Locastro, who ran his way onto a big league roster in 2017.
For decades, September rosters could expand to 40 players. Teams rarely activated that many, but 30-plus was typical, and clubhouses became overcrowded with redundancy and specialization. One-dimensional pinch-runners were not the only September luxury. Third catchers were standard, and top prospects were often promoted despite having little to do but get acclimated to the major leagues -- in 1993, Atlanta called up 21-year-old Chipper Jones and gave him three at-bats.
One major league executive, granted anonymity to speak candidly, noted that the widespread youth and athleticism of modern rosters could be a contributing factor in the decline of September runners -- teams do not necessarily need to pinch-run as often -- but said that the 28-man roster limit was surely the main reason so few teams seem interested in finding the next Terrance Gore.
Last year's Los Angeles Dodgers carried Justin Dean as a dedicated late-season pinch-runner and defensive replacement, but the Dodgers, with their unusual depth, are outliers. Few other teams feel they can devote a roster spot to such a limited player.
There was a brief attempt, a half-century ago, to make pinch-running a season-long occupation. The Oakland Athletics of the 1960s and 1970s regularly gave roster spots to players whose main job, or only job, was to pinch-run. Allan Lewis, Don Hopkins, Matt Alexander and Larry Lintz rarely did much else for the A's, but they did a lot of running, and their teams did a lot of winning. Most famous of the team's runners was Herb Washington, an international track star with a minimal baseball background who never hit or played the field but got into 92 games and stole 29 bases in 1974 as the A's won their third consecutive World Series.
Despite the A's success, their designated runner strategy did not catch on, and even the team's owner, Charlie Finley, seemed to lose interest in the idea (though the Pittsburgh Pirates did sign Alexander and use him in much the same way on the way to their own championship in 1979). September roster expansion, though, allowed the concept to survive as an annual, one-month-only tradition.
September call-ups in the 1980s and 1990s often included running specialists -- from Jeff Stone with the Philadelphia Phillies in 1983 to Eddie Miller for the San Diego Padres in 1984 -- but the practice spiked with the data-driven strategy of the 2000s. In 2009, 13 players stole at least 30 bases in Class AAA, and 12 of them were on major league rosters come September. Only one of the dozen had previously spent more than a couple of weeks in the big leagues. Class AAA leaderboards at that time were always littered with September call-ups.
In 2013, the Cincinnati Reds used September expansion to call up 22-year-old Billy Hamilton, who promptly stole 13 bases in 13 games to help the Reds clinch the final wild-card spot in the National League. Two years later, the Atlanta Braves gave a September call-up to 31-year-old Emilio Bonifácio, whom they had designated for assignment just two months earlier. In 2017, Locastro made his major league debut in September and got his first of 29 consecutive stolen bases without being caught, an MLB record for the start of a career.
"That year I got called up in 2017, all August in the minor leagues, I'm trying to show my speed off more than anything," Locastro said. "I knew if I was going to be called up, it was going to be to run the bases."
Some had memorable names -- Esix Snead, Rico Noel, Charlton Jimerson -- but few had notable careers beyond the fact that in the right moment, they could bring a stadium to its feet. Yet the nature of their jobs made them unforgettable to every fan base that got to see them run.
Most famous of the September runners was Gore, who got to the big leagues every year from 2014 to 2022, won three World Series rings with three organizations and became such a Kansas City Royals icon that his death in February prompted online tributes and an opening day ceremony. Gore started only 14 major league games in his career. But he played in 123, including 11 in the postseason; more than half of Gore's appearances came in September, and his only big league action in 2021 was as an Atlanta pinch-runner in a division series. Baseball Reference considers Gore to have 0.1 wins above replacement, but he stole 43 bases, and most of them came off the bench, late in the year, for playoff-bound teams.
"There have been very few players who can take over a baseball game," Dayton Moore, a former Royals general manager, said after Gore died. "That's exactly what he did."
The Class AAA steals leaders this year, Braiden Ward and Duke Ellis, are experienced outfielders in the Red Sox and Yankees farm systems, each with 50-plus steals and their parent clubs in contention.
That was a reliable call-up formula a decade ago, but neither has been promoted. To get Martin on the roster last week, the Blue Jays had to designate for assignment an underperforming veteran, Jesus Sanchez. The call-up was not as simple as putting Martin on the 40-man roster and stitching his name onto a jersey.
Nearly a decade after the September call-up that started his own big league career, Locastro now works as a minor league instructor with the Padres, and part of his job is to teach young players to run the bases. But he has to warn them: Running cannot be all they do.
"Nowadays," Locastro said, "you need to have all aspects of the game if you want to be called up in September."

title: Yankees’ division dreams hanging by a thread after walk-off loss: ‘It’s gonna be tough’
author: Gary Phillips
body:
PHOENIX — Both the Yankees and Rays saw their respective games end in walk-off fashion on Saturday, but only one of the division rivals emerged victorious.
It wasn’t the Yanks, who suffered a 5-3 loss to the Diamondbacks when Michael Fulmer surrendered a game-ending, two-run home to Pavin Smith with one out in the ninth inning. Aaron Boone said that he considered using Clarke Schmidt, one game back from Tommy John surgery, instead, but he went with the journeyman Fulmer because he’s had more experience in those situations.
“I just felt like Fulmer’s been in these spots and throwing the ball really well for us, and Smith got him there,” Boone said of the reliever, who has a 3.09 ERA this season.
Meanwhile, at Tropicana Field, the Rays pulled off a 2-1 win over the Red Sox thanks to a bloop single from Richie Palacios in the ninth. Tampa now has a five-game lead over the Yankees with just eight games left in the regular season.
The American League East foes will play four of those games against each other at Yankee Stadium from Sept. 22-24, starting with a doubleheader on Tuesday. Boone acknowledged that his club will probably have to sweep the Rays for a crack at a division title.
“We sweep, then it gets interesting,” the manager said with the Yankees’ postseason ticket already punched.
But the odds are already stacked against the Yankees with the team finishing its series in Arizona on Sunday. They entered Saturday with a just a 2.8% chance of winning the division, according to FanGraphs.

title: Benge breaks Mets rookie hits record in victory | Arkansas Democrat Gazette
author: The Associated Press
body:
NEW YORK -- Carson Benge had three hits to break Pete Alonso's Mets season rookie record, homering along with Francisco Alvarez as New York again prevented the Philadelphia Phillies from gaining ground in the National League wild card race with a 10-3 win Saturday.
Benge raised his hits total to 156, one more than Pete Alonso in 2019.
Alec Bohm had a pair of run-scoring singles and Bryce Harper delivered a sacrifice fly for the Phillies, who entered Saturday tied with the Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres for the three NL wild cards, five games ahead of the Arizona Diamondbacks.
Alvarez's three-run home run off Andrew Painter (3-10) put the Mets ahead for good in the fifth.
Benge doffed his cap to an ovation from the crowd of 37,468 following the record-breaking hit, an RBI infield single in the eighth.
CUBS 5, REDS 2 Matthew Boyd ended a six-start winless streak, Dansby Swanson hit his first home run since coming off the injured list and visiting Chicago moved closer to its second consecutive playoff berth by beating Cincinnati. Michael Busch hit a tiebreaking home run off Nick Lodolo (3-6) in the sixth inning for a 3-2 lead, reaching 20 home runs for the third time in four seasons. Swanson added a ninth-inning drive against Zach McCambley, his first since Aug. 12.
NATIONALS 8, CARDINALS 5 (11) Washington scored four runs in the top of the 11th inning to break a 4-4 tie, then worked out of a bases-loaded jam with no outs in the bottom of the inning to get by host St. Louis. Jose Terra hit a two-run double to break the game open, giving the Nationals a 7-4 lead. Dylan Crews' sacrifice fly scored Jacob Young to make it 8-4. JJ Wetherholt hit an RBI single in the bottom of the inning to provide the final margin.
AMERICAN LEAGUE
RANGERS 6, BLUE JAYS 3 Five relievers held Toronto to six hits after Cal Quantrill left 12 pitches in because of right lat tightness, and Texas moved into sole possession of the AL West lead for the first time since late August with a win over visiting Toronto. Texas has won six of seven and moved a half-game ahead of Houston, which holds the tiebreaker. The Rangers have a winning record for the first time since before play on Aug. 11.
WHITE SOX 3, TIGERS 1 Sean Burke pitched six effective innings, Miguel Vargas homered and Chicago topped visiting Detroit. The White Sox dropped at least 101 games in each of the last three years. They could become the first big league team to make the playoffs after finishing with at least 100 losses in each of the previous two seasons. Burke (10-7) allowed one run and five hits in his second consecutive win. Grant Taylor got four outs for his 10th save.
RAYS 2, RED SOX 1 Richie Palacios dropped a fly ball into shallow right in the ninth inning to score Junior Caminero and give Tampa Bay a victory over visiting Boston. The Rays, who've won seven of their last eight, capitalized on two fortuitous bounces in the ninth. First, Caminero's foul popup bounced off the Tropicana Field catwalk and out of the reach of third baseman Caleb Durbin. Caminero then lined the next pitch from Garrett Whitlock (7-2) into left. Three batters later, after Chandler Simpson singled, Connor Wong's passed ball moved Caminero to third.
GUARDIANS 12, ATHLETICS 6 Angel Martínez homered from both sides of the plate and had his second career four-hit game, Chase DeLauter had a three-run home run, and host Cleveland remained in first place in the AL Central with a victory over the Athletics.
INTERLEAGUE
BRAVES 6, ASTROS 3 Ronald Acuna Jr. hit a go-ahead grand slam in the seventh inning, and visiting Atlanta beat Houston to drop the Astros out of the AL West lead. Trailing 2-1, Atlanta loaded the bases against AJ Blubaugh (5-3) and Acuna homered off Bryan Abreu for his second grand slam this season and the fifth of his big league career. Acuna singled and walked twice in his first three plate appearances. He has homered in three of his last four games.
BREWERS 1, ORIOLES 0 Visiting Milwaukee tied a team record with their 97th win of the season, beating Baltimore with the help of a fly ball lost in the sun by Orioles right fielder Rece Hinds. Hinds lost Joey Ortiz's fly ball in the sun in the second inning and tumbled to the ground, and Gary Sánchez hit into a run-scoring groundout.
PIRATES 6, ROYALS 5 Brandon Lowe hit a go-ahead two-run home run in the eighth to lift host Pittsburgh to a victory over Kansas City. Lowe jumped on a pitch from Steven Cruz (2-4) and sent it into the seats in right field for his 33rd home run of the season, the second-most by a player in their first year with the Pirates.
ROCKIES 5, MARINERS 3 Host Colorado used a four-run seventh inning to earn a victory over Seattle. The Mariners built a 3-0 lead, thanks to a two-run home run from Cal Raleigh in the first and a solo shot from Randy Arozarena in the third. Cole Carigg hit a two-run single in the seventh that gave the lead to Colorado, which got an RBI single from TJ Rumfield to tie the game at 3-3 earlier in the inning.
DIAMONDBACKS 5, YANKEES 3 Pavin Smith hit a two-run home run to right-center field in the bottom of the ninth inning to give host Arizona a victory over New York. Jordan Lawlar's triple in the bototm of the fifth scored Nolan Arenado to give Arizona a 2-1 lead, but Heliot Ramos hit a solo home run in the sixth to tie the game at 2-2. Austin Wells hit a home run later in the inning, giving New York the lead, but Arizona tied the game in the bottom of the inning when Ketel Marte scored on Corbin Carroll's sacrifice fly.

title: Dom Amore’s Sunday Read: Coach that launched Sun has his day; big skates to fill at UConn, and more
author: Dom Amore
body:
Mike Thibault was with the Lakers during the early 1980s “Showtime” period, and he was with the Bulls when they drafted Michael Jordan. Then he moved around to different leagues, circumstances, and went back to the NBA as a Bucks assistant.
In 2003, he signed on to be the head coach the original Portland Fire of the WNBA, but Paul Allen, one of the richest men on earth, folded the franchise. Thibault learned the new Connecticut franchise wanted to talk to him, so he flew across the country, made the long drive in pitch darkness down Route 2 to find a shining city on hill.
“Then I look up and see the bright lights of the Mohegan Sun and the hotel and I thought, ‘Oh, this is different,'” Thibault said. “I stayed in the hotel the night before I was going to talk to them, and I went to the casino and won about $80, and the joke was, I told them, ‘well, if you don’t hire me, at least I got a little bit of your money.'”
All of Thibault’s quips landed and he became the first coach of the Connecticut Sun, leading them to the playoffs the first year, to the WNBA Finals in the second and third.
“It was pretty cool to be a part of that first non-NBA (affiliated) WNBA team,” he said, “having to fend for yourself without the backing of an NBA team in the market. I didn’t have trepidations about coaching women, I figured I would coach them just about the same way I coached men. I had been in the NBA, and then in the CBA, now the G League. I had never given much thought to coaching on the women’s side. But if I stayed in the NBA, I probably would have been a career assistant coach. I wanted to be a head coach. So I said, ‘why not?’ I was at a time in my life where if it wouldn’t be fatal (to my career) if it didn’t work out.”
The Sun made the playoffs in eight of their first 10 years, then let Thibault go after a loss in the conference finals in 2013. He went on to win the championship with Washington soon afterward, and he left The W as the winningest coach in its history, 379-289, though he has been passed by Cheryl Reeve. Now, as the Sun’s final season draws to a close, they will honor Mike Thibault during their second-to-last home game, the last name on the banner in the rafters of the arena noting those who were significant in the team’s history, a history both successful and yet oddly star-crossed.
“I was there 10 years and basically got fired in the midst of a good streak,” Thibault said, “and to be honored by the team, I don’t know that that usually happens in these situations. But I have such good memories of my time there. … The way the organization has handled a tough situation, with their “sunset season” theme, honoring former coaches and players, I think it’s very classy.”
Thibault, 75, now coaches Belgium’s national team, a commitment of 14-15 weeks per year, succeeding the final Sun coach, Rachid Meziane, in that position. Belgium finished fifth in the recent World Cup. Coaching in the WNBA in the summers gave Thibault a chance to settle in Connecticut and be around more for his son, Eric, now the coach of the Mystics, and his daughter, Carly Thibault-Dudonis, who is building an impressive legacy coaching Fairfield’s women. In The W, Mike Thibault was one of those who put a stamp on the league.
“Two teams folded that year, and one team moved to Connecticut,” he said. “But I knew the NBA’s commitment, and I knew David Stern’s commitment. so I didn’t worry about the WNBA not making it. Why not be a part of making something work? A lot of the coaches who came in at that time, Cheryl Reeve, Michael Cooper, Bill Laimbeer had a lasting impact. Before that, a lot of the coaches in the league were former college coaches and it was played more like the college game. The NBA influence brought a good blend, and it started to play more like a pro league.”
Today, he compares the league’s growth to the NBA in the 1980s, about 30 years into its history. “I think the game has gotten better, the talent is better, bigger, stronger, faster, better shooters, better athletes,” Thibault said. “It reminds me, I was in the NBA when it was about 30 years old and it started to take off during the 1980s with the talent level really high. The rules changes have allowed the game to be a little more free-flowing. It’s higher scoring, with the athlete taking over on the offensive side of the game. At times it gets physical, and it will be interesting to see how games are called during the playoffs. So TV is excited about it because it’s a more entertaining game.”
The Orlando franchise had been an underachiever, it was perceived. Thibault took over the roster in Connecticut and said his goal was to compete for the title, and he had Nykesha Sales and Rebecca Lobo for the chase.
“At my first press conference there were snickers when I said my first goal would be to play for a championship,” he said. “Everyone was like, ‘Dude!’ But you have to have that mindset going in. Then making the finals two years in a row. There were a lot of coulda, woulda, shoulda’s in both years. In 2006 I think we had our best team, but we were so injury-riddled and ground down when we got to the playoffs.”
In 2009, the Sun traded star Lindsay Whalen to the Lynx, a most painful moment for Thibault.
“I hated that I had to trade Lindsey Whalen,” Thibault said. “She was like a second daughter in my house. It was time because we couldn’t put enough players around her. But then we got Tina Charles and began the rebuild. We had the second youngest team in the league, the second lowest payroll, I was proud of that group. I got fired basically because I didn’t win a championship, even though we had committed two years earlier to the rebuild.”
Ultimately, Thibault jumped into a league struggling to survive and brought the credibility that helped stabilize a new franchise and the league — so in the larger picture he is more than just a “Sun Legend.” The Sun, purchased for $10 million in 2003, began making a profit in 2010, its location one of the reasons. Now it will go to Houston, having been sold for roughly $300 million.
The countdown is on for Sun’s final game in Connecticut is Sept. 24.
“I was sad,” Thibault said. “I understand it from a business standpoint, the league has changed, the money has changed. More for your Sunday Read:
Filling iconic skates at UConn
Tia Chan was in goal for the UConn women’s hockey team for so long, playing at such a high level, one could almost call her an icon — rare for a college athlete. Now the Huskies, who reached the NCAA’s Elite Eight last year, have a strong cast of skaters led by high-scoring Claire Murdoch, but will be looking for the next goalie.
“We were worried when Elaine Chuli left (in 2016), we were worried when Morgan Fisher left (in 2020), we were worried when Annie Belanger left (2018),” coach Chris MacKenzie said. “I just think there is going to be someone who is going to step up. Among the newcomers for MacKenzie are twin sisters Caileigh and Chelsea Tiller, who could have immediate impact as freshman. The UConn season begins at St. Cloud State Sept. 25.
Warnings from Wesleyan
Wesleyan football coach Dan DiCenso posted a video on social media this week in which he called out the New England Small School Athletic Conference for imposing roster limits on football.
“Football is the only sport in the NESAC with a mandated roster limit,” DiCenso begins. “If all the sports had a mandated roster limit and were making cuts, I would have no problem with it. So this week myself, and three or four schools in this situation, will cut kids from our team. Wesleyan won the league title with no roster limits in 2024, and again when roster limits were put in for 2025, citing possible competitive advantages, capping at 84 players. DiCenso noted there are sports where there are large disparities between roster numbers.
“Common sense says, if there isn’t a roster limit in any other sport, why is there one in football?” he said. “… Do we want to talk about it? Or do we want to do something about it. I’m tired of having to meet with kids and not be able to give them a good reason why they can’t be on our team — just to practice and be there.”
Sunday short takes
*The Ivy League is moving its men’s basketball championship to Allentown, Pa., in 2028. Big mistake, I say. With the great, historic venues available in the league, most of which are easy for fans to reach, the Ivy’s four-team format was one of the most exciting and enjoyable of the conference tournaments. Messing with happy is never a good idea.
*Sports performance coaches should commission a study of the spotted lantern fly. Have you tried stepping on one? For a bug its size, it has to have the most explosive first step of any creature on earth.
*UConn men’s hockey coach Mike Cavanaugh filled out his staff with director of player development Ryan Shannon, Darien native, former Boston College and pro player and head coach at Taft School. Earlier, Sean Walsh, who also has pro playing experience, came from Alaska-Fairbanks to join Cavanaugh’s staff.
*Yard Goats manager Robinson Cancel will be a bench coach in the Mexican winter league with Tomateros de Culiacan. He will work with, and hopes to learn a lot from Lorenzo Bundy, a long-time MLB coach with a lot of pro managing experiencing.
*Jim Calhoun and his wife, Pat, will be honored by the University of Saint Joseph on Oct. 9 at the Connecticut Convention Center in Hartford. Tickets and details are available on USJ’s website at usj.edu/give/gala for: ‘A Legacy of Leadership. A Gala Honoring Pat and Jim Calhoun,’ the event to benefit the Calhoun Legacy Fund at USJ. Quite a few of Calhoun’s former players are expected.
*Art Shamsky, the 1969 Met, will be the guest at the Hartford World Series Club’s gathering on Sept. 23.
*Jackie Adams-Cheney, John Benoit, Dr. Kelly Harrigan, Robert Kalat, Sara Plourde-Zirkle, Tom Roberts, Don Sourcy and Jillian Sullivan are the Class of ’26 inductees for the Bristol Sports Hall of Fame. The induction ceremony will be Nov. 20 at the DoubleTree in Bristol, go to bshof.org for tickets and info.
*Dan Lauria, SCSU football player in the late 1960s, who turned to acting and gave us that quintessential 60s Dad on The Wonder Years, was inducted into the New Haven Gridiron Club Hall of Fame earlier this month.
Last word
*Cam Schlittler has been great for the Yankees, but any MVP talk is over the top. When starting pitchers threw complete games, they were viable candidates for both Cy Young and MVP, but it would be silly to give the MVP award to a five- or six-inning starter when there are sluggers like Yordan Alvarez flirting with the Triple Crown in Houston or Junior Caminero blowing past 40 homers for Tampa Bay.

“Then I look up and see the bright lights of the Mohegan Sun and the hotel and I thought, ‘Oh, this is different,'” Thibault said. “I stayed in the hotel the night before I was going to talk to them, and I went to the casino and won about $80, and the joke was, I told them, ‘well, if you don’t hire me, at least I got a little bit of your money.'”
All of Thibault’s quips landed and he became the first coach of the Connecticut Sun, leading them to the playoffs the first year, to the WNBA Finals in the second and third.
“It was pretty cool to be a part of that first non-NBA (affiliated) WNBA team,” he said, “having to fend for yourself without the backing of an NBA team in the market. I didn’t have trepidations about coaching women, I figured I would coach them just about the same way I coached men. I had been in the NBA, and then in the CBA, now the G League. I had never given much thought to coaching on the women’s side. But if I stayed in the NBA, I probably would have been a career assistant coach. I wanted to be a head coach. So I said, ‘why not?’ I was at a time in my life where if it wouldn’t be fatal (to my career) if it didn’t work out.”
The Sun made the playoffs in eight of their first 10 years, then let Thibault go after a loss in the conference finals in 2013. He went on to win the championship with Washington soon afterward, and he left The W as the winningest coach in its history, 379-289, though he has been passed by Cheryl Reeve. Now, as the Sun’s final season draws to a close, they will honor Mike Thibault during their second-to-last home game, the last name on the banner in the rafters of the arena noting those who were significant in the team’s history, a history both successful and yet oddly star-crossed.
“I was there 10 years and basically got fired in the midst of a good streak,” Thibault said, “and to be honored by the team, I don’t know that that usually happens in these situations. But I have such good memories of my time there. … The way the organization has handled a tough situation, with their “sunset season” theme, honoring former coaches and players, I think it’s very classy.”
Thibault, 75, now coaches Belgium’s national team, a commitment of 14-15 weeks per year, succeeding the final Sun coach, Rachid Meziane, in that position. Belgium finished fifth in the recent World Cup. Coaching in the WNBA in the summers gave Thibault a chance to settle in Connecticut and be around more for his son, Eric, now the coach of the Mystics, and his daughter, Carly Thibault-Dudonis, who is building an impressive legacy coaching Fairfield’s women. In The W, Mike Thibault was one of those who put a stamp on the league.
“Two teams folded that year, and one team moved to Connecticut,” he said. “But I knew the NBA’s commitment, and I knew David Stern’s commitment. so I didn’t worry about the WNBA not making it. Before that, a lot of the coaches in the league were former college coaches and it was played more like the college game. The NBA influence brought a good blend, and it started to play more like a pro league.”
Today, he compares the league’s growth to the NBA in the 1980s, about 30 years into its history. “I think the game has gotten better, the talent is better, bigger, stronger, faster, better shooters, better athletes,” Thibault said. “It reminds me, I was in the NBA when it was about 30 years old and it started to take off during the 1980s with the talent level really high. The rules changes have allowed the game to be a little more free-flowing. It’s higher scoring, with the athlete taking over on the offensive side of the game. At times it gets physical, and it will be interesting to see how games are called during the playoffs. So TV is excited about it because it’s a more entertaining game.”
The Orlando franchise had been an underachiever, it was perceived. Thibault took over the roster in Connecticut and said his goal was to compete for the title, and he had Nykesha Sales and Rebecca Lobo for the chase.
“At my first press conference there were snickers when I said my first goal would be to play for a championship,” he said. “Everyone was like, ‘Dude!’ But you have to have that mindset going in. title: Par de jonrones de Bellinger en la paliza de los Yankees, para asegurar la serie ante los Reales - AGP Noticias
author: AGP Noticias
body:
Nueva York, Nueva York.- Cody Bellinger conectó dos jonrones de dos carreras, impulsó cinco carreras y los Yankees de Nueva York aplastaron a los Reales de Kansas City por 13-4 el sábado por la tarde.
El abridor de Nueva York, Will Warren (2-0), igualó su récord personal con 11 ponches y lanzó un juego de dos carreras en siete entradas.
Bellinger conectó un jonrón de dos carreras durante una entrada de cinco carreras en la tercera entrada contra Noah Cameron (1-1) y llevó a Nueva York a su victoria más abultada de la temporada. Bellinger conectó un jonrón de dos carreras contra Mitch Spence en la sexta entrada, después de haber impulsado una carrera con un sencillo en la cuarta.
Bellinger logró su vigésimo partido con múltiples jonrones de su carrera y los Yankees conectaron cuatro jonrones por segunda vez en la temporada.
Bellinger conectó su primer jonrón entre un batazo de dos carreras de Amed Rosario y un jonrón solitario de Ben Rice, aprovechando los Yankees un error de tres bases del jardinero central Kyle Isbel en un elevado de JC Escarra.
Isbel le arrebató la pelota del guante al jardinero derecho Jac Caglianone cuando ambos se encontraban cerca de la zona de advertencia, y los Yankees respondieron con su demostración de poder contra el lanzador zurdo.
Rosario, abriendo el orden al bate por segunda vez en la temporada, envió un lanzamiento cortado a las gradas del jardín derecho. Tras una base por bolas de Aaron Judge, Bellinger conectó un slider en el primer lanzamiento que llegó al segundo piso del jardín derecho, poniendo el marcador 4-0 a favor de su equipo.
Dos bateadores después, Rice conectó un jonrón por tercer partido consecutivo al mandar la bola rápida de Cameron a las gradas del jardín derecho.
Escarra conectó un doble productor y un triple de dos carreras en la séptima entrada. Rosario también impulsó una carrera con un sencillo antes de que Bellinger volviera a conectar. Randal Grichuk impulsó su primera carrera como Yankee con un elevado de sacrificio en las últimas entradas.
Cameron fue castigado con siete carreras, la mayor cantidad en su carrera (cinco limpias), y siete hits en cuatro entradas.
Carter Jensen conectó un jonrón de dos carreras en la séptima entrada, pero los Royals sufrieron su sexta derrota consecutiva y la novena en 11 partidos. title: Spencer Jones Da Un Buen Susto A Los Yankees Por Una Lesión, Ya Que El Césped Del Chase Field Le Ha Hecho Daño En El Talón
author: Sara Molnick
body:
PHOENIX — Los Yankees llegaron a Arizona con el objetivo de mantener su puesto en la postemporada, sin dejar de luchar por una oportunidad cada vez más lejana de ganar la División Este de la Liga Americana. Para el sábado por la noche, la clasificación ya no era más que una parte del problema.
El propio Chase Field se había convertido en algo con lo que Aaron Boone tenía que lidiar.
Nueva York llegaba al domingo con un balance de 89-65 tras perder por 5-3 en la última entrada ante los Diamondbacks, a cinco partidos de Tampa Bay cuando solo quedan ocho partidos por disputar. Los Yankees seguían ocupando el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana, pero su margen para hacer frente a otra lesión se había reducido después de que Aaron Judge volviera a la lista de lesionados de 10 días por una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha.
Las decisiones de Boone del sábado reflejaron esa realidad. José Caballero fue titular en el centro del campo por segunda vez esta temporada. Cody Bellinger se quedó en la izquierda en lugar de cambiar de posición, a pesar de que tiene mucha experiencia jugando en el centro del campo. Boone explicó más tarde que Bellinger también estaba notando el estrés acumulado por la superficie sintética y que no quería aumentar la carga sobre él.
Esa cautela se mantuvo durante todo el partido, que los Yankees acabaron perdiendo por un jonrón de dos carreras de Pavin Smith en la novena entrada. También fue importante porque Nueva York está a punto de marcharse de Arizona para afrontar una serie crucial de cuatro partidos contra Tampa Bay en el Yankee Stadium, que empieza el martes con una doble jornada en la que se repartirán las victorias. Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero el equipo sigue buscando el equilibrio entre la lucha por el título de división y mantener intacta su plantilla para octubre.
La preocupación por el estado del césped dejó de ser un simple detalle de gestión de la alineación en cuanto Boone explicó por qué faltaba otro titular. Los Yankees habían llegado a un punto en el que un pie lesionado más podía complicar tanto su alineación en los jardines como la profundidad de plantilla que podrían necesitar durante la última semana.
Ese cálculo es especialmente importante en el centro del campo, donde Boone tiene menos combinaciones con las que está acostumbrado a trabajar una vez que empieza a proteger a los jugadores de las lesiones. Un ajuste de una sola noche puede convertirse rápidamente en un problema para la plantilla si las molestias persisten de cara a la recta final de la temporada.
Jones se queda fuera tras un repunte del dolor en el talón al jugar sobre césped artificial
Spencer Jones no jugó el sábado por unas molestias en el pie izquierdo y el talón, después de haberse dado un golpe en el talón a principios de semana en Minnesota. Jones dijo que las molestias se agravaron por el desgaste de haber jugado el viernes por la noche en el césped del Chase Field.
El novato restó importancia al tema antes del partido y dijo que esperaba que la baja durara solo un día.
«No es nada grave», dijo Jones.
Jones describió el problema como una molestia más que como una nueva lesión aguda. También lo relacionó directamente con la superficie y con los impactos que habían absorbido sus pies.
«Solo estoy un poco magullado», dijo Jones. «Jugar sobre césped artificial es diferente, es duro para los pies».
Boone dijo que la situación de Jones se evaluaría día a día y que estuvo a punto de dejarlo en la alineación. También dejó claro que los Yankees no consideraban que Jones estuviera fuera de combate.
«Simplemente me pareció que, sobre todo al estar aquí en el césped artificial, se había dado un golpe en el talón en Minnesota y, al volver a jugar en césped [el viernes], creo que es algo que hay que valorar día a día», dijo Boone. «Incluso creo que podría jugar esta noche».
Las declaraciones de Boone tras el partido son lo que más tranquilidad dan
Jones no llegó a salir en el partido del sábado, pero Boone dijo después que la decisión se debió más a la situación del partido que a motivos médicos. El entrenador dijo que habría sacado a Jones si los Yankees hubieran tenido el enfrentamiento adecuado o lo hubieran necesitado al final del partido.
«Estaba disponible, igual que yo lo habría estado… si hubiera surgido una oportunidad de batear o hubiéramos tenido que hacer algo, habría recurrido a él», dijo Boone.
Esa distinción es importante. A Jones no le han dado de baja, ni lo han puesto en la lista de lesionados, ni le han prohibido hacer nada relacionado con el béisbol. El domingo por la mañana, los Yankees seguían considerando el problema como una molestia pasajera.
La profundidad en el centro del campo hace que un día de descanso cobre más importancia
Los Yankees pueden permitirse que se pierda un solo partido. La situación de la plantilla se complica si Jones necesita más tiempo.
Jones ha jugado 80 partidos esta temporada y tiene un promedio de bateo de .248, con un porcentaje de embasado de .318 y un porcentaje de slugging de .433. Lleva 10 jonrones, 12 dobles, un triple, 38 carreras impulsadas y nueve bases robadas en 265 turnos al bate. Baseball Savant le atribuye 23 hits de más de una base, es decir, uno cada 11,5 turnos al bate.
Su valía también se nota en cómo los Yankees pueden colocar al resto del equipo. Caballero puede jugar de central, pero el sábado fue solo su segunda titularidad en esa posición esta temporada. Boone decidió expresamente no cambiar a Bellinger al centro por culpa del césped artificial y de la propia carga de trabajo de Bellinger.
Los Yankees también llamaron a Max Schuemann cuando Judge entró en la lista de lesionados, dando prioridad a la versatilidad defensiva. Esa decisión le da a Boone otra opción en todas las posiciones del campo y en los jardines, pero no sustituye la potencia de Jones como bateador zurdo ni su papel habitual en el centro del campo.
Los Yankees llegan a la última jornada de la serie con una duda sobre su estado físico
Los Yankees cierran la serie contra Arizona el domingo, antes del día de descanso del lunes. Ese descanso le da a Jones un poco más de tiempo para recuperarse antes de los cuatro partidos contra los Rays en tres días en el Yankee Stadium.
Por ahora, el último informe médico sigue siendo alentador. Jones espera que las molestias sean pasajeras, Boone lo consideraba apto para jugar el sábado y el club no ha dado a entender que se esté planteando incluirlo en la lista de lesionados.
La pregunta que queda es si un día de descanso del césped del Chase Field será suficiente para que el talón se recupere antes de que los Yankees empiecen la serie más importante que les queda en el calendario de la temporada regular.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

Los Yankees también llamaron a Max Schuemann cuando Judge entró en la lista de lesionados, dando prioridad a la versatilidad defensiva. Esa decisión le da a Boone otra opción en todas las posiciones del campo y en los jardines, pero no sustituye la potencia de Jones como bateador zurdo ni su papel habitual en el centro del campo.
Los Yankees llegan a la última jornada de la serie con una duda sobre su estado físico
Los Yankees cierran la serie contra Arizona el domingo, antes del día de descanso del lunes. Ese descanso le da a Jones un poco más de tiempo para recuperarse antes de los cuatro partidos contra los Rays en tres días en el Yankee Stadium.
Por ahora, el último informe médico sigue siendo alentador. Jones espera que las molestias sean pasajeras, Boone lo consideraba apto para jugar el sábado y el club no ha dado a entender que se esté planteando incluirlo en la lista de lesionados.
La pregunta que queda es si un día de descanso del césped del Chase Field será suficiente para que el talón se recupere antes de que los Yankees empiecen la serie más importante que les queda en el calendario de la temporada regular.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

title: “Time To Get Him Out of The Lineup” – Yankees Fans Unhappy With George Lombard Jr.’s Defensive Error in Diamondbacks Defeat
author: Karan Tyagi
body:
Fans slammed Yankees rookie SS George Lombard Jr. for his defensive error in Saturday night's game against the Diamondbacks at Chase Field. In the bottom of the seventh, with the game tied 3-3, Lombard dropped an easy infield grounder, allowing D-backs pinch hitter Ildemaro Vargas to reach first base on an error.
While the home side failed to score a run in that inning, fans expressed their displeasure with Lombard's error on social media.
Watch the video here:
Here are some fan reactions:
"Time to get him out of the lineup," one fan commented.
Lombard Jr. went 0-for-4 to end the night as the Yankees lost the contest 5-3, despite a strong start from ace Cam Schlittler and home runs from Heliot Ramos and Austin Wells.
George Lombard Jr. Continues to Make a Positive Impact Despite Some Errors
Lombard Jr. has been a little careless on defense in recent games, which understandably raises concerns among fans. But despite the infield errors, the rookie SS has made a positive impact since joining the roster a day after the trade deadline.
In 36 games this season, the 21-year-old has compiled a .227 batting average, with four home runs, 15 RBIs, and a .643 OPS.
While the Yankee faithful and the front office might have some doubts about his postseason fortunes, Lombard Jr. is sure to come in handy in the batting lineup as the Yankees attempt to adjust their lineup and choose players carefully, with captain Aaron Judge sidelined until September 27 and the Wild Card series starting on September 29.

title: Yankees' Heliot Ramos is Doing Something He's Never Done Before
author: Matthew Schmidt
body:
The New York Yankees made two moves at the MLB trade deadline, acquiring a pair of bats in Luis Garcia Jr. and Heliot Ramos.
Both deals were puzzling at the time given the awkward fit, but now, with Aaron Judge and Giancarlo Stanton potentially both out for the playoffs, it makes sense.
We've already spoken enough about Garcia, so let's focus on Ramos for a second.
Ramos has not been good since arriving in the Bronx.
Heading into Saturday night's matchup against the Arizona Diamondbacks, Ramos was slashing .165/.311/.306 with two home runs and eight RBI over 103 plate appearances in pinstripes. That came after he slashed .264/.304/.424 in San Francisco this season.
Not that Ramos was exactly lighting it up with the Giants, posting a .728 OPS, but he was certainly more productive than he has been with the Yankees.
But there is one area in which Ramos has surprisingly elevated his game since the trade: plate discipline. More specifically, taking pitches.
Ramos owned a 13.6 percent walk rate with New York going into Saturday, which is well above his lifetime median of 7.3 percent.
In fact, in spite of the fact that Ramos is hitting nearly 100 points lower with the Yankees than he did with the Giants this season, his on-base percentage in New York has been higher.
Ramos has never been one for free passes. He topped out at 52 walks last season, finishing with a 7.5 percent walk rate. His OBP in 2025 was .328. He lays claim to a lifetime .316 OBP.
Is it possible there is a legitimate reason why it's suddenly improving with the Yanks? Or is this a classic case of small sample size?
Perhaps being surrounded by better hitters has helped. Ramos is still striking out, having fanned 29 times. But he is doing a much better job of working the count and, as a result, finding other ways to get on base.
Ramos is under club control through 2029, so barring an offseason trade, he could be with the Yankees for a while. If he can start making contact again and hit closer to his career average of .252 while still walking, perhaps New York might have something here.
And with Judge now possibly sidelined for the postseason due to his calf strain, Ramos might have an even bigger role than expected in October.

title: What the Yankees' Lineup Should Look Like Without Aaron Judge In October
author: Michael Zeno; Unknown
body:
Aaron Judge's regular season may be over, but that doesn't mean the Yankees' has to be.
A mystery calf ailment popped up suddenly on Wednesday and has resulted in the Yankees captain being placed on the injured list. It's unclear whether he will return in 2026, even if he's eligible to return next weekend. Aaron Boone did not give any information on the severity of the calf issue, but the timeline is likely not good due to how tricky those injuries prove to be.
A scenario is now potentially unfolding that would have only appeared in Boone's nightmares: a postseason without the best hitter in baseball, with a lineup that struggled mightily without him. Even if they seemed to gradually improve as time went on, particularly in August, it would be a massive blow if he cannot return.
You can't replace a guy like Judge midseason; you can merely do your best to make up for his absence. Fortunately, on a platoon-heavy team like this, they should have plenty of options to build a lineup without him for the playoffs.
What the playoff lineup should look like against right-handed pitching
- Ben Rice (DH)
- Cody Bellinger (LF)
- Luis García Jr. (1B)
- Heliot Ramos (RF)
- Spencer Jones (CF)
- Jazz Chisholm Jr. (2B)
- George Lombard Jr. (SS)
- Austin Wells (C)
- Ryan McMahon (3B)
This lineup simultaneously features the easiest decisions, but also the roughest circumstances. Having a guy like Judge as the ultimate lineup balancer who mashed both lefties and righties allowed you to use plenty of left-handed hitters at the top of the order, something that the team has in abundance.
The best right-handed hitter on the roster without Judge is hard to pinpoint, especially since all of them are significantly worse against same-handed pitching. Heliot Ramos might just be the best option to bat highest among them, which would be cleanup in this scenario.
It's not an ideal situation in the slightest. Even if you don't think it makes sense to bat Ramos that high because of his struggles against righties, there is some merit to breaking up the team's many left-handed bats. In a lineup that will likely only feature one other righty, it has to be considered.
The fate of this lineup when they're out there, which would likely be mostly after a potential Wild Card Series with the Red Sox, would hinge on the middle. Spencer Jones and Jazz Chisholm Jr. got hot in August and helped the offensive turnaround begin, but both are heavily streaky bats with contact issues. If they go cold, this lineup might limp through games like they did in July.
What the playoff lineup should look like against left-handed pitching
- Paul Goldschmidt (1B)
- Cody Bellinger (LF)
- Heliot Ramos (RF)
- Ben Rice (DH)
- George Lombard Jr. (SS)
- Spencer Jones (CF)
- Jazz Chisholm Jr. (2B)
- Anthony Volpe/José Caballero (3B)
- Austin Wells (C)
Here's where it gets interesting. How far do you lean into the platoons on a team with several players designated to specifically hit lefties, especially against a team that will likely lean heavily on those types of pitchers in Boston?
Many Yankees fans believe that it would be improper to take a guy like García, who is likely the team's second-best pound-for-pound hitter with Judge injured, out of the lineup, but you don't really have a choice here. He's slashing just .238/.274/.363 against lefties, while Goldschmidt has been among the team's best hitters against them for the last two seasons. Add in Rice's improvements against same-handed pitching, and it just needs to be done.
Using him in a different position is also just not happening. He has not played second base, where he was extremely poor, since 2025. The only position he's played this season is first base. If he wasn't so dreadful out there, maybe he could replace Chisholm, a mediocre hitter against lefties in his own right.
Speaking of defense, you might notice the lack of Amed Rosario, and that's intentional. Rosario's use on this roster was almost exclusively predicated on his ability to hit left-handed pitching, but he's been significantly worse at it this season. Add in his truly dreadful defense, and you have a conundrum.
Anthony Volpe is a better hitter than José Caballero, but there are questions about how his arm strength would play at third, where he's also very inexperienced with just three games played in Triple-A. Caballero would probably get the nod here, but he's someone who just plays better off the bench with his speed and versatility.
It's also an aggressive placement for Lombard, batting fifth in his first career playoff game. The results haven't quite been there yet for him, but he's always been significantly better against lefties and should be slid up the lineup and be treated as one of those platoon bats who are there to hit that handedness, even if it might lead to consequences in the bullpen.
Boston is loaded with left-handed pitching from the rotation to the bullpen, so there will be few opportunities to get to a guy like García on the bench. The rest of the bench would be situational with pinch runners and pinch hitters.
Things ultimately look particularly shallow, but is there a chance that some last-minute reinforcements could help out?
Could Trent Grisham or Giancarlo Stanton return to provide relief?
It seems unlikely, especially early in the postseason, but the Yankees are refusing to shut the door on either Trent Grisham's or Giancarlo Stanton's return.
Grisham, who suffered a Grade 2 hamstring strain earlier this month, was revealed to be "pretty far along" in his running program, and Boone said it's not out of the question that he returns in the season's final days, although an exact timeline for that has not been spelled out. If Grisham is physically ready to get back on the field, it would provide a boost, even if he might not be starting over Jones at this point.
Stanton, who's been out since April due to two separate calf strains and a re-aggravation, has continued to hit through his rehab, but hasn't resumed running as of last Sunday. Considering how it took several weeks for him to even get close to back from injury with his running program last time, this likely doesn't put him in play until the ALCS at the earliest.
While Stanton seems significantly less likely to get into a game again this season, there is a path for Grisham. The team could use him and Ramos in a platoon situation to add yet another lefty to the lineup against right-handed pitching. They could also utilize him as a pinch hitter on a larger bench than usual, due to the team's propensity to carry fewer than 13 pitchers in the Wild Card Series.
The real question for Grisham is defensive. While Jones has absolutely looked shaky in center field, the struggles of Grisham out there are well documented. Add in his diminished athleticism and likely balky hamstring straight off an injury, would it be better if the team just chanced it by throwing him in right field when he plays?
He hasn't played the position since a disastrous error lost the Brewers the 2019 Wild Card Game against the Nationals, but playing it at Yankee Stadium is significantly easier than dealing with the spacious center field. Of course, this is something the Yankees would have to determine their willingness to do beforehand and have him practice the position, so what plans they have will be determined by that.
As for Stanton if he's ever medically able to get back? There just might not be any room for him with Rice as the permanent DH. You don't want to take the bat out of either of their hands, and with the team seemingly having to juggle multiple guys coming off soft-tissue injuries, can they afford to use a roster spot for a designated pinch hitter as they did with 2022 Matt Carpenter?

Using him in a different position is also just not happening. He has not played second base, where he was extremely poor, since 2025. The only position he's played this season is first base. If he wasn't so dreadful out there, maybe he could replace Chisholm, a mediocre hitter against lefties in his own right.
Speaking of defense, you might notice the lack of Amed Rosario, and that's intentional. Rosario's use on this roster was almost exclusively predicated on his ability to hit left-handed pitching, but he's been significantly worse at it this season. Add in his truly dreadful defense, and you have a conundrum.
Anthony Volpe is a better hitter than José Caballero, but there are questions about how his arm strength would play at third, where he's also very inexperienced with just three games played in Triple-A. Caballero would probably get the nod here, but he's someone who just plays better off the bench with his speed and versatility.
It's also an aggressive placement for Lombard, batting fifth in his first career playoff game. The results haven't quite been there yet for him, but he's always been significantly better against lefties and should be slid up the lineup and be treated as one of those platoon bats who are there to hit that handedness, even if it might lead to consequences in the bullpen.
Boston is loaded with left-handed pitching from the rotation to the bullpen, so there will be few opportunities to get to a guy like García on the bench. The rest of the bench would be situational with pinch runners and pinch hitters.
Things ultimately look particularly shallow, but is there a chance that some last-minute reinforcements could help out?
Could Trent Grisham or Giancarlo Stanton return to provide relief?
It seems unlikely, especially early in the postseason, but the Yankees are refusing to shut the door on either Trent Grisham's or Giancarlo Stanton's return.
Grisham, who suffered a Grade 2 hamstring strain earlier this month, was revealed to be "pretty far along" in his running program, and Boone said it's not out of the question that he returns in the season's final days, although an exact timeline for that has not been spelled out. If Grisham is physically ready to get back on the field, it would provide a boost, even if he might not be starting over Jones at this point.
Stanton, who's been out since April due to two separate calf strains and a re-aggravation, has continued to hit through his rehab, but hasn't resumed running as of last Sunday. Considering how it took several weeks for him to even get close to back from injury with his running program last time, this likely doesn't put him in play until the ALCS at the earliest.
While Stanton seems significantly less likely to get into a game again this season, there is a path for Grisham. The team could use him and Ramos in a platoon situation to add yet another lefty to the lineup against right-handed pitching. They could also utilize him as a pinch hitter on a larger bench than usual, due to the team's propensity to carry fewer than 13 pitchers in the Wild Card Series.
The real question for Grisham is defensive. While Jones has absolutely looked shaky in center field, the struggles of Grisham out there are well documented. Add in his diminished athleticism and likely balky hamstring straight off an injury, would it be better if the team just chanced it by throwing him in right field when he plays?
He hasn't played the position since a disastrous error lost the Brewers the 2019 Wild Card Game against the Nationals, but playing it at Yankee Stadium is significantly easier than dealing with the spacious center field. Of course, this is something the Yankees would have to determine their willingness to do beforehand and have him practice the position, so what plans they have will be determined by that.
As for Stanton if he's ever medically able to get back? There just might not be any room for him with Rice as the permanent DH. You don't want to take the bat out of either of their hands, and with the team seemingly having to juggle multiple guys coming off soft-tissue injuries, can they afford to use a roster spot for a designated pinch hitter as they did with 2022 Matt Carpenter?

title: Los Yankees Pagan Un Alto Precio Al Salir Mal La Curiosa Decisión De Boone En La Derrota Por 5-3 Ante Arizona
author: Esteban Quiñones
body:
PHOENIX — Los Yankees se pasaron casi toda la noche del sábado lidiando con dos realidades en el Chase Field. Cam Schlittler volvió a ofrecerles una gran salida, pero cada entrada cobró más importancia después de que Tampa Bay ya se hubiera llevado la victoria con un tanto decisivo en la última entrada.
Nueva York tuvo la oportunidad de evitar que sus cada vez más remotas opciones en la División Este de la Liga Americana se le escaparan aún más. En cambio, los Yankees se fueron con una derrota por 5-3 ante los Diamondbacks de Arizona, lo que amplió su desventaja en la división a cinco partidos cuando solo quedan ocho por disputar.
Los Yankees hicieron lo suficiente para que el partido se pudiera ganar. Ben Rice conectó un fly de sacrificio en la quinta entrada. Heliot Ramos y Austin Wells conectaron jonrones en la sexta. Schlittler superó su primer bajón serio en el control en semanas y terminó seis entradas concediendo solo una carrera limpia.
Arizona siguió respondiendo. Jordan Lawlar neutralizó la primera ventaja de Nueva York con un triple de dos carreras en la quinta entrada, después de que Schlittler fallara al intentar atrapar un toque. Corbin Carroll empató el partido con un fly de sacrificio en la sexta entrada, tras dos bases por bolas y un sencillo de toque que llenaron las bases.
Lo que estaba en juego ya estaba claro antes del primer lanzamiento. Varios jugadores de los Yankees vieron desde el vestuario de visitantes cómo Tampa Bay vencía a Boston por 2-1, un resultado que situaba a los Rays cinco partidos por delante. Nueva York había ganado ocho de sus últimos diez partidos, pero la racha de Tampa Bay casi no dejaba margen para perder otra oportunidad.
A continuación, los Yankees contaron con dos entradas sin puntos de su bullpen. Brent Headrick consiguió dos outs en la séptima antes de que Paul Blackburn terminara esa entrada y se encargara de la octava. El marcador se mantuvo en 3-3, lo que dejaba a Nueva York a una entrada limpia de tener otra oportunidad al bate.
Schlittler había hecho lo suficiente para mantener a los Yankees en el partido. Cedió tres hits y tres carreras, solo una limpia, y se anotó seis strikeouts en 98 lanzamientos. Su promedio de carreras limpias bajó a 1,94. Para entonces, el margen de error era ya casi nulo.
Fue entonces cuando el partido dio un giro con la decisión más decisiva de Aaron Boone de toda la noche respecto al bullpen.
Boone recurre a Fulmer con el partido en juego
Boone le pasó la parte baja de la novena a Michael Fulmer en lugar de al cerrador David Bednar. Fulmer había lanzado dos tercios de una entrada sin encajar carreras en la victoria del viernes por 9-2, mientras que Bednar no había lanzado desde que hizo dos entradas el miércoles en Minnesota.
Fulmer parecía haber eliminado a Ildemaro Vargas con un strikeout en un lanzamiento con cuenta completa, pero Vargas impugnó la decisión a través del sistema automático de bolas y strikes de la MLB. El lanzamiento se consideró bola, lo que le dio a Arizona una base por bolas para abrir el turno.
Fulmer ponchó a Lawlar. A continuación, Pavin Smith entró como bateador suplente y mandó el segundo lanzamiento de Fulmer, un «cutter», 391 pies al campo derecho para un jonrón de dos carreras que dio la victoria.
Juan Morillo se llevó la victoria para Arizona, mejorando su balance a 5-4. Fulmer sufrió su primera derrota y vio cómo su promedio de carreras limpias subía de 1,59 a 3,09. No hubo salvamento.
La decisión llamó la atención porque Bednar llegaba a la noche con 34 salvamentos y una efectividad de 2,58. Fulmer, fichado por los Yankees a finales de agosto, solo había lanzado 11 1/3 entradas en las Grandes Ligas esta temporada antes del sábado y sigue formando parte de un bullpen muy concurrido de la postemporada.
Schlittler asume la culpa tras una racha irregular
Un error de Schlittler en la quinta entrada ayudó a Arizona a anotar dos veces, y ocho lanzamientos seguidos fuera de la zona al inicio de la sexta propiciaron la remontada que empató el partido. Se recuperó ponchando a Nolan Arenado y a Tim Tawa con dos corredores en posición de anotar.
El lanzador diestro se centró en su propio error tras el partido.
«Asumo toda la culpa por eso», dijo Schlittler. «Cometí un error ahí y dejé que nos marcaran dos carreras. Así es el béisbol, pero esa la tengo yo».
Schlittler ha cedido una carrera limpia o menos en 24 salidas como titular, lo que le convierte, junto a Sandy Koufax y Bob Gibson, en uno de los únicos lanzadores de la Era de la Bola Viva con al menos 24 salidas de este tipo en una temporada, sin contar los «openers».
El descanso de Bednar acentúa el contraste en el bullpen
La secuencia de relevos de los Yankees ofreció un anticipo de la postemporada. Headrick y Blackburn sumaron entre ambos dos entradas sin encajar carreras antes de la novena. Bednar no llegó a salir, mientras que Fulmer lanzó dos días seguidos.
Fulmer llegaba al sábado con una ERA de 1,59 y había limitado a sus rivales a un promedio de bateo de 0,171 en sus apariciones con los Yankees. La diferencia en la carga de trabajo era aún más marcada: Fulmer había lanzado el viernes, mientras que Bednar había tenido dos días completos de descanso tras su salida de dos entradas del miércoles.
Esto es importante ahora que los Yankees están reorganizando una plantilla de lanzadores que se reducirá de cara a octubre. Bednar es una opción consolidada para las últimas entradas. Fulmer ha lanzado lo suficientemente bien como para seguir en la pugna por un puesto en la plantilla, pero su puesto está menos asegurado, ya que varios relevistas compiten por las limitadas plazas de la postemporada.
El sábado supuso otro momento de evaluación, y esta vez se dio en un momento de máxima presión.
Los Yankees pierden más terreno antes del enfrentamiento con los Rays
Con esta derrota, los Yankees se quedan con un balance de 89-65. Tampa Bay sube a 94-60, lo que deja a Nueva York a cinco partidos de distancia en la División Este de la Liga Americana. Los Yankees siguen teniendo una ventaja de 5 partidos y medio sobre Boston en la lucha por el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana.
Boone reconoció lo estrecho que se ha vuelto el camino con cuatro partidos contra Tampa Bay a partir del martes en el Yankee Stadium.
«Si les barreríamos, entonces la cosa se pondría interesante», dijo Boone. «Pero no puedes barrerlos antes del partido [del domingo]».
Los Yankees cierran la serie contra Arizona el domingo, con Will Warren como lanzador previsto para enfrentarse a Corbin Burnes. Tras el partido del sábado, Nueva York debe mantener viva la lucha por el título de división y, al mismo tiempo, decidir en qué relevos confía Boone cuando llegue la próxima novena entrada empatada.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

title: “Aaron Judge Is Falling Apart”; “Hang Up the Cleats” – Fans Rip Yankees Captain for Staying Tight-Lipped About Severity of Injury
author: Shantanu Bhattacharjee
body:
New York Yankees captain Aaron Judge is facing intense scrutiny online for not revealing the severity of his latest right calf strain. The lack of transparency regarding his MRI results and cliffhanger responses has sparked online frustration, with many calling for Judge to retire for good.
Aaron Judge suffered a severe injury to the soleus muscle in his right calf in his first at-bat Wednesday, playing against the Minnesota Twins. Judge felt a stiffness in his lower right leg during the first inning but continued playing. He was eventually removed in the sixth inning. The club put him on the 10-day injured list, which has now raised serious doubts about his availability for upcoming games.
When asked how serious the injury was, Judge reportedly refused to disclose its severity. An MRI was done, but Judge did not reveal the strain's specific grade.
Baseball insider Bryan Hoch posted Judge's statement regarding the injury on X:
"I'd like to be back by the postseason. That's definitely the plan. I got really no answers for you on any timeline or anything like that."
The secrecy of his medical status has only fueled speculation and frustrations among MLB fans.
One user said:
"He's [Aaron Judge] falling apart. This is weirdly familiar to Stanton…."
Another user wrote:
Someone said:
One user wrote:
One more user wrote:
Judge's earliest possible return date is September 27, in the final regular-season game against the Baltimore Orioles at Yankee Stadium.
Yankees Manager Addresses Aaron Judge's Injury
New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone addressed Aaron Judge's injury, admitting that the team is capable of going the distance without its captain:
"The reality is, we've had to play a lot of the season this year without him. There's no replacing a player who is as great as Aaron Judge, but we have high expectations. Those don't change now."
Boone also said:
"I don't have a timeline on him, I'm not going to predict anything. We'll just obviously treat it and see what transpires."
With Judge out, the Yankees, holding the No. 1 wild-card spot, are set to face the Boston Red Sox in a best-of-three series beginning September 29.

title: Cardinals Receive Strong Message Involving Yankees' Anthony Volpe
author: Eduardo Razo
body:
The St. Louis Cardinals missed the playoffs this season and will need to head back to the drawing board to build a team that can qualify for the postseason next year.
Moreover, the question is what moves they should make to improve the team to challenge the Chicago Cubs and Milwaukee Brewers in the NL Central.
It’s been a wild 2026 MLB season for Anthony Volpe, who was optioned to Triple-A in August and then recalled in September. Still, it might be in the 25-year-old’s best interest to get a fresh start elsewhere.
Since reaching the majors in 2023, Volpe has been hitting .225 with 432 hits, 54 homers, 218 RBIs, and 241 runs scored in 537 games for the New York Yankees in his career, per StatMuse.
Despite this production during his four seasons in Pinstripes, FanSided’s Robert Murray believes that the Cardinals could be the change of scenery that Volpe needs after a rollercoaster career with the Yankees.
“Anthony Volpe would be a really good, buy-low option for the Cardinals,” Murray wrote in a Sept. 19 article. “Volpe was supposed to be the Yankees’ long-term answer at shortstop. Instead, he struggled mightily and fluctuated between the majors and minors.
“The Yankees still believe in Volpe and want to hold him, so a trade might be considered unlikely. But this is something that other teams will sniff around this offseason, I believe, and Bloom – who has previously worked with the Red Sox and Rays – should have plenty of familiarity in dealing with the Yankees.”
Anthony Volpe Could Boost Trade Value In the Coming Weeks
Since being recalled on Sept. 9, Volpe has performed well. Entering Sept. 20, Volpe has been batting .290 with nine hits, a home run, seven RBIs, and four runs scored in seven games, per StatMuse.
Moreover, if Volpe can end the season on a high note and have a productive postseason, his trade value might increase, and a team like the Cardinals could feel they can tap into his potential.
Volpe will have an opportunity to step up like every Yankee in that lineup, given that Aaron Judge is back on the injured list. New York can’t replace Judge with one batter, but they can do so with everyone chipping in.
Cardinals, Yankees Get Compelling Trade Idea
Recently, Christopher Kline of FanSided floated a trade idea that would send Volpe along with LHP Brent Headrick and LHP Kyle Carr to the Cardinals for 24-year-old shortstop Masyn Winn.
“The Yankees’ lack of fundamental soundness on the defensive end has bitten them in the you-know-what all season, just like it did last year,” Kline wrote in a Sept. 16 article. “The hope was that top prospect George Lombard Jr. could steady the ship at shortstop, but he has stacked up errors left and right.
“It’s too early to write off the 21-year-old long term, but he could serve more comfortably at third or second — which is notable, since Jazz Chisholm Jr. is about to [be a free agent]. Winn immediately alleviates a ton of defensive issues for the Yankees, while his weaker bat would be well-protected in the American League’s most potent lineup.”

title: Pavin Smith’s 2-run, game-winning homer lifts D-backs over Yankees 5-3, helps slim playoff hopes
author: Associated Press
body:
By DAVID BRANDT
PHOENIX (AP) — Pavin Smith hit a two-run homer in the ninth inning to lift the Arizona Diamondbacks over the New York Yankees 5-3 on Saturday night, giving the D-backs’ slim playoff hopes a boost.
Ildemaro Vargas started the ninth with a walk, winning an ABS challenge on a full-count pitch initially called a strike. After Jordan Lawlar struck out, Smith pinch hit and drove a cutter from Michael Fulmer (0-1) into the right-field seats.
Arizona pulled within four games of Philadelphia for the final NL wild card with seven games remaining, snapping a three-game losing streak on a night the franchise celebrated the 25th anniversary of its 2001 World Series win over the Yankees.
Juan Morillo (1-1) pitched 1 1/3 hitless innings. D-backs right-hander Brandon Pfaadt gave up one run on four hits and a walk over 4 1/3 innings, striking out three.
New York’s 11 walk-off losses are one behind San Francisco, which has the most in the major leagues.
New York ace Cam Schlittler gave up three runs — but only one earned — over six innings. The right-hander allowed three hits and three walks, striking out six and lowering his ERA to 1.94.
Schlitter’s 24 starts with one or no earned runs this year is one shy of the record in the live-ball era since 1920, set by Sandy Koufax in 1963, according to Major League Baseball.
The All-Star didn’t allow a hit until the fifth inning when Nolan Arenado lined a one-out single into left field. The right-hander then made a costly error on Tim Tawa’s sacrifice bunt attempt, dropping the ball as he tried to throw to first. Jordan Lawlar capitalized on the miscue with a two-out triple into the left-center field gap for a 2-1 lead.
Austin Wells and Heliot Ramos hit solo homers off Kevin Ginkel in the sixth to push the Yankees ahead 3-2.
Corbin Carroll hit a sacrifice fly in the bottom half but Schlittler limited damage by striking out Arenado and Tawa to end the threat.
Up next
1. Arizona RHP Corbin Burnes (0-0, 5.87 ERA) and Yankees RHP Will Warren (10-6, 3.89) start Sunday.
___
