title: Type 1 photo with image used for 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle card sells for record $3M
author: Greg Bates
body:
Artwork
Type 1 photo with image used for 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle card sells for record $3M
There’s no slowing down the Mickey Mantle market.
Top-notch examples of the New York Yankees star’s iconic 1952 Topps card have been selling for seven figures for a number of years. Each graded copy continues to increase in value.
Now, the original black-and-white photograph with the image used for his first-ever Topps card is joining the million dollar Mantle club.
Hunt Auctions announced that it brokered the sale of a rare Mantle Type I photo for $3 million through a private deal. That is an all-time record sale for a PSA-authenticated Type I photograph.
“This is huge for the photo collecting community, because it’s such a big number,” Henry Yee, principal authenticator for PSA Photo Authentication Services, told SCD. “When you talk about any collectible that crosses $1 million, whether it be tickets or magazines, it’s huge. Actually, photos have crossed $1 million but they were private sales.”
Related Content:
The previous record sale for an unsigned Type I original photograph was $843,750 on April 7, 2024 through Heritage Auctions. That was also a Mantle photo, which became the image used for his 1951 Bowman rookie card.
“The 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle rookie card remains to date one of the most recognizable American sports and popular culture items of the last 100 years,” said David Hunt, president of Hunt Auctions. “The record-setting price achieved for the related photograph is one of scant few PSA/DNA Type I examples known to exist and is among the most coveted original sports images of any type. This astounding record-setting image further memorializes the elite status of the Topps Mickey Mantle rookie card within the history of American popular culture. We are honored to have facilitated this historic sale, which undoubtedly has established a pricing standard of great significance.”
The Type I Mantle photograph was purchased by Hunt Auctions on behalf of prominent sports memorabilia collector Ron Firman.
“Mickey Mantle was a great player who was universally admired,” said Firman, who became a baseball fan growing up in a New York City suburb. “Our love for sports and its heroes help bring us together in our communities and as a nation, and that’s very important.
“I really want to thank Dave Hunt of Hunt Auctions for his valued assistance in this process and expertise within the market.”
PHOTO CLASSIFICATION
Type I photos, which are first-generation photos that were developed from the original negative within two years of the image being taken, are rare in general. They are also the most valuable and coveted photos by collectors.
PSA has only authenticated three Type I copies of the famous Mantle photograph with the image that Topps ended up using for its 1952 set. Yee has authenticated all three during his tenure at PSA.
In 2005, Yee along with legendary collector Marshall Fogel and Khyber Oser wrote a book titled “A Portrait of Baseball Photography.” The authors created a classification system, labeling photos Type I, II, III or IV, depending on when images were developed.
“Original Type Is are made off of the original negative in a dark room,” Yee said. “It’s as clean as it gets. It’s the most valuable of an image. It’s right off the negative.”
Fogel is a big Type I photograph collector. He knows the importance of this Mantle sale to the entire photography segment of the hobby.
“In a little over 25 years, the value of Type I photos, as evidenced by this sale, have increased exponentially,” Fogel told SCD. “The reason is two-fold: one is the preservation of nostalgia in knowing that this kind of photography, especially the news service photography, is extremely valuable because it’s very limited—including Types II, III and IV. The second is people are starting to realize the importance of the content of these photos. The preservation of our history from the beginning of the early days of baseball in the era of Ty Cobb, Christy Mathewson, Walter Johnson on through the era of Mickey Mantle, Sandy Koufax and Joe DiMaggio. It represents the golden ages of baseball history.”
MANTLE CARD SALES
Prior to this latest sale, the owner of the Type I Mantle photograph wasn’t planning on moving the item.
However, when a PSA 8 example of Mantle’s 1952 Topps card sold for $3.721 million through Heritage Auctions on Aug. 23, that pushed the photograph owner to let go of his prized piece.
The 7-by-9-inch Mantle photograph was taken by a photographer who was either an employee or freelancer—it is not known—for the International News Service (INS). The picture was snapped 75 years ago on March 5, 1951 during a Yankees’ spring training photo shoot.
With Mantle being an almost unknown 19-year-old rookie, having the photographer take his picture was almost an afterthought. However, the image became iconic, and not many original copies of the photograph survived at news services.
“A lot of these photos, they’re valuable simply because they weren’t meant to be collected,” Yee said. “They were basically a byproduct of an industry, and that industry was basically reporting the news of the day. They were made in small quantities. They were sent to various news payrolls of an agency.”
The Mantle Type I photo that just sold was originally discovered in 2012. Legendary Auctions president and COO Doug Allen found the piece in the archives of a regional U.S. newspaper. The back of the photo is plastered with writing. It contains an “International News Photo” stamp, along with stamps from at least five dates that signify the photo was used by the news publication.
After the Type I photo was authenticated and encapsulated by PSA/DNA in 2012, Legendary Auctions sold the photograph for $59,750.
“At the time when this sold for $59,000, that was a massive record price,” Yee said. “At that time, I’m not sure even PSA 8s of Mantle’s Topps rookie card sold for $59,000.
“It kind of mirrors what the PSA 8 goes for, it seems like.”
In November 2019, one of the two other Type I Mantle photographs that exist—stamped on the back with “Newark Sunday News” and with a chipped corner on the upper right—sold for $375,000. Purchased by a private collector, that was a record price at the time.

original_title: Type 1 photo with image used for 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle card sells for record $3M
original_body:
Artwork
Type 1 photo with image used for 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle card sells for record $3M
There’s no slowing down the Mickey Mantle market.
Top-notch examples of the New York Yankees star’s iconic 1952 Topps card have been selling for seven figures for a number of years. Each graded copy continues to increase in value.
Now, the original black-and-white photograph with the image used for his first-ever Topps card is joining the million dollar Mantle club.
Hunt Auctions announced that it brokered the sale of a rare Mantle Type I photo for $3 million through a private deal. That is an all-time record sale for a PSA-authenticated Type I photograph.
“This is huge for the photo collecting community, because it’s such a big number,” Henry Yee, principal authenticator for PSA Photo Authentication Services, told SCD. “When you talk about any collectible that crosses $1 million, whether it be tickets or magazines, it’s huge. Actually, photos have crossed $1 million but they were private sales.”
Related Content:
The previous record sale for an unsigned Type I original photograph was $843,750 on April 7, 2024 through Heritage Auctions. That was also a Mantle photo, which became the image used for his 1951 Bowman rookie card.
“The 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle rookie card remains to date one of the most recognizable American sports and popular culture items of the last 100 years,” said David Hunt, president of Hunt Auctions. “The record-setting price achieved for the related photograph is one of scant few PSA/DNA Type I examples known to exist and is among the most coveted original sports images of any type. This astounding record-setting image further memorializes the elite status of the Topps Mickey Mantle rookie card within the history of American popular culture. We are honored to have facilitated this historic sale, which undoubtedly has established a pricing standard of great significance.”
The Type I Mantle photograph was purchased by Hunt Auctions on behalf of prominent sports memorabilia collector Ron Firman.
“Mickey Mantle was a great player who was universally admired,” said Firman, who became a baseball fan growing up in a New York City suburb. “Our love for sports and its heroes help bring us together in our communities and as a nation, and that’s very important.
“I really want to thank Dave Hunt of Hunt Auctions for his valued assistance in this process and expertise within the market.”
PHOTO CLASSIFICATION
Type I photos, which are first-generation photos that were developed from the original negative within two years of the image being taken, are rare in general. They are also the most valuable and coveted photos by collectors.
PSA has only authenticated three Type I copies of the famous Mantle photograph with the image that Topps ended up using for its 1952 set. Yee has authenticated all three during his tenure at PSA.
In 2005, Yee along with legendary collector Marshall Fogel and Khyber Oser wrote a book titled “A Portrait of Baseball Photography.” The authors created a classification system, labeling photos Type I, II, III or IV, depending on when images were developed.
“Original Type Is are made off of the original negative in a dark room,” Yee said. “It’s as clean as it gets. It’s the most valuable of an image. It’s right off the negative.”
Fogel is a big Type I photograph collector. He knows the importance of this Mantle sale to the entire photography segment of the hobby.
“In a little over 25 years, the value of Type I photos, as evidenced by this sale, have increased exponentially,” Fogel told SCD. “The reason is two-fold: one is the preservation of nostalgia in knowing that this kind of photography, especially the news service photography, is extremely valuable because it’s very limited—including Types II, III and IV. The second is people are starting to realize the importance of the content of these photos. The preservation of our history from the beginning of the early days of baseball in the era of Ty Cobb, Christy Mathewson, Walter Johnson on through the era of Mickey Mantle, Sandy Koufax and Joe DiMaggio. It represents the golden ages of baseball history.”
MANTLE CARD SALES
Prior to this latest sale, the owner of the Type I Mantle photograph wasn’t planning on moving the item.
However, when a PSA 8 example of Mantle’s 1952 Topps card sold for $3.721 million through Heritage Auctions on Aug. 23, that pushed the photograph owner to let go of his prized piece.
The 7-by-9-inch Mantle photograph was taken by a photographer who was either an employee or freelancer—it is not known—for the International News Service (INS). The picture was snapped 75 years ago on March 5, 1951 during a Yankees’ spring training photo shoot.
With Mantle being an almost unknown 19-year-old rookie, having the photographer take his picture was almost an afterthought. However, the image became iconic, and not many original copies of the photograph survived at news services.
“A lot of these photos, they’re valuable simply because they weren’t meant to be collected,” Yee said. “They were basically a byproduct of an industry, and that industry was basically reporting the news of the day. They were made in small quantities. They were sent to various news payrolls of an agency.”
The Mantle Type I photo that just sold was originally discovered in 2012. Legendary Auctions president and COO Doug Allen found the piece in the archives of a regional U.S. newspaper. The back of the photo is plastered with writing. It contains an “International News Photo” stamp, along with stamps from at least five dates that signify the photo was used by the news publication.
After the Type I photo was authenticated and encapsulated by PSA/DNA in 2012, Legendary Auctions sold the photograph for $59,750.
“At the time when this sold for $59,000, that was a massive record price,” Yee said. “At that time, I’m not sure even PSA 8s of Mantle’s Topps rookie card sold for $59,000.
“It kind of mirrors what the PSA 8 goes for, it seems like.”
In November 2019, one of the two other Type I Mantle photographs that exist—stamped on the back with “Newark Sunday News” and with a chipped corner on the upper right—sold for $375,000. Purchased by a private collector, that was a record price at the time.

title: Jazz Chisholm Jr. casts doubt on long-term future with NY Yankees
author: Santiago Tovar
body:
Another season, another spot secured in the postseason for the New York Yankees. Mirroring last year’s path, the Yanks are once again hunting for a World Series berth. With Jazz Chisholm Jr.’s return date drawing near, New York is aiming to finally snap its long championship drought.
However, when speaking with Randy Miller of NJ.com, Chisholm revealed that his long-term future in the Bronx remains uncertain, noting he hasn’t discussed a contract extension since spring training. “It was just like, ‘We don’t do extensions,'” Chisholm admitted.
While trade rumors have occasionally linked Chisholm to the crosstown rival New York Mets, his latest candid comments suggest he could very well be playing elsewhere next season.
Meanwhile, the Yankees confirmed a target return date for starter Clarke Schmidt as the postseason approaches. Manager Aaron Boone expects to have the right-hander fully stretched out and ready to bolster the rotation for October.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. #13 of the New York Yankees.
Chisholm Jr. ‘reaches out’ to the Yankees front office
When asked if he had formally approached the front office or General Manager Brian Cashman about an extension, Chisholm clarified that it wasn’t a sit-down meeting, but rather a brief exchange in passing.
“I wouldn’t say I reached out. It was more of a mutual thing, just me walking around saying something to Cashman as he walked past me,” Chisholm said, as reported by Miller.
How well did Chisholm Jr. play this season?
Chisholm has delivered his signature blend of dynamic speed and raw power during his 2026 campaign with the Yankees, even if his overall production has suffered from brief stretches of inconsistency. Here is a look at his statistical output this year:
- Slash Line: .232 / .312 / .403
- OPS: .715
- Home Runs: 19
- RBIs: 55
- Stolen Bases: 40
- Plate Appearances: 520
SurveyWill Chisholm Jr. play with the Yankees next season?

title: Yankees could be making a huge October mistake
author: Alexander Wilson
body:
The Yankees beat Minnesota 8-3 on Sunday, and Jose Caballero did not sneak through that game. He went 2-for-4, hit a home run, and drove in two runs. For a club that has spent plenty of time trying to sort out its infield, that is the sort of day people will remember when October lineups get picked.
Caballero has not suddenly turned into a middle-of-the-order bat. His season line sits at .235/.292/.376. But he has 14 homers, 32 stolen bases, and enough defensive versatility to make every good game feel a little more important than it would for a normal bench player.
The Yankees can keep calling him a utility option, and technically that is still true. I just do not think the role feels that simple anymore. There are only so many ways to build a playoff bench, especially when the team is still trying to decide how much offense it can live with at shortstop.
Yankees have an October lineup choice coming
Caballero gives the roster a speed element that does not need a full-time starting job to matter. He can enter late, cover multiple spots, run for a slower bat, and make a routine ground ball feel less routine. That stuff plays when one run can flip a game.
His player profile also makes the recent production easier to understand. He is not sitting around waiting for somebody else to create the action. He puts pressure on the defense, then forces the pitcher to deal with the next hitter while he is moving around the bases.
There is a difference between being useful and being automatic. Caballero is still on the useful side of that line. Sunday gave the Yankees another reason to test where the ceiling actually is.
Jose Caballero cannot be treated like an afterthought
Anthony Volpe remains part of the picture, and the Yankees do not have to make a permanent declaration after one afternoon in Minneapolis. Nobody is saying Caballero should be handed the job because he ran into a fastball.
Still, the club cannot pretend the gap between them is a non-issue when the offensive production keeps stacking up. A playoff lineup is not a reward for who held a spot in April. It is about who gives the team a better chance to score, defend, and survive a close game.
Caballero is making that case in his own way. The Yankees should listen before they lock themselves into an answer out of habit.

title: José Caballero despierta a la ofensiva y los Yankees se meten a la postemporada
body:
José Caballero conectó un HR, remolcó dos carreras y Aaron Judge volvió a pegar un cuadrangular para ayudar a los Yankees a vencer a los Minnesota Twins 8-3 y asegurar su pase a la postemporada.
"Chema" se fue de 4-2 con 2 remolcadas, 2 anotadas. En la tercera entrada conectó HR para poner en ventaja a su equipo ante los envíos de Dean Kremer quien le lanzó una curva de 77.6 mph y mandarla a 103.7 mph a 372 pies hacia el jardín izquierdo.
El santeño volvió a conectar un batazo oportuno en la octava entrada al pegar un sencillo por el jardín central e impulsar a George Lombard Jr.
Números de José Caballero
Hasta el momento batea para .235 con 14 cuadrangulares, 49 producidas, 32 bases robadas y .668 de OPS.

José Caballero conectó un HR, remolcó dos carreras y Aaron Judge volvió a pegar un cuadrangular para ayudar a los Yankees a vencer a los Minnesota Twins 8-3 y asegurar su pase a la postemporada.
"Chema" se fue de 4-2 con 2 remolcadas, 2 anotadas. En la tercera entrada conectó HR para poner en ventaja a su equipo ante los envíos de Dean Kremer quien le lanzó una curva de 77.6 mph y mandarla a 103.7 mph a 372 pies hacia el jardín izquierdo.
El santeño volvió a conectar un batazo oportuno en la octava entrada al pegar un sencillo por el jardín central e impulsar a George Lombard Jr.
Números de José Caballero
Hasta el momento batea para .235 con 14 cuadrangulares, 49 producidas, 32 bases robadas y .668 de OPS.

title: Inside George Lombard Jr.’s private breakfast with Yankees legend Derek Jeter
author: Brendan Kuty
body:
MINNEAPOLIS — As Derek Jeter spoke, George Lombard Jr. listened.
It was January in Miami, and a mutual friend had set up a meeting between Jeter, the legendary New York Yankees shortstop, and Lombard, then the club’s top shortstop prospect. Over breakfast, Jeter answered Lombard’s questions about life in the big leagues and life with the Yankees, and offered advice.
Advertisement
On Monday, in an interview with The Athletic in the visitors clubhouse at Target Field, Lombard could still vividly recall the morning he spent with the Hall of Famer.
Jeter was “a great dude” and “a normal dude,” Lombard said. He was also “humble and down to earth.”
But as Lombard reminisced, one piece of advice from Jeter, in particular, stood out.
“The big one — and it seems pretty simple and probably one of the most important things — is to be a stand-up dude,” Lombard said Jeter told him.
“Whether that’s in the clubhouse or with the media or the fans, whatever it is. Be authentic and be a good person. It goes a long way, doing those little things. Whether that’s always being upfront and honest or remembering people’s names. Just being an overall good human being. It keeps you grounded and keeps you humble and it allows you to keep doing the stuff on the field and producing on the field and helping out the team wherever you can, while keeping all the unnecessary distractions away.”
Lombard played a major role in Monday’s 8-3 victory over the Minnesota Twins, which came after a loss by the Toronto Blue Jays that clinched a spot in the playoffs for the Yankees.
In the eighth inning, the Yankees were losing 2-1 when Lombard crushed Andrew Morris’ 98 mph fastball for a double off the wall in left-center field. He moved to third on an infield single and then scored on José Caballero’s one-out hit up the middle.
“It was unbelievable,” Aaron Judge said of Lombard’s clutch hit. “I saw him, even leading up to that at-bat, he was on the iPad. He’s doing his homework. First-pitch swinging to be able to do that off a guy like that who has been so lock-down for the Twins all year was impressive.”
This double was the hardest hit ball of George Lombard Jr.’s career ‼️
(Details below) pic.twitter.com/3sobpw6ONV
— Jacob P.M.🌔 (@JacobBSpeaks) September 15, 2026
It was a display of the kind of natural hitting ability that has the Yankees so high on Lombard, who they hope will take over as shortstop of the future the way Jeter did in 1996.
Advertisement
At the time of their January meeting, neither Jeter nor Lombard could have known how soon he would potentially be following in Jeter’s footsteps. Still, Lombard jumped at the chance to make a connection with Jeter, now 52.
Lombard, 21, wasn’t exactly new to meeting great players. As the son of retired outfielder and current Detroit Tigers bench coach George Lombard Sr., he used to take ground balls at Dodger Stadium next to Corey Seager, mimicking his movements. He also used to run around the outfield with a young Cody Bellinger, now one of his teammates.
But meeting Jeter was different, Lombard said.
“There definitely was some emotion involved in all that,” he recalled. “You’re going to go talk to Derek Jeter. I don’t know if I was nervous, but I was excited and looking forward to it.”
Lombard said Jeter was immediately cool with him “picking his brain and talking about his experiences.” They talked about “everything.”
“I think the better questions — and the ones that are more valuable — are all the non-baseball (questions),” Lombard said. “How he approached dealing with New York. Dealing with everything that comes with it. The media. The off-the-field stuff. How, in his case, being the captain, dealing with all of those responsibilities. All of it. Just good conversation. Very insightful. Definitely someone that you can take a lot from having a short conversation.”
To Lombard, Jeter stressed the importance of having a strong character.
“In New York, the on-field impact is extremely important,” Lombard said. “But the character and who you are person-wise is just as important.”
Derek Jeter & George Lombard Jr.’s swing comparisons are nearly IDENTICAL 👀🤯 pic.twitter.com/MRjyuGLHeW
— Concrete City Sports (@concretecityccs) August 11, 2026
Back then, Lombard was preparing for major-league spring training, and he would begin the season in Double A. But after dominating there and eventually acing his Triple-A assignment, he was called up by the Yankees on Aug. 4 — right after the trade deadline — and was asked to take over shortstop and also help their push to the playoffs. At the time, he was the youngest player in franchise history since Jeter to start at shortstop, at 21 years and 63 days old. Jeter was just 20 years and 350 days old when he debuted as a starting shortstop on June 11, 1995.
So far, Lombard’s first experience in the majors has been uneven.
Advertisement
Entering Monday, he was hitting just .215 with three home runs, 11 RBIs and a .619 OPS. His 73 wRC+ was sixth worst among shortstops with at least 100 plate appearances. Lombard homered in his first game in the majors, but has often swung and missed (25.9 percent) and he hasn’t exactly been crushing the baseball (85.5 mph average exit velocity).
Defensively, Lombard has looked more than capable, displaying a strong arm, good range and smooth actions. But he also had a stretch in which he made an error in six straight games. At the time, it was the longest consecutive error streak since Cleveland’s Mark Lewis had an error in seven straight games in 1992.
Lombard’s simply wanting a chance to ask Jeter questions that would prepare him for life as the Yankees’ shortstop was impressive, manager Aaron Boone said.
“I love when our players have an interest in connecting themselves to the organization,” Boone said. “Doing something like that and going and talking to Derek — those are cool things, when your players are curious. Look, everyone’s not that way. You respect that. But you do love when guys are curious and understand the magnitude of this organization and wanting to be an important part of it.”
Jeter returned to Yankee Stadium on Friday for the 25th anniversary of 9/11. While he was there, he visited the Yankees’ clubhouse and reconnected with Lombard. This time, it wasn’t over breakfast, but at a big-league ballpark.
“It’s been kind of a crazy year,” Lombard said. “But he’s happy for me, and he told me to keep doing my thing and to stay focused.”
Just another slice of advice to Lombard from Jeter, who knows what he’s talking about.

title: Un Comentarista De Los Twins Arremete Contra Ben Rice, De Los Yankees, Con Acusaciones Sin Fundamento
author: Inna Zeyger
body:
MINNEAPOLIS — Durante siete entradas, la ofensiva de los Yankees apenas hizo nada contra Minnesota, mientras que los errores defensivos complicaron una noche en la que ya había mucho en juego de cara a octubre.
Pero la octava entrada lo cambió todo.
George Lombard Jr. abrió el partido con un doble, Ryan McMahon llegó a base y José Caballero empató el partido con un sencillo. Anthony Volpe y Caballero encadenaron un doble robo antes de que Ben Rice conectara un sencillo de dos carreras al centro. De repente, los Yankees se pusieron por delante 4-2.
Aaron Judge asestó el golpe definitivo. Después de que Cody Bellinger llegara a base, Judge mandó un cutter de A.J. Minter a las gradas del campo izquierdo para un jonrón de tres carreras, el primero para él desde el 24 de mayo. Austin Wells añadió un jonrón solitario en la novena entrada, y los Yankees cerraron la victoria por 8-3, lo que les aseguró su 61.ª clasificación para la postemporada y la novena en las últimas diez temporadas.
Según el marcador oficial, la victoria fue para Tim Hill, la derrota para Andrew Morris y John Schreiber sumó su segundo salvamento. Will Warren encajó dos carreras no ganadas en 5 2/3 entradas. Tras el partido, los Yankees quedan con un balance de 87-63, a 3,5 partidos de los Tampa Bay Rays, líderes de la División Este de la Liga Americana.
Ben Rice acabó con 2 de 3, dos carreras impulsadas y una base por bolas. Judge por fin se desató después de llegar al partido con un registro de 3 de 20 y 11 strikeouts desde que volvió tras una ausencia de 84 partidos por una fractura en la costilla derecha.
La primera carrera de los Yankees llegó con el jonrón de Caballero en la tercera entrada, pero Minnesota se puso por delante en la sexta después de que un error de Ryan McMahon ayudara a alargar la entrada y Emmanuel Rodríguez impulsara dos carreras con un triple. Los Yankees solo habían conseguido dos hits en siete entradas. La victoria de Detroit por 6-5 sobre Toronto aseguró matemáticamente la clasificación de Nueva York para la postemporada durante el partido, pero los Yankees aún así remataron la faena con su 35.ª remontada de la temporada.
Ese contexto fue importante el lunes por la noche.
Pero lo más raro ocurrió después de que los Yankees se pusieran por delante, cuando la retransmisión televisiva de Minnesota pasó de mostrar el jonrón de Judge a enfocar los movimientos de Rice en la segunda base.
La cabina de los Twins pone a Rice bajo la lupa
La retransmisión de Twins.TV volvió a mostrar a Rice durante el turno al bate de Judge y comparó su lenguaje corporal ante los distintos lanzamientos de Minter. Rice pareció hacer un movimiento evidente antes de un cambio de velocidad, pero no lo repitió antes del cutter que Judge conectó para el jonrón de tres carreras.
Eso llevó a los comentaristas a preguntarse si Rice había captado algo de Minter y le estaba pasando información sobre los lanzamientos a Judge.
La retransmisión también reconoció la diferencia clave: no presentó ninguna prueba de que los Yankees utilizaran dispositivos electrónicos, vídeo o cualquier otro sistema prohibido.
Un comentarista de los Twins dijo mientras se mostraba la repetición:
«Solo estamos contando lo que vimos. Por la derecha lanzaba un cambio de velocidad, por la izquierda una bola rápida. Por la derecha nunca se agacha hasta las rodillas. Entonces, ¿había algo ahí? Solo ellos lo saben, pero todo dentro de las reglas del juego».
El equipo de Twins.TV del lunes estaba formado por Corey Provus, Justin Morneau, Trevor Plouffe y Audra Martin. La transcripción disponible no permite identificar con certeza a quién pertenecía la voz que hizo el comentario, así que en este artículo no se atribuye a ningún comentarista en concreto.
Esa última frase es importante. La MLB distingue entre la observación en el campo y el uso prohibido de dispositivos electrónicos o de vídeo para descifrar las señales. Las restricciones sobre el robo de señales mediante dispositivos electrónicos se aclararon y reforzaron en 2017 y 2018. Nada de lo que se mostró el lunes demostró que los Yankees hubieran cruzado esa línea.
El juez hace que cuente cada lanzamiento
La sospecha llamó la atención por lo que pasó después.
Judge había parecido un poco fuera de forma durante gran parte de su primera semana tras el regreso. Había hecho un roletazo que se convirtió en doble play y se había ponchado dos veces antes de que Minter lanzara un cutter por dentro que Judge mandó fuera. Ese jonrón fue el decimoctavo de Judge en la temporada y convirtió una ventaja de dos carreras en un colchón de cinco.
La reacción de Rice dejó claro lo rápido que ese turno al bate cambió el rumbo de la noche.
«¡Madre mía, menuda jugada!», dijo Rice. «Menudo golpe. Uno se podría acostumbrar a ver algo así, sobre todo en esta época del año».
El repunte de Rice en septiembre le da un nuevo matiz
Las estadísticas actualizadas de la temporada hasta el 14 de septiembre muestran que Rice tiene un promedio de bateo de .263, con 38 jonrones, 92 carreras impulsadas, 96 carreras anotadas y un OPS de .888 en 143 partidos.
Un análisis de PinstripesNation de esos resultados partido a partido muestra una racha reciente aún más impresionante. En nueve partidos desde el 4 de septiembre, Rice ha conectado 13 de 31, un promedio de .419, con tres jonrones, cinco carreras impulsadas y siete bases por bolas.
Esa aportación fue clave durante la larga ausencia de Judge. El sencillo de dos carreras de Rice el lunes dio a los Yankees su primera ventaja después de que Minnesota se pusiera 2-1 por delante en la sexta entrada.
No hay pruebas de que los Yankees hayan urdido un plan ilegal
La repetición de la retransmisión creó un momento polémico, pero las pruebas disponibles distan mucho de demostrar que se haya producido un robo ilegal de señales.
No ha habido ningún indicio público de que la MLB esté investigando a Rice, a Judge o a los Yankees por esa jugada. Tampoco hay pruebas de que se utilizara tecnología para descifrar los lanzamientos de Minter.
Aún no se ha aclarado públicamente si los movimientos de Rice fueron señales intencionadas o simplemente el comportamiento habitual de un corredor de bases.
Los Yankees ganaron porque su octava entrada desbordó al bullpen de Minnesota. Caballero empató el partido, Rice conectó el hit que les dio la ventaja y Judge aprovechó un cutter para sumar tres carreras más. Schreiber cerró luego la victoria por 8-3 con una doble jugada que puso fin al partido.
Para los Yankees, el resultado general está asegurado. Vuelven a octubre. No hay nada que se haya hecho público que demuestre que Rice o los Yankees hayan infringido las normas de la MLB.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

La victoria de Detroit por 6-5 sobre Toronto aseguró matemáticamente la clasificación de Nueva York para la postemporada durante el partido, pero los Yankees aún así remataron la faena con su 35.ª remontada de la temporada.
Ese contexto fue importante el lunes por la noche.
Pero lo más raro ocurrió después de que los Yankees se pusieran por delante, cuando la retransmisión televisiva de Minnesota pasó de mostrar el jonrón de Judge a enfocar los movimientos de Rice en la segunda base.
La cabina de los Twins pone a Rice bajo la lupa
La retransmisión de Twins.TV volvió a mostrar a Rice durante el turno al bate de Judge y comparó su lenguaje corporal ante los distintos lanzamientos de Minter. Rice pareció hacer un movimiento evidente antes de un cambio de velocidad, pero no lo repitió antes del cutter que Judge conectó para el jonrón de tres carreras.
Eso llevó a los comentaristas a preguntarse si Rice había captado algo de Minter y le estaba pasando información sobre los lanzamientos a Judge.
La retransmisión también reconoció la diferencia clave: no presentó ninguna prueba de que los Yankees utilizaran dispositivos electrónicos, vídeo o cualquier otro sistema prohibido.
Un comentarista de los Twins dijo mientras se mostraba la repetición:
«Solo estamos contando lo que vimos. Por la derecha lanzaba un cambio de velocidad, por la izquierda una bola rápida. Por la derecha nunca se agacha hasta las rodillas. Entonces, ¿había algo ahí? Solo ellos lo saben, pero todo dentro de las reglas del juego».
El equipo de Twins.TV del lunes estaba formado por Corey Provus, Justin Morneau, Trevor Plouffe y Audra Martin. La transcripción disponible no permite identificar con certeza a quién pertenecía la voz que hizo el comentario, así que en este artículo no se atribuye a ningún comentarista en concreto.
Esa última frase es importante. La MLB distingue entre la observación en el campo y el uso prohibido de dispositivos electrónicos o de vídeo para descifrar las señales. Las restricciones sobre el robo de señales mediante dispositivos electrónicos se aclararon y reforzaron en 2017 y 2018. Nada de lo que se mostró el lunes demostró que los Yankees hubieran cruzado esa línea.
El juez hace que cuente cada lanzamiento
La sospecha llamó la atención por lo que pasó después.
Judge había parecido un poco fuera de forma durante gran parte de su primera semana tras el regreso. Había hecho un roletazo que se convirtió en doble play y se había ponchado dos veces antes de que Minter lanzara un cutter por dentro que Judge mandó fuera. Ese jonrón fue el decimoctavo de Judge en la temporada y convirtió una ventaja de dos carreras en un colchón de cinco.
La reacción de Rice dejó claro lo rápido que ese turno al bate cambió el rumbo de la noche.
«¡Madre mía, menuda jugada!», dijo Rice. «Menudo golpe. Uno se podría acostumbrar a ver algo así, sobre todo en esta época del año».
El repunte de Rice en septiembre le da un nuevo matiz
Las estadísticas actualizadas de la temporada hasta el 14 de septiembre muestran que Rice tiene un promedio de bateo de .263, con 38 jonrones, 92 carreras impulsadas, 96 carreras anotadas y un OPS de .888 en 143 partidos.
Un análisis de PinstripesNation de esos resultados partido a partido muestra una racha reciente aún más impresionante. En nueve partidos desde el 4 de septiembre, Rice ha conectado 13 de 31, un promedio de .419, con tres jonrones, cinco carreras impulsadas y siete bases por bolas.
Esa aportación fue clave durante la larga ausencia de Judge. El sencillo de dos carreras de Rice el lunes dio a los Yankees su primera ventaja después de que Minnesota se pusiera 2-1 por delante en la sexta entrada.
No hay pruebas de que los Yankees hayan urdido un plan ilegal
La repetición de la retransmisión creó un momento polémico, pero las pruebas disponibles distan mucho de demostrar que se haya producido un robo ilegal de señales.
No ha habido ningún indicio público de que la MLB esté investigando a Rice, a Judge o a los Yankees por esa jugada. Tampoco hay pruebas de que se utilizara tecnología para descifrar los lanzamientos de Minter.
Aún no se ha aclarado públicamente si los movimientos de Rice fueron señales intencionadas o simplemente el comportamiento habitual de un corredor de bases.
Los Yankees ganaron porque su octava entrada desbordó al bullpen de Minnesota. Caballero empató el partido, Rice conectó el hit que les dio la ventaja y Judge aprovechó un cutter para sumar tres carreras más. Schreiber cerró luego la victoria por 8-3 con una doble jugada que puso fin al partido.
Para los Yankees, el resultado general está asegurado. Vuelven a octubre. No hay nada que se haya hecho público que demuestre que Rice o los Yankees hayan infringido las normas de la MLB.

title: Carlos Rodón Making Case for Bigger Postseason Role
author: Joseph Randazzo; Unknown
body:
On paper, the New York Yankees rotation is set. Cam Schlittler earned his role as the Game 1 starter and AL Cy Young frontrunner, and right behind him is Gerrit Cole, the longtime ace with a wealth of postseason experience. Where things get a little tricky is who comes out for that pivotal swing game, which is Game 3: Carlos Rodón or Max Fried.
If the Yankees were in a healthier position, that question would be easy to answer. It's Max Fried. The issue is that both starters seem to be going in different directions.
In eight starts, Fried looks like he could be regressing. In his most recent start, he pitched 3.1 innings, struggling to get through at-bats against a bad Rockies team. It does feel like he should be at his 100-pitch count already, but his laboring and a decrease in velocity in that start were his biggest red flags. He did strike out seven, and allow one earned run, but his stuff just looked off.
Fried saw a drop in velocity across the board on his cutter, sinker, curveball, sweeper, changeup, and fastball. He saw 2 MPH dips on the sweeper and curve, as well as a 1.2 MPH drop on his fastball.
Rodón is trending upward
Rodón, on the other hand, pitched his best game against the Mets on an emotional night in New York. He threw 6.1 innings with one earned run and eight strikeouts against a Mets team that has rebounded after the deadline. Against Juan Soto and a solid youthful core in A.J. Ewing, Carson Benge, and Francisco Alvarez, he struck out eight, walked just one batter, allowed one earned run, and gave up just three hits. The red flag for his start was six hard-hit balls.
Rodón's velocity was stable, too. He saw a small uptick in fastball velocity, up 0.3 MPH.
Basing the entire trajectory of a postseason rotation on two starts against sub-.500 teams isn't something teams should do, but what happened is worth monitoring in the future. That is especially true if Fried's velocity continues to dip, or stays around where it was against Colorado, without increasing over the next few weeks.
At that point, it would be fair to wonder if Fried could be a liability in October, with Rodón being the better option to be that third starter. The Yankees would probably prefer Fried in that role, but at that point, they should also consider playing the hot hand. If Rodón continues to pitch well and Fried struggles, their performances will answer the question of who should be the third starter in October.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

title: Un Giro Inesperado Empaña La Primera Fiesta Del Champán De George Lombard Con Los Yankees
author: Esteban Quiñones
body:
MINNEAPOLIS — El champán aún goteaba de las lonas de plástico cuando George Lombard Jr. saboreó por primera vez aquello a lo que había aspirado toda su vida. El lunes por la noche, en el vestuario de visitantes del Target Field, empapado de champán, este novato de 21 años celebró su primera clasificación para la postemporada en su carrera en las Grandes Ligas.
Se había ganado su puesto en el equipo. Lombard ayudó a dar el empujón definitivo que sentenció el partido, y durante unas horas se mostró tal y como los Yankees se lo imaginaban en octubre cuando ascendieron a su mejor promesa en agosto.
Los Yankees vencieron a los Twins por 8-3 y así hicieron oficial la celebración. La derrota anterior de Toronto ante Detroit ya les había asegurado matemáticamente la clasificación, pero la remontada de Nueva York garantizó que la clasificación llegara con una victoria, en lugar de con un simple encogimiento de hombros mientras miraban el marcador.
Para Lombard, fue el tipo de noche que justifica un ascenso meteórico. Apenas lleva un mes en las grandes ligas y ya tiene una celebración por el título en su haber. La euforia, sin embargo, no duró toda la noche.
Lombard enciende la mecha en la octava
Los Yankees iban perdiendo 2-1 al comenzar la octava y apenas habían hecho nada contra el pitcheo de Minnesota durante siete entradas. Lombard cambió el rumbo con un solo swing, abriendo la entrada con un doble que colocó a la carrera del empate en posición de anotar.
Por fin, la alineación se despertó detrás de él. José Caballero conectó un sencillo que llevó a Lombard a home y empató el partido; después, Anthony Volpe y Caballero lograron un doble robo. Ben Rice conectó un sencillo con el bate roto que impulsó dos carreras, y Cody Bellinger siguió con otro sencillo.
Aaron Judge dio el golpe de gracia. El capitán conectó un jonrón de tres carreras de 415 pies, su aportación a una entrada de seis carreras que convirtió un 2-1 en contra en una ventaja de 7-2. Austin Wells añadió un jonrón solitario en la novena, y los Yankees mejoraron su balance a 87-63.
Lombard estaba al frente de todo eso. Esa es exactamente la situación que se imaginaban los Yankees cuando le dieron el puesto de campocorto a una promesa que apenas había jugado en las ligas menores superiores. Su bate, que antes era una incógnita, no deja de dar respuestas.
«Ha sido genial», dijo tras la victoria. «Obviamente, fue un momento clave del partido y hice todo lo que pude para llegar a base en esa jugada».
El error que empañó la celebración
Entonces llegó el giro inesperado que impidió que la noche fuera un triunfo rotundo. Más adelante en el partido, Lombard cometió otro error, una nueva entrada en un historial defensivo que se ha alargado demasiado para un jugador cuyo guante se suponía que era su punto fuerte.
El momento fue un golpe duro. Justo la noche en que los Yankees se aseguraron el título, su shortstop novato les volvió a recordar el único punto débil que podría ser clave cuando cambie el año. Ese contraste —un gran impacto ofensivo seguido de un fallo defensivo— se ha convertido en la tónica dominante de su joven carrera.
No se suponía que fuera así. Cuando los Yankees ascendieron a Lombard, los ojeadores consideraban que su defensa era la parte más sólida de su juego. En cambio, los errores se han ido acumulando de una forma que casi nadie había previsto.
El momento más bajo llegó en agosto. Lombard cometió un error en seis partidos seguidos, convirtiéndose en el primer campocorto de los Yankees en hacerlo desde Roger Peckinpaugh en 1915. Acumuló siete errores en sus primeros 20 partidos de las Grandes Ligas, una cifra sorprendente para un jugador considerado un activo defensivo.
Un novato que asume la responsabilidad
Lombard no ha eludido el tema. Tras su sexto partido consecutivo con un error en agosto, abordó directamente su mala racha en lugar de restarle importancia.
Cuando le preguntaron por los errores de esa racha, Lombard se mostró sincero sobre el trabajo que le queda por delante.
«Es algo que estoy intentando averiguar», dijo Lombard.
Su entrenador le ha seguido apoyando. Aaron Boone ha calificado en varias ocasiones las dificultades de agosto como un bache pasajero y no como algo característico, y ha destacado el alcance, la potencia de lanzamiento y la capacidad atlética de Lombard como prueba de que su defensa mejorará. El novato también ha dejado entrever ese potencial con unas paradas en picado que demostraron por qué los Yankees confiaron en él de inmediato como shortstop.
El talento no está en duda. Lo que sí se cuestiona es la regularidad. Por ahora, los Yankees están dispuestos a aguantar los tropiezos iniciales porque el potencial es enorme y, al mismo tiempo que cometen errores, siguen rindiendo bien al bate.
Por qué octubre sube la apuesta
El margen de error se reduce en la postemporada, y eso es lo que convierte el desarrollo de Lombard en una de las historias más interesantes de los Yankees. Un error en agosto se diluye en una temporada de 162 partidos. Un error en un partido de playoffs puede decidir una serie.
Los Yankees apuestan por que la recompensa compense el riesgo. El bate de Lombard ha empezado a dar momentos que justifican la paciencia. Unos días antes del partido decisivo del lunes, conectó el primer grand slam de su carrera en las Grandes Ligas contra Colorado.
Ese batazo tenía su propia historia. Con 21 años y 99 días, Lombard se convirtió en el tercer jugador más joven de los Yankees en batear un grand slam, solo superado por dos jonrones de Mickey Mantle, que los bateó siendo aún más joven. Para una franquicia que se mide por sus leyendas, es un honor muy exclusivo para un novato.
«Obviamente, es intenso y cada lanzamiento cuenta, y todo importa, pero estamos preparados para ello», añadió Lombard. «La preparación va a ser la misma, la misma rutina. Solo tenemos que salir ahí fuera y hacer lo nuestro».
Ahora ha ayudado a los Yankees a llegar a otro octubre, y la recompensa por ello es una prueba aún mayor. El lunes se pudieron ver sus dos caras en tan solo unas entradas: el bate que ayudó a que Nueva York celebrara con champán y el guante que nos recordó una vez más el trabajo que aún queda por delante. Puede que su prueba más dura de este octubre no haya hecho más que empezar.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

Los Yankees iban perdiendo 2-1 al comenzar la octava y apenas habían hecho nada contra el pitcheo de Minnesota durante siete entradas. Lombard cambió el rumbo con un solo swing, abriendo la entrada con un doble que colocó a la carrera del empate en posición de anotar.
Por fin, la alineación se despertó detrás de él. José Caballero conectó un sencillo que llevó a Lombard a home y empató el partido; después, Anthony Volpe y Caballero lograron un doble robo. Ben Rice conectó un sencillo con el bate roto que impulsó dos carreras, y Cody Bellinger siguió con otro sencillo.
Aaron Judge dio el golpe de gracia. El capitán conectó un jonrón de tres carreras de 415 pies, su aportación a una entrada de seis carreras que convirtió un 2-1 en contra en una ventaja de 7-2. Austin Wells añadió un jonrón solitario en la novena, y los Yankees mejoraron su balance a 87-63.
Lombard estaba al frente de todo eso. Esa es exactamente la situación que se imaginaban los Yankees cuando le dieron el puesto de campocorto a una promesa que apenas había jugado en las ligas menores superiores. Su bate, que antes era una incógnita, no deja de dar respuestas.
«Ha sido genial», dijo tras la victoria. «Obviamente, fue un momento clave del partido y hice todo lo que pude para llegar a base en esa jugada».
El error que empañó la celebración
Entonces llegó el giro inesperado que impidió que la noche fuera un triunfo rotundo. Más adelante en el partido, Lombard cometió otro error, una nueva entrada en un historial defensivo que se ha alargado demasiado para un jugador cuyo guante se suponía que era su punto fuerte.
El momento fue un golpe duro. Justo la noche en que los Yankees se aseguraron el título, su shortstop novato les volvió a recordar el único punto débil que podría ser clave cuando cambie el año. Ese contraste —un gran impacto ofensivo seguido de un fallo defensivo— se ha convertido en la tónica dominante de su joven carrera.
No se suponía que fuera así. Cuando los Yankees ascendieron a Lombard, los ojeadores consideraban que su defensa era la parte más sólida de su juego. En cambio, los errores se han ido acumulando de una forma que casi nadie había previsto.
El momento más bajo llegó en agosto. Lombard cometió un error en seis partidos seguidos, convirtiéndose en el primer campocorto de los Yankees en hacerlo desde Roger Peckinpaugh en 1915. Acumuló siete errores en sus primeros 20 partidos de las Grandes Ligas, una cifra sorprendente para un jugador considerado un activo defensivo.
Un novato que asume la responsabilidad
Lombard no ha eludido el tema. Tras su sexto partido consecutivo con un error en agosto, abordó directamente su mala racha en lugar de restarle importancia.
Cuando le preguntaron por los errores de esa racha, Lombard se mostró sincero sobre el trabajo que le queda por delante.
«Es algo que estoy intentando averiguar», dijo Lombard.
Su entrenador le ha seguido apoyando. Aaron Boone ha calificado en varias ocasiones las dificultades de agosto como un bache pasajero y no como algo característico, y ha destacado el alcance, la potencia de lanzamiento y la capacidad atlética de Lombard como prueba de que su defensa mejorará. El novato también ha dejado entrever ese potencial con unas paradas en picado que demostraron por qué los Yankees confiaron en él de inmediato como shortstop.
El talento no está en duda. Lo que sí se cuestiona es la regularidad. Por ahora, los Yankees están dispuestos a aguantar los tropiezos iniciales porque el potencial es enorme y, al mismo tiempo que cometen errores, siguen rindiendo bien al bate.
Por qué octubre sube la apuesta
El margen de error se reduce en la postemporada, y eso es lo que convierte el desarrollo de Lombard en una de las historias más interesantes de los Yankees. Un error en agosto se diluye en una temporada de 162 partidos. Un error en un partido de playoffs puede decidir una serie.
Los Yankees apuestan por que la recompensa compense el riesgo. El bate de Lombard ha empezado a dar momentos que justifican la paciencia. Unos días antes del partido decisivo del lunes, conectó el primer grand slam de su carrera en las Grandes Ligas contra Colorado.
Ese batazo tenía su propia historia. Con 21 años y 99 días, Lombard se convirtió en el tercer jugador más joven de los Yankees en batear un grand slam, solo superado por dos jonrones de Mickey Mantle, que los bateó siendo aún más joven. Para una franquicia que se mide por sus leyendas, es un honor muy exclusivo para un novato.
«Obviamente, es intenso y cada lanzamiento cuenta, y todo importa, pero estamos preparados para ello», añadió Lombard. «La preparación va a ser la misma, la misma rutina. Solo tenemos que salir ahí fuera y hacer lo nuestro».
Ahora ha ayudado a los Yankees a llegar a otro octubre, y la recompensa por ello es una prueba aún mayor. El lunes se pudieron ver sus dos caras en tan solo unas entradas: el bate que ayudó a que Nueva York celebrara con champán y el guante que nos recordó una vez más el trabajo que aún queda por delante. Puede que su prueba más dura de este octubre no haya hecho más que empezar.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

title: Why the Yankees feel each step of their postseason journey is worth celebrating
author: Gary Phillips
body:
MINNESOTA — As the second-place Yankees celebrated their ninth playoff berth in 10 years on Monday night, Michael Fulmer stood off to the side.
Far enough from the blast radius of champagne spritzes and exploding beers, the reliever, signed in late August, watched his new teammates let loose. With a Budweiser in his hand and protective goggles resting on his forehead, Fulmer soaked in not only the booze, but the first big league postseason party of his nine-year career.
That he had contemplated retirement after undergoing his second Tommy John surgery in 2023 only made the moment sweeter.
“It’s been a long road, especially the last few years,” said Fulmer, the oft-injured 2016 American League Rookie of the Year. “A lot of surgeries, but I tried to just keep grinding away and wasn’t ready to call it quits yet.”
There’s no guarantee that Fulmer, 33, will be on the Yankees’ postseason roster in a couple of weeks. But his presence in Monday’s festivities, held after an 8-3 win over the Twins at Target Field, illustrated why Aaron Judge was so insistent when asked if the championship-or-bust Bombers would celebrate a simple playoff berth.
“There’s a lot of guys in this room that are going to wear this pinstripe jersey one time, and they might not have [another] opportunity to ever make it to a postseason,” the captain said Sunday. “So you gotta celebrate that because, at the end of the day, you work your butt off in spring training and all season long to get an opportunity to go out there and win a World Series.”
To Judge’s point, eight players in Monday’s celebration have never played in the postseason. That group includes two rookies in George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones, but also the veteran Fulmer, trade acquisitions Heliot Ramos and Luis García Jr., and bullpen breakout Brent Headrick.
A few members of the coaching staff also got their first taste of a playoff bash.
“We want to celebrate, even the little successes,” said infield coach Dan Fiorito, who grew up a Yankees fan and played in their minor league system but didn’t become a big leaguer until this year. “There’s so much that goes into it, so much time and effort, sacrifices like being away from the family throughout the season. So to make the playoffs is something special.”
There are certainly fans and pundits who feel that anything short of a title shouldn’t be celebrated in sports, and some who think carousing over anything less is especially beneath the Yankees, who have won 27 World Series but zero since 2009.
Even the Knicks, New York’s most recent champions, barely acknowledged their run of dominance in June before winning the NBA Finals and throwing a rager that was 53 years in the making. Heck, their owner, James Dolan, was so desperate for a ring that he suggested his team give up sex during the playoffs, all for the sake of staying locked in.
But as Judge and others explained, celebrating every step on the unpredictable path to and through the postseason has become a no-brainer for the Yankees, who last went to the World Series in 2024.
“Not everyone gets to do it,” Jones noted when asked why he felt it was important to celebrate each playoff milestone before Monday’s game. While he hopes that many more parties are in his short- and long-term future, he was eager to experience his first.
“You gotta celebrate, man, c’mon,” the 25-year-old said. “It’s such a long season. Any chance to celebrate with your team right after a game, you gotta take it. So I’m all for it. I’m down.”
Aaron Boone, who only made the postseason once as a player before becoming an October regular as the Yankees’ manager, shared a similar sentiment.
“Look, it’s such a grind, this season,” the skipper said. “It’s such a game of failure. You celebrate opportunities to play for all the marbles. That’s how I look at it.”
Some will scoff at the Yankees’ decision to revel in a mere playoff berth, but it is not lost on them that there is more work to do.
Once they finish their road trip to Minnesota and Arizona, they will host four games against the division-leading Rays at Yankee Stadium from Sept. 22-24. Tampa Bay has a 3.5-game lead on the Yankees with 12 games left in the regular season. The Rays lead the season series, 6-3.
The pinstripers also need to protect their five-game lead over the Red Sox for the top Wild Card spot. The Yankees, having already won the season series against Boston, hold a tiebreaker over their fiercest foes.
And once the postseason begins, there is only one acceptable outcome in the Bronx: a victory in the Fall Classic. That’s when the party moves beyond the clubhouse, parading down the Canyon of Heroes and throughout the heart and soul of New York City.
“We’re here for a World Series. We’re here to win,” Judge said. “[Celebrating is] about getting into the postseason and giving ourselves a chance. If you don’t get in, you can’t win a World Series, right?”
It’s been a while since the Yankees have pulled that off, an eternity by their stated standards. They know this, and they hope to put an end to their drought in the coming weeks.
In the meantime, however, they don’t see any harm in celebrating Step 1 of that process, especially since some may not get to do it again.
“You gotta understand, this is a huge accomplishment,” Fulmer said. “No matter who you are, no matter how long you’ve been around, this is a very big accomplishment that should be celebrated. But every hug I got today from everybody, the one phrase that’s been said is, ‘Job’s not finished.’
“So we know what’s at stake still. We want to keep climbing that ladder. Obviously, the ultimate goal is to bring a World Series back to the Yankees organization. We’re going to continue to strive for that.”

title: Will Warren strikes out six in no-decision Monday
author: Nick Shlain; Will Warren
body:
Will Warren allowed two runs (none earned) in 5 2/3 innings and got a no-decision in the Yankees’ 8-3 victory over the Twins on Monday.
            
                Warren gave up five hits, walked two and struck out six. He’s allowed two earned runs and recorded 21 strikeouts in 18 2/3 innings (0.96 ERA) over his last three starts. Warren has a 3.89 ERA this year. He’s lined up to face the Diamondbacks on the road on Sunday.

title: Yankees' Austin Wells: Homers in second straight game
author: RotoWire Staff
body:
Wells went 1-for-4 with a solo home run against Minnesota in an 8-3 win Monday.
Wells struck out twice over his first three plate appearances but ended on a high note with a solo shot to right field in the ninth inning. The long ball was his second in as many days following an 11-game span without any extra-base hits. Despite the mini power surge, the backstop has also struck out four times across those two games and is batting a meager .074 (2-for-27) across his past nine contests. It's been a tough campaign for Wells, as he's notched an ugly .180/.278/.315 slash line through 115 games.

title: Will Yankees' postseason first-timers prove to be ready for the moment?
author: Patrick Donnelly
body:
It’s common to think of the Yankees as a playoff-tested team. After all, this is the eighth time in nine years that they’ve made the postseason under manager Aaron Boone. And a quick look at some of their regulars shows a lineup that varies between a little bit and a wealth of October experience.
Player No. of Career Playoff Games
Cody Bellinger                     76
Aaron Judge                        65
Paul Goldschmidt                29
Trent Grisham                      26
Jazz Chisholm, Jr.                 24
Austin Wells                          21
Anthony Volpe                     21
Amed Rosario                      11
Ryan McMahon                   10
Ben Rice                               6
José Caballero                     3
But a few names are missing from that list: Shortstop George Lombard Jr., outfielder Spencer Jones, first baseman Luis García Jr. and outfielder Heliot Ramos. Those four have never played in the postseason, either with the Yankees or -- as is the case with García and Ramos -- with their previous teams.
Now, it’s possible that some of the injured veteran players -- Grisham and Chisholm, specifically -- could return to the lineup and send some of those new faces to the bench or off the playoff roster entirely. But it’s safe to say the Yankees are going to be counting on at least a few playoff newbies next month in their quest to win their first World Series since 2009.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone said his youngsters and playoff newcomers have another advantage over players who are coming of age in other markets.
“You play for the Yankees, you play in New York,” he said, “it has a way of getting you ready for the postseason.”
This has been something of a transitional year in the Major Leagues. Check out the first round of the 2023 Draft if you want proof. No fewer than 19 of the 37 first-round and sandwich picks have debuted, and many of them are already impact players with their teams.
“Players are getting to the big leagues at a very quick pace now and at a young age,” said Tigers manager A.J. Hinch, who has welcomed No. 3 pick Max Clark and AL Rookie of the Year favorite Kevin McGonigle to Detroit this year. “I don't think they're as wowed by the big steps that they're taking.”
For the Yankees, that class includes Lombard, who has acclimated nicely since being called up in early August. And Jones was recently lauded by none other than Aaron Judge, who said the rookie outfielder has “really evolved every single time he got called up, gotten a little bit better and a little bit better.”
Of course, there will be hiccups along the way. On Wednesday, Jones went 0-for-6 with five strikeouts and committed an error when he dropped a fly ball in center field. And Lombard couldn’t come up with a Victor Caratini grounder in the 13th that was ruled a single as the Twins walked off the Yankees.
But anyone who follows baseball knows bad days and bad plays are all part of the growth cycle of a Major League player. The key is to learn from them so you can limit them going forward. And all of it -- the good, the bad and the occasionally ugly -- helps prepare a young player for his first time playing in the crucible of October baseball.
The world is about to find out just how ready the young Yankees are. But Jones offered a bit of reassurance on Monday as he soaked up the post-clinch locker room celebration at Target Field.
“I think for us, we play better when the crowd gets louder,” he said. “I’m really excited for what’s to come.”

title: Yankees' Jose Caballero: Homers, swipes bag Monday
author: RotoWire Staff
body:
Caballero went 2-for-4 with a home run, two total runs, two total RBI and a stolen base Monday in an 8-3 victory versus the Twins.
Caballero got the scoring started in the contest with a solo shot to left field in the third inning. He added an RBI single in the eighth and then stole second before subsequently coming around to score on a Ben Rice single. Monday marked the fourth time this season Caballero has stolen a base and homered in the same game. It was a much-needed productive performance by the utility man, as he entered the contest in a 1-for-19 tailspin at the plate. That's one of the factors that has cost Caballero playing time, as he's started just three times across New York's past eight games.

title: Yankees' John Schreiber: Credited with save Monday
author: RotoWire Staff
body:
Schreiber earned a save against the Twins on Monday, issuing one walk over 1.1 hitless and scoreless innings. He did not record a strikeout.
Schreiber entered with two outs in the eighth inning after Minnesota put two runners on base while trailing by four runs. He retired the only batter he faced in that frame and returned for the ninth, working around a one-out walk and an error to close out the contest. Schreiber thus notched his first save since joining the Yankees off waivers Aug. 31. The right-hander had a save with the Royals earlier in the campaign, but he's no threat to David Bednar's closing role. Still, he's been excellent so far in his tenure with New York, pitching seven scoreless innings over six outings, giving up just one hit.

title: Yankees' Will Warren: Solid again Monday
author: RotoWire Staff
body:
Warren allowed two runs (both unearned) on five hits and two walks while striking out six batters over 5.2 innings in a no-decision against Minnesota on Monday.
Warren cruised through five scoreless frames before giving up two runs in the sixth. The right-hander was hurt in that inning by a one-out error and a two-out infield single before yielding a two-run triple. Warren was pulled after that hit and was thus unable to notch a second straight quality start, but this was nonetheless another positive outing for him. Across his past four appearances, he's given up just two earned runs over 21 innings while posting a 21:6 K:BB. Warren has lowered his season ERA to 3.89 during that span, and he's projected to next take the mound in Arizona.

title: Yankees news: Austin Wells offers bold All-Star rotation take
author: Colin Loughran; ClutchPoints
body:
Yankees news: Austin Wells offers bold All-Star rotation take appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees secured their place in the 2026 postseason after the Toronto Blue Jays lost 8-3 to the Detroit Tigers. Following an 8-3 road win against the Minnesota Twins on Monday night, catcher Austin Wells complimented the club's starting rotation who has been a major key to their success.
"They're the best in baseball," Wells remarked.
New York ranks first in terms of starter ERA and fourth in WHIP. Despite dealing with injuries to key arms like Max Fried, Gerrit Cole, and Carlos Rodon at different points in the campaign, individuals like Will Warren and Cam Schlittler have been consistent contributors.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Schlittler has been particularly lethal in his first full big-league season. Across 31 starts, the 25-year-old has gone 14-6 with a sizzling 1.95 ERA. He leads the sport in ERA and is third in terms of WHIP.
Wells has worked closely with the staff as the Yankees' starting catcher and has been an effective defensive force. According to Baseball Savant, he ranks in the 91st percentile in terms of Blocks Above Average and the 93rd percentile in Framing.
The former first-round pick has struggled offensively overall, but has shown pop that could be beneficial. He homered in both the Yankees' Sunday win over the New York Mets and their Monday victory in Minnesota.
The Yankees' rotation is nearly at full strength, and while only time will tell whether or not the team will be able to bring home the franchise's 28th World Series title, it is apparent that Wells is confident that the group has what it takes to make a serious push.

title: New York Yankees Announce Surprise Cody Bellinger Decision After Bad Game
author: Michael DeRosa
body:
The New York Yankees defeated the New York Mets by a 2-0 final score in their most recent game on Sunday.
Now, the Yankees will be taking on the Detroit Tigers for the first game of their series on Monday.
As New York prepares for their series opener against the Tigers, they have made a surprising decision with Cody Bellinger.
Cody Bellinger Still Batting Second After Tough Game
Bellinger had a tough day at the plate for the Yankees in their series finale against the Mets. This star slugger went 0-for-4 in the matchup, which included him grounding into a double play.
Yet, the Yankees are still having Bellinger bat second in their Monday matchup against the Tigers despite his hard day at the plate last game.
It seemed possible that the Yankees could have switched Bellinger to a different spot in their batting order after he struggled at the plate last game. Yet, they will instead keep him in their second spot.
Here is the Yankees' full batting order for Monday's game against the Tigers:
B. Rice DH
C. Bellinger LF
A. Judge RF
L. García Jr. 1B
S. Jones CF
G. Lombard Jr. SS
R. McMahon 3B
A. Wells C
J. Caballero 2B
Bellinger Looking to Have Bounce-Back Game
With Bellinger once again batting second for the Yankees, he will be looking to heat back up against the Tigers.
Before his bad day at the plate, Bellinger had been on a seven-game hitting streak. With this, he certainly has the potential to turn things back around, and it will be interesting to see if he can do just that.
Bellinger has posted 15 home runs, 69 RBI, and a .268 batting average in 122 games so far this season with the Yankees.

title: José Caballero pierde minutos con los Yankees: Volpe y Lombard Jr. le quitan protagonismo en la recta final
author: Eric Conte
body:
José “Chema” Caballero ha ido perdiendo protagonismo con los Yankees en los últimos partidos, desplazado por el ascenso de Anthony Volpe y la presencia de George Lombard Jr. en el cuadro neoyorquino. El panameño, que había ganado terreno tras la lesión de Jazz Chisholm Jr., ahora vuelve a la banca en dos partidos consecutivos mientras el equipo busca definir su alineación para la postemporada.
Números de la temporada 2026
En lo que va de esta temporada, “Chema” tiene un promedio de .232 con 13 cuadrangulares, 47 impulsadas, 31 bases robadas, .657 de OPS, .290 de OBP y .367 de SLG. Además suma 46 carreras, 89 hits, 13 dobles, 26 bases por bolas y 103 ponches en 59 juegos disputados con Nueva York.
El infielder de 30 años llegó a los Yankees como agente libre después de una temporada sólida con los Seattle Mariners, donde estableció nuevos récords personales en jonrones y carreras impulsadas. Sin embargo, su rendimiento en el Bronx ha sido irregular, con rachas ofensivas que lo han mantenido en la rotación del equipo pero sin consolidarse como titular indiscutible.
Su desempeño ante los Mets
“Chema” en esta serie del Subway ante los Mets entró como corredor emergente donde anotó una carrera en el primer juego. En el segundo no vio acción y en el tercer encuentro se fue en blanco en dos turnos y recibió una base por bolas. La gran novedad para la afición latinoamericana fue su regreso al lineup abridor en el juego dominical, figurando en el orden al bate ocupando la novena casilla y cubriendo el campo corto.
En el primer juego de la serie, Caballero pegó un incogible en la parte alta del décimo episodio y luego cruzó el home plate mediante un hit de Austin Wells en la victoria de los Yankees por 6-3 sobre los Angelinos de Los Ángeles. Con esa actuación, su promedio de bateo subió a .236.
La batalla por la segunda base
La situación se complicó para Caballero cuando los Yankees llamaron a Anthony Volpe desde Triple-A el 9 de septiembre, después de que el joven infielder dominara en las menores con promedio de .333, ocho jonrones y 14 impulsadas en sus últimos 13 juegos. Volpe produjo un regreso impresionante con tres hits, incluyendo un grand slam durante una sexta entrada de seis carreras, en la victoria de 10-3 sobre los Rockies.
Volpe había sido enviado a Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre el 4 de agosto después de batear .240 con un jonrón y 19 impulsadas en 56 juegos como campocorto antes de ser reemplazado por Lombard. Desde su opción a las menores, Volpe conectó .295 con 10 jonrones y 21 impulsadas en 27 juegos, ganándose otra oportunidad en las mayores.
La lesión de Chisholm abre y cierra puertas
Todo cambió cuando Jazz Chisholm Jr. fue colocado en la lista de lesionados por esguince en el pulgar el 10 de septiembre. El panameño José Caballero sustituyó al jugador en la intermedia para el noveno inning, situación que lo apuntaba para recibir mayor cantidad de turnos y titularidad en la posición durante la ausencia de su compañero.
Sin embargo, el manager Aaron Boone dejó abierta la posibilidad de una batalla por la posición. “Caballero ha estado entrando y saliendo del lineup últimamente”, reconoció el estratega. En agosto, el segunda base jugó en cinco series seguidas sin perderse un solo juego del 18 de agosto al 2 de septiembre. Pero en el último mes, ya había sido sacado de la alineación en un par de partidos.
La competencia se intensifica
El último imparable de Chema fue el pasado miércoles 2 de septiembre contra los Angels en la victoria 6-3 de los Yankees, donde se fue de 4-1 con una anotada y jugando en el campo corto. Desde entonces, ha tenido dificultades para mantener la consistencia ofensiva que el equipo necesita en la recta final de la temporada regular.
Con Volpe de regreso y Lombard Jr. consolidado en el campocorto, los Yankees tienen opciones para el cuadro interior de cara a los playoffs. La decisión final dependerá del rendimiento en los últimos juegos de septiembre y de cómo se recupere Chisholm de su lesión en el pulgar.

title: Austin Wells just complicated the Yankees' catcher decision again
author: Alexander Wilson
body:
Austin Wells homered in Sunday’s 2-0 win over the Mets, and it was a big one. In a game where the Yankees only put three hits on the board, his solo shot supplied half the offense.
The Wells conversation never stays simple for long. He has 11 homers and can still run into a baseball that changes a game. He also entered the day hitting .179 with a .586 OPS over 114 games. Both things are true, and neither can be ignored because of one clean swing.
The Yankees need a catcher they trust when October gets tight. Wells has shown enough pop to keep the door open. The bigger question is whether the rest of his at-bats can get to a place where the club does not have to plan around the empty ones.
Nobody should be rooting against him. A good Wells changes the lineup in a real way, especially because he is a left-handed catcher with power. The power has never been the concern.
Austin Wells gave the Yankees a needed jolt
Sunday was a good reminder of why he is still here. He did not need a three-hit game to matter. He got one pitch he could drive and gave Cam Schlittler a lead to protect.
That kind of production plays in October. The Yankees have seen too many playoff innings die because nobody could put a mistake in the seats. Wells can do it.
Yankees cannot call the catcher issue fixed
One homer cannot erase a .179 average, just as a cold week would not erase his power. The Yankees have to decide whether the next few weeks show a hitter who is actually finding a groove or one who remains wildly difficult to predict.
That decision has real consequences. Catcher is not a spot where a contender can shrug and hope the good version shows up in a playoff series. Wells earned himself another loud moment Sunday. Now he needs to stack a few normal, useful nights behind it.

title: Yankees Have a Ryan McMahon Problem They Might Not Address
author: Matthew Schmidt
body:
Will the New York Yankees replace Ryan McMahon at third base this offseason?
The results have not been what Yankees fans were expecting.
Since arriving in the Bronx in July 2025, McMahon is slashing just .211/.290/.346 with 14 home runs and 52 RBI over 522 plate appearances.
This season, he owns a .212/.280/.353 slash line with 10 homers and 34 RBI across 337 trips to the dish, and while McMahon does seem to have an odd knack for getting big hits, his offensive production has been generally unacceptable at the hot corner.
New York was willing to look past that because of his defense, as McMahon posted 10 defensive runs saved and seven outs above average at third base last year. He also regularly posted similar numbers during his time with the Colorado Rockies.
While McMahon has still been wholly solid in the field, a 2026 decline has been evident, as he has posted zero defensive runs saved and three outs above average this season.
Has he been bad at third? Absolutely not. But he has been good enough to justify his $16 million salary while posting a .633 OPS? No.
The problem for the Yankees is that McMahon is under contract for another $16 million next year, which significantly decreases the chances of New York going out and finding an upgrade at the position.
These aren't your dad's Yankees; this is the more financially shrewd, cost-conscious version that initially balked at making any major moves last year due to Marcus Stroman's $18 million salary ... which they eventually ate after releasing him in August 2025.
You can bet that Hal Steinbrenner has every intention of going into 2027 with McMahon as the club's starting third baseman unless Brian Cashman can somehow find a trade for the veteran in which he can offload that money.
McMahon is 31 years old. He'll turn 32 in December. It's entirely possible that the former All-Star is declining, so it's possible that his defensive downturn this season is not a mirage.
Can New York win with McMahon on the roster? Sure. But is it preferable to keep him in a starting role? No.
An alternative solution is fighting a right-handed third baseman who isn't Amed Rosario to man the starting job while keeping McMahon in a reserve role ... but then you are paying $16 million for a pedestrian bench player. That isn't exactly advisable. Especially not for a team that, in recent years, has been trying to cut costs.
And it becomes even less realistic if the MLB does, indeed, institute a salary cap for 2027.
Is it possible the Yankees can trade McMahon? I guess, but good luck finding a team willing to take on the final year of his contract. New York would likely have to absorb some of that $16 million salary, and I'm just not sure how amenable Steinbrenner would be to doing that.
You would think if it meant upgrading the team for just a little bit of extra case, the Yankees would do it. I mean, they're the Yankees, right? But those Evil Empire days appear to be long gone.
The most probable scenario is New York opening up 2027 with McMahon as its starting third baseman, and while it could be worse, it could also be a lot better.

title: Yankees ace Cam Schlittler is getting MVP attention -- just don't ask teammate Aaron Judge
author: Mike Axisa
body:
Yankees ace Cam Schlittler added to his American League Cy Young case Sunday afternoon at Yankee Stadium, throwing six shutout innings against the crosstown rival Mets (NYY 2, NYM 0). Schlittler struck out eight and allowed one hit. He is tied with Jacob Misiorowski with a 1.95 ERA, lowest among qualified pitchers, and also with 6.0 WAR, best among all pitchers.
"I think valuable is a good word. He might be the MVP, too," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said after Sunday's game (via MLB.com). "He's been awesome. Just an awesome season and hopefully there's a lot left in the tank."
The is between Schlittler and Dylan Cease, with Parker Messick and Drew Rasmussen trying to nudge their way in as the third finalist. The AL MVP race is more wide open. Yordan Alvarez has hit an un-MVP-like .238/.375/.393 over the last calendar month and his Triple Crown chances are fading, opening the door for Schlittler and others.

| FanGraphs WAR | Baseball Reference WAR |
